#5689. Why Builders May Be More Motivated To Sell Than Homeowners

Here’s something most homebuyers don’t think about. When the housing market slows down, homeowners and builders don’t always respond the same way.

Think about it. If you’re selling your house and aren’t getting the offers you want, you could make the choice to take it off the market and stay put, and wait for things to improve.

But builders? They may be more motivated to stay the course.

They’ve already invested money in building those houses. And every completed home that sits unsold means money tied up in a property, plus ongoing costs that can add up.

That’s why some builders may be more motivated to negotiate right now. And that could work in your favor.

You’ve probably seen the headlines. According to the latest report from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), pending home sales – homes that have gone under contract but haven’t closed yet – fell 7.3% in September and 11.3% compared to last year.

Why? Higher mortgage rates are making it harder for buyers to make the numbers work. Now, that report tracks existing homes, not new construction. But we’re seeing signs of the same slowdown on the builder side, too.

According to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), builder confidence dropped to 29 in October, its lowest level since June 2012. Traffic from prospective buyers also dropped to its lowest level in more than a decade, excluding the start of the pandemic.

As Robert Dietz, Chief Economist at NAHB, explains:

“Demand persists, but higher mortgage rates, elevated construction costs and weaker consumer confidence are keeping more buyers on the sidelines.”

A homeowner may be able to wait for the right offer. But a builder with several finished houses sitting unsold may have more reason to get those homes sold sooner rather than later.

And that means they may be more willing to work with you than you think.

If you’ve always assumed builders don’t negotiate, take a look at what they’re actually doing. According to the latest survey from NAHB, in October:

65% of builders are offering sales incentives.

43% are cutting prices, the highest share recorded between 2020 and 2026.

And 6% is what they’re typically taking off the price.

So, yes. Builders absolutely do negotiate. And with demand slowing, there’s good reason to explore just how flexible they may be right now.

That could mean asking for a lower price. But it could also mean asking for a mortgage-rate buydown, help with closing costs, or upgrades that would otherwise cost you extra.

And here’s a tip that could make a real difference.

Don’t just look at the newest communities or the prettiest model homes. Look for builders with completed houses that haven’t sold yet.

Those are sometimes called quick move-in homes or spec homes. And the longer one of those move-in ready homes sits unsold, the more reason a builder may have to consider an offer that helps get it off their books.

Don’t assume the advertised price or incentive package is the best they’ll do.

This is where having your own agent can really pay off. An agent who knows the local market can help you compare what builders are offering, identify communities with more available homes, and understand where there’s room to negotiate.

Of course, not every builder will offer the same incentives. And some may be more flexible on closing costs or mortgage rates than on the price itself.

The trick is knowing where to look, what to ask for, and how much room there may be to negotiate. And that’s where having your own agent is key.

#5688. Scientists discover a surprising clue to autism's origins hidden in the placenta

Scientists are still working to understand why autism develops. Genetics are known to play a major role, but researchers have also found that conditions during pregnancy can influence the likelihood of autism spectrum disorder.

A new study from Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory (CSHL) has uncovered a surprising connection between inflammation during pregnancy, changes in the placenta, and the development of autism-like traits in male mice. The findings suggest that certain developmental disruptions may begin much earlier than previously recognized, potentially offering new clues about autism's origins.

"To truly understand autism spectrum disorder, we have to look beyond the brain," CSHL Associate Professor Lucas Cheadle says. "Our work suggests that maternal immune activation and changes within the placenta are a gateway to autism for some unique individuals."

Scientists Identify an Early Window of Vulnerability

To investigate how inflammation affects fetal development, Cheadle and his colleagues triggered an immune response in pregnant mice at different stages of pregnancy. They used a substance that mimics the immune system's reaction to a viral infection without actually introducing a virus.

The researchers discovered that mouse fetuses were especially vulnerable when inflammation occurred 12.5 days into pregnancy. According to Irene Sanchez Martin, a postdoctoral researcher in Cheadle's laboratory, approximately one-third of the fetuses showed developmental abnormalities within just 24 hours.

Scientists have investigated the effects of maternal immune activation for decades, but these findings reveal signs of developmental disruption earlier than researchers had previously observed.

Even more striking was the difference between male and female fetuses. Across every experiment, autism-like traits appeared only in males, while females continued developing normally.

This unexpected distinction could provide insight into why autism is diagnosed substantially more often in boys than girls. What makes the finding especially intriguing is how early the difference appeared, before many of the biological changes normally associated with sex-specific development.

"It's really fascinating, because we're looking at an age which precedes hormonal surges. It precedes sexual differentiation in the brain and many other regions. So, it's surprising there would be a sex-based difference this early."

A Surprising Connection Between the Placenta and Autism

To determine why some developing mice were affected while others appeared protected, Cheadle and Sanchez Martin examined the placenta, the organ that connects a developing fetus to its mother and supports its growth throughout pregnancy.

Their attention centered on specialized cells called spongiotrophoblasts, which occupy a region of the mouse placenta where maternal and fetal cells interact.

In fetuses that developed normally, this part of the placenta remained healthy. However, male fetuses showing developmental abnormalities also had visible damage to these specialized cells.

Spongiotrophoblasts play an important role in helping the mother's immune system tolerate the developing fetus. This protection is essential because the fetus carries genetic material from both parents and is not genetically identical to the mother.

The researchers found that maternal immune activation could interfere with this protective function. When these placental cells become damaged, the mother's immune response may begin affecting the developing fetus in harmful ways.

Why Female Fetuses May Have a Hidden Advantage

The findings raise another intriguing question: Why were male fetuses vulnerable while females appeared unaffected?

One possibility is that male embryos produce distinctive proteins that can trigger an unfavorable maternal immune response following a viral infection. Another explanation is that female embryos possess some form of protection that helps them withstand inflammation during this sensitive developmental period.

Cheadle says, "A protective mechanism may exist within the female that could be harnessed to help the male. We're trying to understand how autism emerges in both sexes," he explains. "The evidence says that there are potentially different mechanisms."

These possibilities suggest that biological pathways involved in autism-like development may differ between males and females. Understanding those differences could help researchers identify why some individuals are more vulnerable to certain environmental influences during pregnancy.

Cheadle's team plans to investigate both male and female mice more closely to uncover the mechanisms responsible for these contrasting responses. Their work could eventually identify new targets for treatments and lead to strategies for intervening earlier in developmental processes associated with autism.

Although the findings come from experiments in mice and do not establish that the same mechanisms cause autism in humans, they highlight an unexpected possibility: Important clues to autism's earliest development may lie not only in the brain, but also in the placenta and its interactions with the maternal immune system.

#5687. Who’s Buying Homes with Cash Right Now?

Ryan Serhant, CEO of SERHANT, says there isn’t just 1 housing market right now. There are really 4: cash buyers, buyers who need a mortgage, homeowners with low mortgage rates, and builders.

Today, let’s zoom in on the 1st group – cash buyers.

According to the National Association of Realtors (NAR), 27% of homes sold in September were bought with all cash. That’s more than 1 in 4 buyers. And that’s a pretty big number, especially when so many people are struggling with affordability.

So where is all that cash coming from? When you hear a number like that, it’s easy to picture wealthy investors buying up houses left and right. But that’s not necessarily the case. Some of those cash buyers are actually homeowners who’ve built up enough equity to buy their next home outright.

Here’s what you should know about who’s paying cash and what that really means for the market.

Cash buyers tend to fall into a few groups, according to NAR:

Homeowners who sold a house and are using that money to buy their next one

So, it’s not all those big investors social media talks about. That 1st group may include people a lot more like you. Here’s how. According to Cotality, the average homeowner with a mortgage has about $310,000 in equity.

That’s a big deal right now. Many homeowners feel stuck because they don’t want to give up the low mortgage rate they have today. But once they learn they may have enough equity to move and pay cash for their next home, today’s rates don’t matter nearly as much. Because buying in all cash means…

No need to borrow at today’s mortgage rates

No loan approval process, so you may be able to close faster

And even if the equity won’t cover the whole purchase, putting more of it toward the next home means borrowing less. That can mean a smaller monthly payment, too.

But cash buyers like this are more common in some places than others. And how big of a segment of your local market this is, is going to depend on where you live.

For example, Realtor.com data shows cash buyers made up almost 47% of sales in Mississippi and 46% in Montana earlier this year (see map below).

According to Realtor.com, the states with the most cash buyers reflect “a mix of affordability, wealth and buyer demographics.” Think places with lower home prices, or lots of retirees and 2nd-home buyers.

So, depending on where you live, you may see a lot more (or a lot fewer) cash buyers than the national number suggests. An agent who knows your area can tell you who’s actually buying near you.

And if all of this has you thinking everyone’s paying cash, they’re not. If you’re planning to buy and need a mortgage, you’re actually in the majority.

Based on NAR’s numbers, nearly 3 out of 4 home purchases still involve financing. And for homes priced between $200,000 and $750,000, only about 1 in 5 sold for cash, according to Realtor.com (see graph below):

That means most people buying in that price range are financing their purchase, too. So, there’s no need to assume you’re at a disadvantage just because you’re using a loan.

So, what does all this mean for you? Maybe more than you think.

If you already own a house, you may have enough equity to make your next move more affordable than you realize. And if you’re buying with a mortgage, remember, you’re in good company. Most buyers are financing their purchases, too.

The takeaway? Don’t make assumptions about what’s possible based on how other people are buying homes. What really matters is your equity, your budget, and what’s happening in your local market.

#5686. Don't Let the Fear of a Buyer Backing Out Scare You Away from Selling

There’s nothing quite like the excitement of getting an offer on your house. You’re one step closer to moving on to what’s next. But what happens if that buyer backs out or ghosts you before closing?

If you’ve been seeing headlines about more home sales falling through lately, that possibility may be keeping you up at night. And it’s true. According to Redfin and Cotality, canceled contracts have been on the rise.

But here’s what those headlines don’t always tell you…

Most sales still go through. Only 10-15% hit this snag. And even so, there are things you can do to help keep your sale from becoming one of them.

The key is knowing what tends to scare buyers away and getting ahead of those issues before they have a chance to derail your move.

Today’s buyers are being more cautious. Mortgage rates are stretching budgets, and with more homes to choose from, buyers have more freedom to walk away if something doesn’t feel right. As Redfin explains:

“That gives house hunters more options and makes them more likely to walk away if an inspection uncovers problems, an appraisal comes in low or the seller doesn’t agree to concessions.”

That’s why an accepted offer isn’t always a guaranteed sale. But it doesn’t mean you should be afraid to put your house on the market, either.

It just means getting ahead of potential problems matters more than ever.

A Redfin survey asked real estate agents why some buyers are backing out. And their answers give you a short of cheatsheet into what could go sideways and how you can get ahead of those headaches (see graph below):

This is the big one. And the good news? It’s also one of the areas where you can be the most proactive.

One simple way to head this off is by getting a pre-listing inspection before your house goes on the market. That way, if something needs attention, you can decide whether to fix it upfront (before you sell), adjust your price, or disclose it and come in already prepared for what’s likely to pop up in negotiations. It’s a lot better to find the skeletons in the closet before a buyer does.

Even buyers who are pre-approved can run into financing issues before closing. And with mortgage rates putting extra pressure on affordability, some buyers are finding it harder to make the numbers work.

While you can’t control whether a buyer’s loan goes through, you can work with your agent to look closely at their financing before accepting an offer. And if affordability is the concern, your agent can help you explore whether incentives like closing cost credits or a mortgage-rate buydown could make a difference.

Sometimes, your buyer needs to sell their house before they can buy yours. And if their sale falls through, yours could be affected too.

That’s why it’s important to understand any home-sale contingencies before accepting an offer. Your agent can help you look at where the buyer is in their own selling process and what protections you may want in place.

The goal isn’t to eliminate every possible risk. It’s to avoid being caught off guard by the ones you can plan for.

Just remember when you read headlines about canceled deals, they don’t give you the full picture. Most home sales still make it to closing.

And if a sale does fall through, that doesn’t automatically mean your house won’t sell. Sometimes a buyer’s circumstances change. Sometimes an issue comes up that can be addressed before the next offer.

What matters is having an agent who knows how to spot potential problems early, help you navigate negotiations, and keep your sale moving forward.

Because while you can’t control every twist and turn, you can control how prepared you are.

There's no need to let the fear of a buyer backing out hold you back. While no sale comes with guarantees, a little preparation upfront can go a long way toward making the whole process smoother.If you're ready to make a move, talk to a local agent about whether a pre-listing inspection makes sense for you.

#5685. Credit Scoring Is Changing: 3 Things Homebuyers Should Know

Quick, what credit score do you need to buy a home? If a number pops into your head, there’s a pretty good chance it’s wrong. And the right answer is getting harder to pin down, because the way credit scores are determined and delivered is changing – for the better.

Here’s what you need to know in today’s changing credit climate.

Fannie Mae has been tracking consumer perceptions about mortgage requirements since 2015 and found that consumers consistently overestimated the minimum credit score lenders required to qualify for a mortgage. As recently as 2023, the average guess was 652.

In reality, the long-standing benchmark for loans backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac is lower, at 620, and today even that isn’t a hard rule for every mortgage they back.

Like the Fannie Mae research, a recent survey from Veterans United found consumers continue to overestimate what it takes to qualify for a home loan:

The takeaway? Guessing wrong can cost you.

A renter who assumes their score is too low and they can’t qualify for a mortgage may never take steps to find out for sure.

For decades, the mortgage industry relied on one set of scores – Classic FICO. Thanks to a push to promote competition, make credit scoring more inclusive, and help more Americans become homeowners, the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) has approved the use of new credit score models such as FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0.

A different model can mean a different number for the same person. VantageScore says its model can score about 33 million adults that the Classic FICO’s model can’t. So the score you saw on an app last month may not be the one your lender pulls.

Remember: the models may be new, but the basics haven’t changed.

Your credit score is important – no matter how it’s measured. Following the same basic rules will benefit your profile in the old and new score models:

Because while credit models may change, the general advice for you to improve your score doesn’t. Financial awareness and consistency mixed with a little willpower can go a long way.

Don't make credit or homebuying decisions from a chart, an app, or a friend's advice. #5684. The Home Insurance Move That Could Save You $440 a Year

When you’re planning a move, every monthly cost counts. That’s why it can be frustrating to see home insurance keep creeping up. According to Intercontinental Exchange, it now makes up 9.6% of the average monthly mortgage payment.

But the latest numbers show some progress on that front – as the increases start to slow down. Here’s what you need to know and what you can do about it.

A look at the past two years shows how much things have cooled down. In mid-2024, home insurance premiums rose 4.3% in a single quarter. By the second quarter of this year, that was down to 1.8%. That’s the smallest quarterly growth in almost 3 years – and that’s a good thing (see graph below):

As Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at Intercontinental Exchange, explains:

“Property insurance has been a fast-growing component of the monthly mortgage payment, but this quarter’s data shows the pace of increase is finally slowing.”

While your premium will likely still go up over time, it may not climb as quickly as it did a couple of years ago. And that’s, at the very least, a step in the right direction.

Here’s where you have some say in what you pay. Let’s take current homeowners as an example. Intercontinental Exchange found that when homeowners shopped around and switched insurance companies, their premiums went down 6.6% on average. Those who stayed with their current company saw an increase of 10.4% (see graph below):

Think about that. That’s a big difference and it goes to show that looking for a new provider can literally pay off.

That works out to about $440 a year in savings for the people who switched. And they didn’t have to give up coverage to get it. Their deductibles dipped 1.4%, and their coverage limits actually rose 7.3%.

While this example is current homeowners, the same general idea applies for first-time buyers too. Shop around and get multiple quotes before you pick your insurance provider. Then, once you’re settled in, review your policy each year when it comes up for renewal. You’re not locked into the first price you get.

The home itself plays a role as well. According to John Burns Research and Consulting (JBREC), newly built homes are 10% to 15% less expensive to insure than older ones nationally.

And while a brand-new home won’t necessarily be the right fit for every buyer, if you’re open to one, it could be one more way to keep your monthly insurance costs down.

Home insurance is certainly a bigger part of the monthly costs than it used to be, and that can feel like just one more thing to juggle when you’re buying a home or moving. But knowing you have ways to keep it in check can take some of the pressure off. Compare a few options before you buy, revisit your policy each year, and lean on trusted local professionals as you plan for your next move.

#5683. What Experts Forecast for Mortgage Rates and Home Prices in 2027

When it comes to housing, two of the biggest questions on everyone’s mind right now are:

And if you’re weighing whether to move in the next few months or wait until 2027, here’s what you should know.

When experts look ahead to 2027, they see a steady housing market. No wild swings. No big surprises. Just a calmer, more balanced market.

And steady makes planning a whole lot easier. Let’s break it down.

Lots of people are holding out for lower rates. But the latest forecasts from Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo show rates holding fairly flat through 2027 (see graph below):

Lenders see it the same way. In a recent survey from HousingWire, 70% of mortgage executives said they expect rates to be around 7.5% or higher six months from now (see graph below):

And if you’re wondering why, the answer is fairly simple. Chen Zhao, Head of Economics Research at Redfin, says:

“Until the underlying economic fundamentals—everything from oil prices to AI–that are keeping rates high change, mortgage rates are unlikely to fall significantly.”

So what does that mean for you? Instead of trying to guess where rates go next, focus on what you can control. Even if rates don’t budge, there are still ways to get the best rate possible. When you talk with your lender, ask about:

Your credit score. Even a small bump in your score could help lower your rate.

Different loan types. Some programs offer lower rates or smaller down payments than you might expect.

Buying down your rate. Paying a little more upfront (called “points”) can lower your rate and your monthly payment.

That way, you’ll know exactly where you stand and what a comfortable monthly payment looks like for you.

But what about prices? Here’s where steady really works in your favor.

Experts don’t see a home price drop coming. On average, forecasts from Fannie Mae, MBA, and Wells Fargo show prices rising about 1% to 1.5% a year through 2027 (see graph below):

In plain terms, in most places prices are still going up, just not as fast. For sellers, that means your home should hold onto its value. For buyers, slower growth gives you a little more breathing room. Just don’t count on prices getting cheaper while you wait.

But keep in mind, these are national forecasts. Prices can look very different from one area to the next, so what matters most is what’s happening where you live.

When the market is steady, you don’t have to try to time it perfectly. There’s no big swing to wait out.

That puts the focus back on you. Maybe you need more space for a growing family. Maybe you’re ready for less upkeep. A steady market makes it easier to plan for either one.

If you’re asking yourself should you move now or wait? You should know experts see a steady market through 2027, with rates holding near today’s levels and prices rising slowly. So, rather than waiting for a big shift that may not come, connect with a local real estate agent and run the numbers on what a move looks like at today’s rates and prices, so you can decide based on your goals instead of the headlines.

#5682. What the Silver Tsunami Means if You’re Planning To Sell

If you’re following the housing market, you may have heard the term “silver tsunami” lately. It’s the idea that millions of homes owned by older Americans could come onto the market as more homeowners reach retirement age and make their next move.

And when you hear a phrase like that, it’s easy to picture a flood of houses hitting the market all at once. But that picture doesn’t match the data.

And if you’re planning to sell, it’s not a reason to put your plans on hold. Let’s look at what the research actually says.

According to Realtor.com, about 13.9 million homes owned by older Americans are expected to change hands by 2036. Sure, that’s a big number. But these homes aren’t all expected to come onto the market at once.

The projections show this happening gradually over the next decade, with roughly 1.3 to 1.5 million homes changing hands each year (see graph below):

Rather than a sudden wave of houses flooding the market, this is a gradual shift as longtime homeowners make decisions about where and how they want to live.

The term silver tsunami makes for a dramatic headline, but the actual data tells a much less dramatic story. And there’s another reason these homes won’t overwhelm the market.

After the 2008 housing crash, builders significantly slowed construction. And for years afterward, they didn’t build enough homes to keep up with demand. That led to a housing shortage we’re still dealing with today.

And just how big a gap are we talking about? Estimates vary, but many experts say the U.S. is still millions of homes short. For example, a recent report from the White House Council of Economic Advisers explains:

“If homebuilding and the growth of the single-family housing stock had continued at their historical pace instead of falling dramatically after 2008, there would be 10 million or more additional single-family homes today.”

As more longtime homeowners sell, those homes will help a gap that’s already there. But they won’t push us over the edge. That’s because, at the same time, more households are expected to form in the decade ahead, and they’ll need homes, too.

So, more homes becoming available over time isn’t automatically a bad thing. It can give buyers more options and help create a more balanced housing market moving forward.

Here’s the takeaway if you’re thinking about selling your house. The silver tsunami isn’t something you need to plan your move around. What’s happening in your local market is far more important than a national projection about the next decade.

That’s because real estate is local. Some markets have more homes for sale than others. Some are seeing houses sell relatively quickly, while others are taking longer.

And those are the conditions that matter when you’re deciding how to price, prepare, and market your house.

For example, an agent who knows your area can help you understand:

How many homes are for sale nearby. This tells you how much choice buyers have and how your house will compare.

What similar houses are actually selling for. That’s one of the most important factors in setting a competitive asking price.

What buyers are looking for right now. Knowing which features and improvements matter most can help your house make a strong first impression.

And that’s something you can act on today, regardless of what happens with the silver tsunami over the next decade.

The right strategy starts with understanding your local market and making decisions based on what’s happening there, not what a dramatic national headline suggests might happen years from now.

The silver tsunami may sound like a major wave of homes coming onto the market, but the research points to a gradual shift over the next decade, not a sudden flood of listings.If you're thinking about selling, don't let that headline make you second-guess your plans. Talk to an agent about what's happening in your local market.

#5681. The Famous ‘Orange County Choppers’ Compound Just Got a $100K Price Cut—and It’s a Gearhead’s Dream

A 38.3-acre ultimate collector’s playground, formerly owned by master mechanic Paul Teutul Sr. of the popular reality TV show "American Choppers," has received a $100K price chop.

Located in Montgomery, NY, the adventure estate has a pond with a waterfall, fenced paddocks, animal run-in sheds, a two-story auto showroom, and a 6,000-square-foot commercial-grade mechanic’s garage and workshop.

Teutul sold the iconic Hudson Valley retreat to the current owners for $1,500,000 in 2019 after originally listing it for $2,895,000 in 2017.

The farm, garage, and family compound, known locally as the “Orange County Choppers House,” would be ideal for an equestrian, auto enthusiast, or investor seeking a legacy compound.

“It’s a substantial property that offers a lifestyle beyond the main house that feels like its own retreat,” said listing agent Danielle Bartula of Howard Hanna | Rand Realty. “The Orange County [Teutul] family had goats, llamas, and horses.”

A gated entrance opens to meadows that lead to the primary log home. The 3,448-square-foot house has a gourmet eat-in kitchen with high-end appliances, custom wood cabinetry, granite countertops, and an island with a prep sink.

The wood-clad interior also includes a two-story great room with vaulted wood ceilings, skylights, a floor-to-ceiling stone fireplace, and French doors that open to a wraparound covered porch.

“This part of Montgomery is known for hiking, mountain biking, and horse farms,” Bartula added. “It’s in the heart of the Hudson Valley with a wide range of everything nearby.”

The main level offers an executive office and a primary suite with a walk-in closet and a spa-inspired bath with a jetted soaking tub, oversized shower, and double vanity.

An upstairs loft that could be used as additional living space overlooks the great room. A partially finished lower level with a bar area awaits a buyer’s finishing touches.

“I could see a family who loves to entertain with family and friends buying this property or an athlete who has to go back and forth from the city,” she said. “It’s only an hour and 20 minutes away to New York City but offers a true retreat setting.”

Other highlights include a mudroom with a dog washing station, a whole-home generator, manicured gardens, and koi ponds.

“The current owners used it as a secondary residence but for the previous owners, it was their primary,” Bartula noted. “I think it would be great to have it used as a primary but would certainly work well either way because it is very private yet very convenient.”

Outdoors, a multi-level heated pool has a slide and wading area. It is surrounded by a sundeck for lounging, plus an outdoor kitchen and shaded pergola for entertaining. The nearby pool house has a tiki bar, full bath, and outdoor shower.

A spectacular heated 7,000-square-foot garage features two guest quarters that could also be used for staff or extended family.

The two-story barn can accommodate up to five horses and has a hay loft and “room for expansion.”

A mechanic’s garage and workshop provides additional flexible space for hobbyists, collectors, or business pursuits.

The 1-acre pond has docks and a grilling patio, ideal for fishing, relaxing, or entertaining.

“There is no way you could rebuild this for that price,” she said. “We have shown it to a lot of people and they are all enamored. It’s a really special property but the hardest part is finding someone who wants to maintain all of this.”

#5680. AGNT Posts 6% Revenue Growth in Q3, Expects ‘Difficult’ Market Into 2027

AGNT, the parent company for eXp Realty and NextHome, posted revenue growth despite economic headwinds of high rates and sluggish home demand, the company announced during an earnings call Thursday.

Closed real estate sales transactions reached 131,000 in the third quarter of 2026, up 8% year-over-year, alongside a 10% jump in sales volume to $59.3 billion, executives said. That productivity pushed AGNT revenues to $1.4 billion over the quarter, up 6% from $1.3 billion a year ago.

Meanwhile, the company saw a net loss of $4.3 million over the quarter and 7% higher operating expenses from a year ago. AGNT’s adjusted EBITDA closed out the quarter at $17.1 million, down 3% from $17.7 million compared to the previous year.

Newly minted AGNT CEO Leo Pareja acknowledged the market is challenging, with existing-home sales expected to be near 4 million, inventory up about 7% year-over-year but still below pandemic levels and mortgage rates above 7.3%. He said the market was “not broken” but “resetting to normal” after two unusually strong booms.

Overall, the company saw agent count grow to 87,457 by the end of the third quarter, up 5% year-over-year (including NextHome, which was acquired earlier in the year).

Pareja attributed most of its agent attrition mostly to unproductive agents leaving eXp or NextHome, with 49% of those nonproductive agents leaving the real estate industry altogether in Q3. Newer agents to the company tend to join a team, where they get a stronger start, he added.

“With 44% of new agent joiners on teams in Q3, and this is important because agents on teams are 77% more productive than individual agents,” Pareja said.

The company’s Q3 earnings call came on the heels of AGNT, along with Keller Williams, HomeServices of America and Real REMAX Group, forming Open Real Estate, a new shared listing-data company. The new initiative uses standard fields for listings to be entered then distributes the data out to participating members, local MLSs, search portals and other platforms.

“When listings are fragmented or kept out of view, buyers can miss homes, and sellers reach fewer potential buyers,” Pareja said. Pareja noted that Open Real Estate’s startup costs have limited exposure for the rest of the business.

As mortgage rates stay north of 7% and home sales slow heading into the final stretch of the year, AGNT updated its guidance for the remainder of 2026. AGNT Chief Financial Officer Jesse Hill acknowledged the tough market conditions the company—and the entire industry—is facing.

“Rising interest rates continue to weigh significantly on housing demand, and we’ve seen that softening as we’ve headed into Q4 here,” Hill said. He added that market conditions, along with AGNT seeing “higher-than-baseline” legal expenses peaking in 2026, caused it to update its financial outlook for the year.

In late October, eXp reached a settlement with agent Anya Roberts who sued former eXp agents Michael Bjorkman and David Golden in 2023, alleging they drugged and sexually assaulted her at company events. Roberts also named the brokerage and founder Glenn Sanford in her federal lawsuit for allegedly ignoring or covering up a sex trafficking/recruiting scheme tied to its revenue-share model. The company has consistently denied all wrongdoing in connection to the lawsuit.

While the case was settled for an undisclosed amount, a separate, larger civil lawsuit from four other female eXp agents with similar allegations is ongoing. Hill said the company expects legal costs to “normalize” in 2027, but remain higher for the rest of the year.

Overall in 2026, AGNT expects revenue to reach $4.85 billion to $5.05 billion and adjusted EBITDA in the neighborhood of $40 million to $47 million, Hill noted.

#5679. Selling Your Home? What You Should Know About Price Cuts vs. Rate Buydowns.

In today’s market, a growing number of sellers are opting to do something called a price cut – especially when their house has been on the market for a while without any bites.

According to HousingWire Data as many as 4 in 10 (43%) sellers are going this route – that’s the highest it’s been in 4 years. But what if there’s another (potentially better option) for your bottom line? And it’s just as appealing, if not more so, to today’s buyers?

First, let’s set the stage on why some compromise may be necessary in today’s market.

In September, Redfin says there were 63% more sellers than buyers in the market. And with so many sellers active and relatively few buyers by comparison, those purchasers are realizing they have more power. And as mortgage rates continue to put a squeeze on their budgets, they’re leaning in and using it.

One of the most common negotiation points? The price.

That’s because they want to feel like they’re getting a deal and they want to see their monthly payment drop. And since buyers can’t control rates, the price feels like the most obvious lever to pull.

But the savviest sellers realize being flexible doesn’t always mean a lower price, paying for a buyer’s rate buydown might work better.

A buydown is money paid at closing to lower the buyer’s mortgage rate. When you pay it as the seller, you are paying some of the buyer’s interest ahead of time, so the buyer gets a lower rate and monthly payment. And that’s especially appealing to today’s buyers.

Temporary buydowns lower the rate for the first few years, then it goes back to the full rate. The more years a buydown covers, the more it costs. These work well for buyers who expect to refinance within a certain amount of time.

A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the whole loan. These are paid for with “discount points.” One point costs 1% of the loan. According to FICO, each point generally lowers the rate by about a quarter of a percent. This type of buydown works well for buyers who plan to stay in the home for a long time.

And here’s why these can be a win-win for both buyers and sellers. Rate buydowns help sellers stand out in a crowded market and they can have a bigger impact on your buyer than a price cut would.

Here’s an example to show you what that could look like.

Let’s say you’re willing to make a $10,000 concession to help get the deal done. Take a look at these three ways to spend that money and the impact they could have on a buyer’s $420,000, 30-year fixed loan at 7%:

It’s the same $10,000 from the seller. But a 2-1 buydown saves the buyer about eight times more each month in the first year.

And since most buyers shop by monthly payment, that’s what grabs their attention.

That’s what makes a rate buydown worth considering. Instead of reducing your asking price, you may be able to use that same money to have a bigger impact on your buyer’s monthly payments. And depending on what matters most to that buyer, the immediate savings could be more appealing than a price reduction.

The key is working with your agent and the buyer’s lender to compare the options and see which one makes the most sense.

Loan programs cap how much a seller can pay toward a buyer’s costs.

Money toward buydowns doesn’t limit what else a buyer may ask a seller to pay for. Buyers may still ask for repairs or other concessions.

Putting the buydown offer in your listing lets agents and buyers know it’s an option.

Your agent can run scenarios on buydowns and other costs of selling in advance so you’re prepared when an offer comes in.

As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers.”

And sellers who offer solutions like buydowns can make meaningful impact where home buyers need it most: in their wallets.

When you're looking for ways to make your house more appealing to buyers, a price reduction isn't your only option. #5678. Meet the 27-Year-Old Who’s Trying To Bring Housing Back to Rural Ohio

When it comes to the hottest locations that attract young 20-somethings, Mansfield, OH, probably isn't the first place that comes to mind.

For years, Mansfield’s nickname was “The Fun Center of Ohio” because of its family-friendly attractions and its status in the 1970s as a mini-bike manufacturing hub.

More recently, the town of 47,000, located halfway between Columbus and Cleveland, earned the local nickname of “Danger City” after the Westinghouse electric plant left in 1990 and the town fell into deep economic decline.

The 27-year-old serial entrepreneur, who started a painting and landscaping business as a teenager, relocated to Mansfield from Seattle a year ago, hoping to revitalize rural housing through his vertically integrated housing development company, Western Dominion Land.

Vertical integration is a development model in which a single company controls the full life cycle of a housing project.

“In other countries, they’ve figured out that vertically integrating construction means you’re not paying a margin out to every single step," Goehner explains. "If you own the system—from a lumberyard, to producing panels or modular, to buying the land, to developing the land, to building the homes—you're not paying everyone’s markup along the way, and you can actually deliver that home at a reasonable price.”

Goehner is building a factory in Mansfield to produce structured panels that he says will cut single-family home construction from months to weeks and allow him to charge much less than other builders. The first panels are expected to roll off the production line in early 2027.

Currently, it takes 8.8 months to construct a home from start to finish, according to the National Association of Home Builders. Goehner says his process allows a home to be built and move-in-ready in 40 days.

Western Dominion has already built about 500 housing units across Ohio, starting at $200,000 for a single-family home.

Western Dominion focuses on what it calls "attainable housing"—homes priced below what the median household income in the area can afford but not income-limited, meaning they work for the vast majority of families and buyers.

In Mansfield, where the median listing price is $229,000, he says, "single-family homes at $215,000 sold instantly. At $260,000, they sat for months."

As he sees it, 25% of the homes on the market are priced for 60% to 70% of buyers, while the rest of what’s being built is at the top end of the market. Furthermore, only 8% of construction happens in rural areas, despite 20% of the population living there.

"The government is too focused on low-income housing" and low-income housing tax credits, he says. “And the last few housing bills they passed were only structured to deliver essentially more urban multifamily units and incentivize builders to build more low-income housing with tax credits."

In rural communities, he adds, “We have a terrible amount of aged housing inventory. Most of our homes are from before 1970, which would be fine if it didn't cost so much to remodel.

“From the '90s to the 2000s, we’re building a good amount of homes. As a country, we were doing about 1.6 million a year. And then in rural America, we were doing about 220,000 homes a year. And then 2008 hits, and that drops down to about 60,000 homes a year in rural America."

Along the way, smaller builders disappeared, and larger builders were disincentivized from building in rural areas because of the red tape involved.

"If you want to build in rural America and you go to a bank, unless you have all the cash, you have to show comps," he says. "You've got to be, like, ‘All right, we think these homes are going to sell for this much because these guys sold for this much.' And if no one's built for five to 50 years, which is the case in a lot of these communities, that can be difficult."

The added costs of building in rural areas, like having to pull utilities, "mean you're spending $25,000 to $50,000 per lot before you can even start putting a house on it or connecting your utilities to the lot."

Since the COVID-19 pandemic, home prices in rural communities have risen sharply. A Realtor.com® housing analysis of home prices from November 2019 to November 2025 found that median listing prices increased more than 70% in rural counties while in-metro counties saw home prices increase around 30% during the same time period.

"A lot of the politicians we talk to, they go, 'I didn't know that that county needed housing. I didn't know rural needed housing because the population is shrinking.' But then when you look at why the population is shrinking, it's because they haven't gotten any new homes for 20 to 40 years."

"You've got this huge demand. But on paper, on the surface, it looks like there's no demand because the population's declining," he continues. "And that's how you get cities like Holiday City."

Holiday City, near the Ohio border with Indiana and Michigan, has a population of just 48 people, but it is home to three large businesses—Chase Brass & Copper Co., 20/20 Custom Molded Products, and a Menards Distribution Center—which draw around 1,500 commuters from out of state.

"Let's put up, you know, 300 homes, and a portion of the workforce can actually stop commuting an hour or two every day," Goehner says.

Goehner hopes Ohio's new slate of elected officials will help advance rural building by offsetting some of the infrastructure-related costs of building in rural areas. In exchange, he would sell homes at his “attainable” housing rates.

"The government needs to stop spending thousands of dollars a month per unit to subsidize rents when they could simply spend a little bit upfront to make it viable to build at a reasonable price point again," he says.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5677. A Rare $7M Double Townhome Hits the Market in DC—Complete With a Heated Terrace and ‘Fortress’ Garage

The word "compound" is very rarely associated with townhouses in bustling city neighborhoods, but a $7 million property in Washington DC’s Dupont Circle might just be the exception.

Offered together, the connected luxury residences at 1617 and 1619 19th Street NW are an incredibly rare opportunity to own some serious square footage in one of the capital’s most vibrant areas.

The property is anchored by 1619—a four-bedroom, 4.5-bathroom residence that spans four impeccably-renovated levels. Next door, 1617 serves as a complementary rowhome with three fully-leased residences—a spacious one bedroom with a private patio, and two additional two-bedroom, two-bathroom units.

Spanning 6,600 square feet and boasting nine bedrooms and 9.5 half-bathrooms between them, the pair of buildings has "all kinds of unique use cases," according to listing agent Barak Sky with Serhant.

Sky explains that there are plenty of impressive features that could make this the perfect situation for a "needle in a haystack buyer who can’t find exactly what they need."

Perhaps a notable public figure would like to reside in the four-level residence, and dedicate one of the smaller units in the secondary building to a round-the-clock security team. A family could take advantage of the opportunity to create a multigenerational home.

Maybe it’s just right for a buyer who wants to live in a gorgeous home and generate rental income. The three units currently pull in $136,200 annually, according to the listing.

“It’s definitely special,” says Sky. “We thought this was a unique opportunity to present this compound as one offering.”

Aside from the fact that the sheer volume of space is ripe with possibility, there’s another feature of the property that brings endless potential.

“The detached garage is completely like a fortress,” Sky adds.

A steel two-car garage is structurally engineered for future expansion, and could be used to add a private, elevated pool deck or even an additional accessory residence. Given the historic nature of the property, which was built in 1910, the chance to add to the building’s legacy is certainly exciting.

Should the buyer choose to leave everything as-is, they’re still in for a treat.

The primary residence has been painstakingly renovated, and features an “uncompromising commitment to craftsmanship,” according to the listing, which touts the dwelling’s “soaring ceilings and extensive custom millwork.”

A private elevator services each floor, connecting the sprawling formal spaces, gourmet kitchen, and inviting family room to the private retreats upstairs.

An entire level is dedicated to the primary suite, which includes a private terrace, dual walk-in closets, and a spa-inspired marble bathroom equipped with heated floors, a steam shower, and a sauna.

Of the additional bedrooms, two are ensuites.

The lower level hosts a recreation lounge, a temperature-controlled wine cellar, a guest suite, and space for what could become an efficiency kitchen.

The outdoor space is just as lavish, and is described as a “spectacular private sanctuary” in the listing. There’s a wood-burning fireplace, outdoor audio and television, heat lamps for the winter, a misting system for the summer, and heated walkways.

There are also a number of seemingly invisible amenities that were carefully selected to make life more comfortable, such as seamlessly-integrated smart home technology and whole-house water filtration.

As for the location, this gem is located on one of Dupont Circle’s "most coveted tree-lined blocks,”"according to the listing.

“This exceptional offering places the very best of Washington at your doorstep, from acclaimed restaurants, boutique shopping, and neighborhood cafes to Embassy Row, downtown business districts, cultural institutions, and Metro access,” it reads.

#5676. Two Neighboring $9.9 Million Oceanfront Homes Just Listed in Kauai’s South Shore—And They Can Form an Ultra-Luxe Compound

Tucked into a private-club community in Hawaii called Kukui‘ula, two luxury homes just hit the market on Kauai's South Shore.

Set right on the ocean, and set among lush tropical vegetation, this walkable community is only 25-minute drive from Lihue Airport.

"The close proximity of everything is very convenient. You’re not having to spend a lot of time in the car,” says Pancho Sullivan of Hawaii Life, who is co-listing the two homes with Haunani Sullivan as well as Suzanne Harding and Jeff Skinner of Kukui‘ula Realty Group. The asking price sits at $9,900,000 each.

Both were built in 2025 and have never been occupied. Aepo Nei 18 and Aepo Nei 19 are neighboring 3,372-square-foot homes with four bedrooms and 4.5 baths each. They can be purchased together, to create a private compound, or by separate buyers.

Even better, the homes are fully furnished and stocked with items like bed and bath linens, beach towels, and everything you need to cook and serve in the kitchen, such as bowls, plates and glasses.

But it’s the design by Brazil-based Architects+CO that’s truly unique. Kauai Bahia Construction and their in-house material company, Kayu, handled all of the finish material production and millwork installation.

"Brazil is known for incredible resort-club communities," says Pancho. "We actually traveled to Brazil to look at some of the clubs they designed. It’s the same tropical feel (as Hawaii) that blends in really well with nature."

Aepo Nei 18’s layout features connected pavilions while Aepo Nei 19’s living spaces open onto a lawn courtyard. Design features at both include deep roof overhangs, walls of glass and multiple outdoor living spaces such as an infinity-edge pool; jacuzzi; swim-in, swim-out sauna; and in-water fire pit.

"They both have beautiful 180-degree ocean views looking across the Tom Weiskopf-designed golf course. The swim-in, swim-out dry sauna facing the ocean is a unique feature," says Pancho, adding that the usage of natural materials like lava stone, coral and teak "fit into the landscape very beautifully."

Referred to as the Garden Island, Kauai is home to about 73,000 people.

"We get the majority of the island’s sunshine down here," says Haunani, about the South Shore. "People flock here for the beaches and the sunshine, Hawaiian monk seals on the sand, and a lot of ocean activity including surfing.

"A lot of people that venture to Kauai are adventure seekers. We have great hiking. You can get on a boat and dive on the Nā Pali Coast and do ziplining and ATV tours."

Stand-up paddleboarding, diving and fishing are two other activities easy to do in this community.

Homeowners become club members with access to dining, a pool, spa (boasting a steam rook and lava-rock dry sauna), pickleball and tennis courts, and an 18-hole golf course.

"There’s an incredible gym with classes daily, from yoga to sound bathing to fitness training," says Pancho. "All of that is part of your club membership. It’s a great place to be in tune with nature and get healthy."

A 10-acre organic garden features a farm stand as well as opportunities to create floral bouquets. There’s also a conscious effort to honor Hawaiian history through cultural-heritage walks; sunrise ceremonies; hula performances; and classes in Hawaiian featherwork, quilting and basket weaving.

“Members who are part of the club become life-long friends,” says Haunani. “They’re going to each other’s second homes and weddings. They travel around the world together.”

The community also organizes annual golf and pickleball tournaments for members, and three golf courses are within a seven-minute drive.

Another incentive is that the community’s zoned as a Vacation Destination Area.

This means properties can join the short-term rental pool, for minimum seven-night stays.

"Some of the owners put their homes in the rental pool and block out time for themselves and their families. That’s a great added benefit," says Haunani, as few club communities on Kauai allow this.

The Sullivans think the buyer will likely hail from the West Coast, enticed by a direct flight from hubs in cities like Los Angeles, San Francisco, Seattle, Phoenix and Denver that arrive on the island by mid-day.

“Kukui‘ula is a great place for families to gather and spend time together. We see a lot of members bring their entire families so they can vacation together multiple times per year,” says Pancho.

“With all these activities it’s easy to curate an incredible vacation with the convenience of being on property. A lot of people enjoy coming here and decompressing.”

Based in Milwaukee, Kristine Hansen writes for TravelandLeisure.com, ArchitecturalDigest.com, Vogue.com, and other outlets. She’s also the author of “Frank Lloyd Wright’s Wisconsin: How America’s Most Famous Architect Found Inspiration in His Home State.” She lives in a 1924 bungalow.

#5675. Midterm elections will put AI and data centers on trial, but will Big Tech end up winning anyway?

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof

It may be a little soon to determine the ultimate winners and losers among enterprise suppliers after the midterm elections, but the early line is: Big Tech wins and data center suppliers operators such as chipmakers and neoclouds lose. Or will everybody lose?

The day after the elections, stocks of many tech companies shot up, a bit paradoxically because investors apparently believe potential limits on AI and data centers could tamp down spending on compute and thus improve tech company margins that have made investors nervous. But then on Thursday, tech stocks almost across the board plunged back down even more for a collective loss of $2.5 trillion in market cap — the Nasdaq fell more than 5.5% — on more generalized worries that, well, the AI boom could slow. Suffice to say, investors are still sorting things out.

Marvell Semiconductor this week made a surprisingly huge acquisition with Lumentum, a bet on the AI boom continuing. That is, if it comes off: The drop in Lumentum’s stock price has some speculating it could hunt around for another offer.

And the AI juggernaut indeed continues apace, judging from strong tech earnings, though even pre-election, they reflected investor wariness. AMD, Supermicro and Arista all beat easily, as well as Palantir and Kyndryl, whose stock rocketed 30%. But chipmakers Qualcomm, Arm and Globalfoundries didn’t get the love despite good quarters — especially in Thursday’s bloodbath.

All of which raises the question that Dave Vellante posed in his Breaking Analysis last weekend: Can enterprise AI pay for the boom? Dave and analyst Crawford Del Prete discussed the prospects.

Next week’s earnings reports include Cisco, CoreWeave, Applied Materials, Cerebras and Nebius, any or all of which could move markets.

Here’s all of this week’s enterprise and emerging tech news, analysis and commentary from SiliconANGLE and beyond:

Amazon, Microsoft and other tech giants close higher after Democrats’ midterm sweep No, data centers won’t get shut down, and AI will continue apace — just regulated as it needs to be, and we can hope it’s in the right way to protect people and communities and innovation all at the same time. We can walk and chew gum at the same time if we put our mind to it. Hard to imagine the Dems could do worse than Trump and the GOP have been doing for years now.

#5674. Housing Week Ahead: Hottest Markets, Inflation, and Existing-Home Sales

The coming week brings a steady stream of new reports from the Realtor.com economics team, as well as a number of key indicators for the housing market.

On Monday, senior economist Anthony Smith published the October Luxury Report, which looks at pockets of growth where luxury prices are still rising.

On Tuesday, ahead of Veterans Day, we honor America’s military service members and veterans with a report on Veterans Affairs loans. Senior economist Jiayi Xu explores what they are and how they help with homeownership.

On Wednesday, senior economist Hannah Jones examines how the lock-in effect has evolved and where today’s homeowners with a mortgage face larger or smaller payment shocks if they are thinking about moving.

On Thursday, Hannah is back to examine what the first full week of November data reveals about the housing market, and on Friday, Hannah publishes the October Hottest Markets report, which identifies the markets where homes are moving the fastest and getting the most attention from online shoppers.

Turning to the economic indicators that will be released, we’ll see the consumer price index reading on inflation as well as mortgage rates and existing-home sales.

Inflation has run above the Fed’s target, 2% growth in headline PCE, for 5.5 years, and it’s clear from exit polls that the cost of living was very much on the mind of voters in last week’s election.

This week, we’ll see the first inflation reading for October from the consumer price index, which was up sharply in September largely due to higher energy prices. I’m expecting the annual inflation reading to be similarly high in October even if the month-to-month momentum wanes a bit.

Although inflation remains elevated, mortgage rates could continue to ebb. Last week the 30-year fixed mortgage rate, according to Freddie Mac, dropped to 7.18% as the 10-year hovered near 4.9%.

Late in the week, the 10-year yield dropped further as uncertainty over artificial intelligence investments led to a pullback in stocks. Even if the 10-year were to remain at 4.9%, it has adjusted faster than mortgage rates, so I think there is room for spread compression that could help nudge rates lower, which will help late-season home shoppers.

The last indicator of the week is existing-home sales data from the National Association of Realtors®. That October home sales data is likely to be very disappointing.

Mortgage rates rose sharply in the month, and NAR’s pending home sales hit a series record low in September, while Realtor.com housing data suggests that the buyer pullback continued into October. I’m watching to see if the pullback is sufficient to push months supply even higher.

For full reports, the Market Clock, and raw housing data, visit realtor.com/research.

Danielle Hale is the chief economist of Realtor.com.

#5673. Fayetteville’s Growth Continues, but Affordability Is Testing the Market

The Fayetteville metro enters the final months of 2026 with several indicators pointing to continued economic growth. Total households are expected to increase 1.9% year over year to 236,740 in 2026, with annual growth of roughly 2% projected through 2028. Labor market conditions have also remained favorable, as total nonfarm employment grew 3.0% year over year to 311,300 in August and the unemployment rate fell to 3.1%, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Several notable projects are moving forward across the region. Northwest Arkansas National Airport (XNA) is advancing a nearly $79 million terminal expansion after recording its highest monthly passenger volume on record in July 2026 and surpassing Little Rock in annual enplanements last year. In Bentonville, the Alice L. Walton School of Medicine Whole Health Campus recently broke ground, an investment that could help meet rising health care needs as the metro’s 65 and older population continues to grow through 2028.

While demographic indicators and economic activity remain positive, housing market data tells a more mixed story.

Despite continued household and employment growth, home sales activity has slowed. As of July, annualized new home closings totaled 2,033, down 20.4% year over year, compared with an essentially flat decline for annualized existing home closings over the same period.

Pricing remains an important consideration. The median new home closing price reached nearly $380,000 in July, compared with $365,000 for existing homes. Despite that premium, new home demand remains concentrated at more attainable price points. In fact, the largest share of both detached and attached annualized new home closings occurred between $300,000 and $350,000 in July.

Meanwhile, single-family permitting is expected to decline 20.4% year over year in 2026 before decreasing another 15.1% in 2027. What was previously characterized as a housing shortage could become a more competitive environment as supply catches up with demand.

Fayetteville’s important storyline will be turning household and employment growth into qualified housing demand. The fundamentals remain compelling, but affordability and a shifting supply-demand balance are likely to separate the market’s strongest performers from the rest.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth market reports published in Zonda Enterprise.

#5671. Mortgage Mix: Buyers Turning to ARMs Due to Elevated Rates; Compass Expands Its Mortgage Business

Editor’s Note: The Mortgage Mix is RISMedia’s highlight reel of need-to-know mortgage-industry happenings. Watch for it every other Friday afternoon.

The numbers: While mortgage rates had hit a peak and were nearing the high-end of the 7% range, they have now decreased for the third straight week to 7.18% for the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage and 6.57% for the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage. Notably, this was the lowest level seen in over a month.

What this means: A stronger jobs report was partially attributed to this week’s improvement, as Realtor.com® Senior Economist Hannah Jones said that “while solid hiring supports housing demand over time, a stronger-than-expected report could also lift bond yields and slow the pace of rate declines in the near term.

The “blue wave” that occurred in the elections this past Tuesday may also contribute to further improvements down the road, as Jones noted that “many newly elected representatives have voiced discontent with the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, which has contributed to rising inflation, so any progress toward resolution could mean lower inflation and softer mortgage rates ahead.”

Using their ARMs? Despite a come down, many buyers are still holding off from the market due to rates remaining over 7%. Mortgage applications this week were down 1.2%.

With the fixed-rate mortgage elevated, more buyers have turned to adjustable rate mortgages (ARMs) instead.

“As we have highlighted in recent weeks, more borrowers are choosing ARMs in this environment to lower their initial payments, with the ARM share at its highest level since September 2025,” said Mike Fratantoni, the Mortgage Bankers Association’s SVP and chief economist.

A Better battle comes to an end: After a tumultuous struggle between the lender and its founder, Better.com has dropped its federal securities lawsuit against Vishal Garg, who was ousted in August. The case was dismissed with prejudice, meaning it cannot be refiled.

The lender had been suing Garg for allegedly violating federal securities laws, arguing that he did not engage in the proper process to solicit shareholders in a bid to regain his position.

That bid ended up being successful, with Garg back in a leadership role.

Compass takes mortgage JV to the big leagues: Expanding its mortgage business to become a top-10 lender, Compass announced a merger between its own OriginPoint mortgage platform and Rate’s Guaranteed Rate Affinity to unite the two mortgage ventures under the OriginPoint brand.

Guaranteed Rate Affinity was founded in partnership with Anywhere Real Estate back in 2017, making the merger an unsurprising move due to Compass’s acquisition of Anywhere last year.

The merger expands OriginPoint’s resources and geographic reach, the companies noted in a release, while backing the business with Rate’s AI technology, products and lending platform.

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5670. Columbia, South Carolina, Balances Growth and Affordability Challenges

Columbia remains a market defined by competing forces. Demand fundamentals continue to support housing activity, but elevated home prices, affordability pressures, and a cooler sales environment are creating some new challenges for builders operating in the region.

The market’s long-term outlook remains supported by solid demographic trends. Columbia’s population is approaching 890,000 residents, while household growth continues to outpace many mature markets. Household formation is expected to remain positive through 2028, providing a steady stream of potential buyers and renters. Meanwhile, median household income continues to rise, helping support housing demand even as affordability remains strained.

Adding to the area’s economic foundation is the presence of the University of South Carolina, which enrolled more than 40,000 students in 2025. According to a university study, the institution generates billions in annual economic activity across the region through payroll, purchases, and tax contributions.

While market conditions have cooled from the rapid growth period seen earlier in the decade, Columbia remains structurally undersupplied. Zonda’s analysis indicates the market is currently undersupplied by roughly 3.7%, suggesting that long-term housing demand still exceeds available inventory.

Builders have responded by expanding community offerings. Active projects increased year over year, with 109 communities currently operating across the market. At the same time, quick move-in inventory remains relatively manageable, signaling that builders have largely avoided excessive speculative inventory buildup.

Like most other markets across the country, affordability remains one of the market’s biggest hurdles. Columbia’s housing market is currently considered overvalued relative to local income levels, with home prices continuing to exceed income-supported pricing.

Still, the broader economic backdrop remains supportive. Employment levels continue to grow, unemployment remains relatively low, and household growth is forecast to continue over the next several years. Combined with the market’s ongoing housing deficit, those factors should help sustain demand even as affordability challenges limit the pace of future growth.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth market reports published as part of Zonda’s Enterprise subscription.

Zonda’s experts provide objective analysis on housing trends, supply and demand dynamics, and economic drivers. The team of economists, researchers, and analysts blends proprietary data with expert interpretation to help you navigate changing markets and make smarter decisions.

#5669. Luxury Home Prices Are Falling, but These Pockets of Growth Are Defying the Slump

Luxury home prices are sinking in much of the country, but there are significant exceptions, where high-end home prices just keep rising.

The national threshold for luxury homes—defined as the top 10% of listings—in October came in at $1,197,014, down 2.3% from one year ago, according to the latest Realtor.com® monthly luxury report.

The downward trend held in the upper tiers of the luxury market, with the 95th percentile down 4.1% to a threshold of $1,873,040 and the 99th percentile down 6.2% to $5,125,874.

However, in certain golden pockets, the luxury market is thriving. Of the 43 metros in the report's dataset, 12 posted a year-over-year increase of 1% or higher.

"Although the price point for entry luxury has had 31 consecutive months of annual decline at the national level, there are markets where prices are climbing and, in some cases, well above the year-ago levels," says the report's author, Realtor.com senior economist Anthony Smith.

Of those 12 robust luxury markets, the South massively dominates, with five markets in Florida alone. Only two Northern metros—Atlantic City and Detroit—made the cut.

Nor are these necessarily the most expensive markets in the U.S. While those pricey markets—with familiar names like Bridgeport-Stamford-Danbury, CT, and Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim, CA—have the highest entry thresholds to luxury, their prices are slipping.

Of the 12 most expensive markets, only Naples-Marco Island, FL, with an entry threshold of $3,753,333, continues to show price gains. Nor are these gains negligible—the metro's luxury threshold is up a very healthy 9.0% year over year.

While this is only 1.3 percentage points over second-place finisher North Port-Bradenton-Sarasota, FL, with a much lower entry to luxury at $1,796,850, it is a full 4.3 percentage points over third-place finisher Charleston-North Charleston, SC.

Naples comes ahead in another key way, too. Luxury properties are moving a median 27 days faster than last year, or 21.1% quicker, by far the fastest pace increase of all the growth metros. The second-place finisher, Cape Coral-Fort Myers, FL, is moving 18 days faster than last year, or 16.1%.

The price gains aren't limited to entry-level luxury, or the top 10%. Eight of the 12 metros saw all three luxury tiers rise from a year ago, a sharp contrast with the national picture, where all those thresholds fell.

The largest gain for the top 1% of listings (ultraluxury) came from Charleston-North Charleston, SC. Here, the entry-level luxe threshold rose 4.7% (the third-highest in the nation), but its top 1% of properties blasted past that with a median price increase of 18.7%, for a threshold of $8,044,460.

These are the top 12 growth markets for entry-level luxury:

North Port-Bradenton-Sarasota, FL (up 7.7%)

Miami-Fort Lauderdale-West Palm Beach, FL (up 4.1%)

Nashville-Davidson-Murfreesboro-Franklin, TN (up 3.6%)

Las Vegas-Henderson-North Las Vegas, NV (up 2.2%)

Tampa-St. Petersburg-Clearwater, FL (up 2.1%)

On the southwestern edge of the Sunshine State, dubbed the Paradise Coast, Naples has long lured snowbirds eager to escape Northern winters and embrace the blue-green waters and white sandy shores of the Gulf.

But it hasn't always been a top luxury haven; in fact, that aspect of the area is rather new.

Luxury broker Taylor Canada of Gulf Coast International Properties, who was born and raised in Naples, says that in the 1980s, the town was "nothing."

"On the beach, there were like four buildings," he tells Realtor.com.

But over the decades, the agent has seen the metro change dramatically, with booming development and sprawling Tuscan-style mansions and high-end retail. Still, the town has managed to retain much of its "small town" charm, thanks to tight building regulations.

"They are really trying to make it not Miami," he says of the city. "That attracts a lot of affluent buyers to the lifestyle and the quietness."

The wealthy in Palm Beach County are "more showy," he says. "Here, you could be behind a billionaire in the grocery store and never know."

The broker, who currently represents a $9 million, four-bedroom, 4.5-bath 5,000-plus-square-foot estate in Old Naples, isn't surprised that his hometown is bucking the national trend, with luxury prices on the rise.

"We're seeing records broken monthly," he says of certain exclusive and waterfront neighborhoods. Even the luxury condo market, which he says "struggled for a few years," is showing signs of a recovery, with the occasional bidding war.

Buyers at this level are the usual suspects, hailing from more expensive states such as New York, Washington, and California. But, uniquely, the area also sees a lot of local buyers who "shuffle around" from one luxury property to another.

"Every three to five years, they figure out where they want to go next," Canada says of mobile Naples lovers. "They go, 'Oh, maybe I want to be on the water, or maybe I want to get closer to the beach, or maybe I want to be in a golf community.'"

And while Naples still draws an older crowd, the agent says it is more common now to see buyers "in their 40s and their families." While the techies tend to head to Miami and the West Coast, the CEOs and business leaders prefer the East Coast, he says.

And what they want are properties that are brand-new, turnkey, and furnished.

"They're willing to pay a premium for that," he adds.

Florida's plethora of tax breaks—including the newly approved measure that would reform the state's property tax system—is luring high net worth individuals more than ever before.

"The tax break is paying for their property, almost," he says.

The metro with the second-highest annual growth in the nation, with a 7.7% increase, is 120 miles north of Naples, nestled along Sarasota Bay. Luxe homes, with an entry threshold of $1,796,850, are moving nine days faster than they did last year.

The North Port-Bradenton-Sarasota metro encompasses multiple barrier islands, including Longboat Key and Siesta Key, with famous Siesta Beach, which often tops "beat beaches" polls due to its nearly 100% quartz-crystal sand.

Like Naples, Sarasota wasn't always a luxury haven.

Local broker Joel Schemmel of Douglas Elliman has been representing the area for 25 years and concentrates on the top 1% of properties, or those over $4 million.

Those with fat pocketbooks began pouring into Sarasota during the COVID-19 pandemic, he says. Now, buyers continue to be lured by the pristine white beaches, cultural attractions (Sarasota has a vibrant arts community), and top-notch schools, including the renowned IMG Academy sports prep school in Bradenton.

"We've really seen movement in the ultraluxury market," he tells Realtor.com, noting that sales priced at $4 million and over are up about 80% since last year.

The broker attributes the soaring luxury market to the end of a buying funk, when people were "thinking a bit more" about investing in waterfront properties due to storms. In fall 2024, Sarasota County had just caught its breath from Hurricane Helene when it was slammed by Hurricane Milton.

But apparently those hurricane hesitations have been swept away.

"Newer construction went through the storms unscathed," says Schemmel. "All of those people who were on the fence are like, 'If I want a house in Florida, why not buy now?'"

The typical multimillion-dollar estate buyer is already familiar with the area and upgrading, says the broker. Then there are the out-of-towners—mostly from the New York-New Jersey-CT tristate area—who are discovering Sarasota for its comparable affordability.

"We have a lot more waterfront options, and our price point is in a different zone from the East Coast and Naples," he says. "The value is here."

Not every property seems like a value play—Schemmel currently represents a $38.45 million 11-bedroom, 17,200-square-foot estate on Longboat Key—but that price tag would double or triple in Naples or Palm Beach.

The threat of erosion, storms, and climate change isn't stopping the wealthy from plunking down millions on properties mere feet from the water.

"Any time I'd think there would be an exodus from those barrier islands," he says. "I'd be proven wrong."
