#5633. Wall Street Power Grab? Anti-Crypto Elizabeth Warren Could Put Day Trading in the Crosshairs

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Elizabeth Warren is preparing to take control of the Senate Banking Committee, putting one of Washington’s most outspoken financial regulators at the center of America’s next market policy battle. Her expected appointment could bring renewed scrutiny to Wall Street, crypto, and the rules governing retail day trading.

With Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress in the November 2026 midterms, Warren will have a stronger platform to investigate financial firms and challenge federal regulators. Her priorities could extend beyond traditional banking, bringing day trading platforms, market structure, and prediction markets into the congressional red-list.

JUST IN: 🇺🇸 Anti-crypto Senator Elizabeth Warren expected to become Chair of Senate Banking Committee, giving her major power over the financial industry. pic.twitter.com/t2nvMSdo1U

The Massachusetts senator has spent years arguing that financial markets need stronger protections for ordinary Americans. Now, she could have the committee authority to turn those arguments into hearings, investigations, and legislative proposals.

The connection to day trading is not simply about whether Americans can buy and sell stocks freely. It is about the market infrastructure that determines how retail orders are executed, priced, and routed.

Elizabeth Warren has already taken a position on one important part of that debate. On October 1, she joined four Democratic senators in urging SEC Chairman Paul Atkins to preserve key Regulation National Market System protections.

The lawmakers opposed proposed changes to Rules 611 and 610(e), warning that removing protections could allow retail orders to execute at worse prices. They argued that larger market participants could benefit while ordinary investors faced higher trading costs.

For day trading platforms and their customers, these rules matter. Fast-moving traders depend on competitive execution, transparent pricing and reliable access to market liquidity.

Warren’s intervention shows that retail trading infrastructure is already on her regulatory agenda. Her committee leadership could give her more opportunities to question the SEC about how brokers, exchanges and market makers handle individual investors’ orders.

This does not mean Warren has proposed restrictions on day trading itself. There is currently no confirmed proposal from her to limit how frequently retail investors can trade.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Day trading is only one potential part of Warren’s expanding financial oversight agenda. The senator has also raised concerns about prediction markets, particularly the possibility of insider trading involving contracts tied to political and economic events.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Warren intends to examine alleged insider trading in prediction markets alongside private equity, major banks and crypto companies. Meanwhile, Democrats are preparing investigations into financial relationships between the crypto industry, Trump and his family.

Warren is expected to lead the Senate Banking Committee and has pledged to examine alleged deals connecting the industry with the president.

Senator Elizabeth Warren accuses President Donald Trump of using his presidency to benefit wealthy donors and corporate allies at the expense of ordinary Americans. In a video posted on X, Warren points to corporate donations, dropped lawsuits, cryptocurrency ventures and airline… pic.twitter.com/bQ1twXJfvN

Those investigations could put companies with political and financial connections under greater pressure. They could also consume congressional attention that the crypto industry had hoped to devote to market structure legislation.

On day trading businesses, the consequences may be less direct but still important. Congressional scrutiny of retail trading protections, prediction markets, and financial intermediaries could influence how regulators approach trading platforms.

Warren’s critics may argue that additional regulation risks increasing compliance costs and limiting competition. Her supporters, meanwhile, point to investor protections and fair market access as reasons for stronger oversight.

The bigger question is how far Elizabeth Warren intends to take that agenda once she assumes the committee chairmanship. With subpoena powers, control over hearings, and a stronger legislative platform, she will have more influence over the financial industry’s relationship with federal regulators.

#5632. Home prices rise in 78% of metros while weekly demand sinks to a low

Prices climbed in 78 percent of metros in the third quarter, according to NAR, as Redfin data shows pending sales at the lowest level in its records.

Home prices rose in 78 percent of U.S. metro areas during the third quarter, while pending sales in the four weeks ending Oct. 25 fell to the lowest level in Redfin’s records.

The national median single-family existing-home price rose 1.7 percent year over year to $432,900, matching the second quarter’s revised annual growth rate, the National Association of Realtors reported Thursday. Prices rose in 78 percent of the some 235 metros NAR tracks, down from 80 percent in the second quarter, and fell in 21 percent, up from 20 percent. Four percent of metros posted double-digit gains, down from 5 percent.

“Even with affordability challenges causing the housing market to stagnate, home prices continue to set record highs in most parts of the country,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. “Homeowners are the beneficiaries of the price gains. Over the past seven years, the average house has appreciated by $146,000.”

Redfin’s data for the four weeks ending Oct. 25 shows prices dipping. The median U.S. home-sale price fell 0.1 percent year over year to $389,601, according to Redfin, following a 0.2 percent decline the prior week. The two drops are the first in more than three years.

NAR and Redfin measure different things. NAR tracks quarterly sales of existing single-family homes, while Redfin’s figures cover homes listed or sold across more than 900 metros on a rolling four-week basis.

The Northeast posted the largest annual gain, and the West was the only region where prices fell, according to NAR.

Prices declined in many Florida markets over the past year, Yun said.

“This quarter, however, homes in nearly all Florida markets are showing price gains,” he said. “In a similar vein, price declines in other markets may also be brief if the local job market and economy are solid.”

Gulfport-Biloxi-Pascagoula, Mississippi, led large markets with an 11 percent price increase, followed by Rochester, New York (10.9 percent) and Jackson, Mississippi (10.1 percent). Grand Rapids-Wyoming, Michigan; Cleveland-Elyria, Ohio; and Fort Wayne, Indiana, were among the Midwest markets in the top 10.

“Many markets in the Midwest offer exceptional value with more affordable homes, making homeownership more attainable,” Yun said. “Meanwhile, the artificial intelligence technology boom continues to push Bay Area home prices higher, keeping the region the most expensive in the country.”

San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, California, remained the most expensive market at a median of $1.92 million, up 0.3 percent. Anaheim-Santa Ana-Irvine, California ($1.47 million) and San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward, California ($1.35 million) followed. Nine of the 10 most expensive markets are in California or Hawaii.

The monthly mortgage payment on a typical existing single-family home with a 20 percent down payment was $2,251 in the third quarter, up $48 from the second quarter and $69 from a year earlier, according to NAR. Typical families spent an average of 24.1 percent of income on mortgage payments, up from 23.9 percent last quarter and down from 24.5 percent a year ago.

First-time buyers faced a monthly payment of $2,208 on a typical $368,000 starter home with 10 percent down. That payment took up 36.3 percent of income, up from 36 percent last quarter and down from 37 percent a year earlier.

Pending sales fell 1.8 percent from a week earlier and 15.9 percent year over year, declining in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metros for the third straight week, according to Redfin. Seattle (down 31.6 percent) and Atlanta (down 25.9 percent) posted the steepest annual drops.

Redfin’s median monthly mortgage payment, calculated at a 7.32 percent rate, reached $2,786, up 10.7 percent year over year and the second-highest level in its records. The weekly average rate is down from 7.4 percent a week earlier and near a three-year high.

New listings fell 0.6 percent from a week earlier to their lowest level since January. Total inventory rose 0.3 percent because pending sales fell faster than new listings, Redfin reported. The share of listings with price drops rose to 21.5 percent from 20.9 percent a year earlier.

Redfin reported hundreds of thousands more sellers than buyers nationwide, giving buyers more negotiating power than they have had in more than a decade.

A First American analysis found that since 1991, rising mortgage rates have coincided with falling national home prices in some cases. In eight periods of sustained mortgage-rate increases since 1993, national home prices generally continued to appreciate, though the pace varied, First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming found.

During the rate run-up from December 2021 through October 2023, national prices rose an estimated 14 percent, according to the analysis. Affordability worsened at a steeper rate than prices, Fleming found. First American’s Real House Price Index, which adjusts prices for changes in income and mortgage rates, rose more than 70 percent over the same period.

Limited inventory can offset weaker demand when rates rise, Fleming wrote. Homeowners with mortgages below current rates may hold off on selling, and some sellers pull homes from the market rather than accept lower prices.

“Higher mortgage rates can put pressure on home prices, but the economy, household incomes and the number of homes for sale all play a role in what happens next,” Fleming wrote.

#5631. Significant Pent-Up Demand Could Be Released If Supply, Affordability and Confidence Improve

A wave of sidelined homebuyers could be poised to flood the housing market if a trifecta of housing supply and affordability improve and consumer confidence picks up. How likely that is remains unclear, however.

That was the theme of a market outlook delivered this past Friday by National Association of Realtors® Chief Economist Lawrence Yun at the Residential Economic Issues and Trends Forum at NAR NXT in New Orleans.

According to a release, Yun compared today’s economy with the year 2000, noting since then, the U.S. population has grown from 281 million to 350 million, and payroll jobs have risen from 132 million to 159 million. He said housing wealth has grown from $7 trillion to $35 trillion, yet existing-home sales are running near 4 million this year, below the 5.2 million homes sold in 2000.

“Affordability is tough, but people’s incomes are rising, and if somehow mortgage rates go down, think about the potential housing demand that could be released to the marketplace,” Yun said.

On supply, Yun noted that inventory has risen as sales have slowed. Months’ supply is at its highest level since 2015, and the median home took 33 days to go from listing to contract in September.

“Homes are staying on the market a little longer than before,” Yun said. “With longer days on market, you have to be realistic to the market condition. Otherwise, buyers will reject the homes on the market.”

Yun said a rebound in consumer confidence would also be key. Consumer sentiment has fallen to roughly half its 2000 level and is now worse than during the Great Recession, even as the economy has added jobs, he said.

“If we can boost confidence levels, maybe that can also change the dynamics,” Yun said.

Jessica Lautz, NAR deputy chief economist and vice president of research, presented highlights from the newly released 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. First-time buyers made up 22% of all buyers, near the historic low, and the median age of first-time buyers held at a record-high 40.

“First-time home buyers are struggling,” Lautz said. “They’re not struggling just with housing affordability. They’re also struggling with rent. They’re struggling with student loan debt, and a rising issue for first-time home buyers is childcare costs.”

Sellers stayed in their homes for a median of 12 years before selling, the longest on record.

“The golden handcuffs of low interest rate mortgages is true. People are holding on to those properties for longer periods of time,” said Lautz. “It’s why we need to build more housing inventory—especially affordable housing inventory—for the potential first-time home buyers who are out there.”

Use of real estate professionals remained strong: 90% of buyers purchased through an agent, the highest share in four decades, and a record 92% of sellers used an agent.

“Sellers want agents to price that home competitively, find that qualified buyer, help with marketing, and make sure they get to the closing table in a time frame that they need to do so,” Lautz said.

Routine maintenance, sensible storage, suitable flood protection and a clear emergency plan can help homeowners prepare more effectively. The right approach depends on the property, its surroundings and the conditions it may face. Read more.

#5630. AWS commits $100M in AI and cloud credits to health groups in underserved communities

Amazon Web Services Inc. today committed $100 million worth of artificial intelligence and cloud technology over five years to health organizations working in underserved communities around the world, provided to recipients as AWS credits.

The new AWS Health Impact Initiative is taking aim at a cost problem that AWS says is keeping many of those organizations out of the current wave of AI adoption. AWS points to survey data to explain the focus on credits.

An independent survey of 83 of the more than 400 organizations supported under the company’s earlier AWS Health Equity Initiative found that 60% saw cost as the main barrier to cloud adoption where they operate. Most ranked AWS credits as their highest-priority need. That program began in 2021 with $40 million behind it, and the total had grown to $60 million by the time the last of it was handed out in July 2024.

Timing matters too. A World Economic Forum forecast cited by AWS has generative AI use climbing faster in health care than in any other field. If the organizations closest to underserved patients fall behind on adopting it, AWS argues, health gaps will widen.

Agents and AI are reshaping health services, said Dr. Rowland Illing, chief medical officer and director of health care and life sciences at AWS, and they “too often don’t reach the communities that need them most.” Illing framed the initiative as an extension of the company’s stated aim of democratizing AI and cloud-based health technology.

Any area of health care is eligible, and AWS has singled out three for added weight. The first is access to health services, where AWS wants to support diagnostic testing and stronger health infrastructure in places such as rural areas and low- and middle-income countries.

A second area covers research into women’s and children’s health, with better data and more inclusive studies as the goal. Women’s health draws just 5% of health research funding, the company said, and as many as half the medicines given to children lack pediatric clinical validation.

Healthy food is the third area. AWS said malnutrition among pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers and adolescent girls has climbed 25% since 2020 in the 12 countries hit hardest by the global food and nutrition crisis. Projects there could improve food distribution or predict food security patterns.

Recipients AWS highlighted include women’s health data nonprofit Eve’s Ark, which collects research datasets that are at risk of disappearing when a lab closes or a grant ends. Co-founder and Chief Executive Melissa Antal Iftimie said the group started with a small AWS award and “a single at-risk dataset.” The archive now holds more than a petabyte of women’s health data on AWS, and the group is building a secure research environment where scientists can work with it.

In Haiti, primary care provider Care 2 Communities runs a network of community clinics that has served 350,000 people and handles almost 120,000 patient visits a year. Its electronic medical records sit on AWS, which brings centralized, real-time data to clinics in rural parts of the country. School meals for more than 2.35 million children in India come out of kitchens run by the Akshaya Patra Foundation every school day, and the foundation uses AWS to run those kitchens and get meals out to schools.

Eligibility runs well past health charities to government agencies, research institutions and companies, and AWS will consider a project at any stage up to full production.

Organizations with an AWS account team can submit proposals through it, and a public portal is open to everyone else. Each application has to estimate how many lives the project will improve, and AWS goes through submissions every week. Successful applicants receive credits sized to their own AWS Pricing Calculator estimate of what a project needs, or a starting allocation of up to $10,000. Awardees have 12 months to use the credits and can ask to have that window stretched to 24.

#5629. David Muir Shares Rare Look at Personal Life Ahead of His Birthday—Inside His $7 Million Lakeside Estate in Upstate New York

When it comes to his personal life, famed journalist David Muir tends to keep quiet, but the “World News Tonight” anchor recently pulled back the curtain just before his 53rd birthday.

In a Nov. 7 Instagram post, the ABC News anchor shared a wholesome update—a snap of his German short-haired pointer, Axel, as the pair set out to enjoy the fall foliage.

Although Muir let the photo speak for itself—offering nothing more than an autumnal leaf emoji as the caption—he occasionally uploads content of Axel, usually to show off their outdoor adventures.

In a 2025 interview with People magazine, the broadcaster shared some rare insight into his home life, noting that while he’s based in Manhattan for work, he enjoys retreating to a spot just outside his hometown of Syracuse.

“I’d say my most comfortable element is being outside, covered in mud,” he told the publication, adding that he had recently taken a trip to his property in upstate New York, enjoying the surroundings despite the fact that it had been “pouring rain.”

In 2019, Muir purchased a $7 million property on Skaneateles Lake—a small town about a 30-minute drive from Syracuse.

“This job takes me all over the world, and I can’t think of a better place to catch my breath,” he told Syracuse.com at the time.

The 4,300-square-foot abode is a single-family home set on a 6-acre plot of land with water access. The six-bedroom, 2.5-bathroom dwelling was built in 1890 and seems to be the perfect place to escape from the bustle of the city—or a job as demanding as Muir’s.

“When you’re out there on the lake, smelling the same air that you smelled when you were on your BMX bike back when you were a kid, there’s something really fueling about that and connected about it,” he told People magazine in 2025. “You just feel like you’re home again.”

Over the years, Muir has invited his Instagram followers to enjoy the dazzling lake views he enjoys during his weekends away.

In a 2020 post, he remarked, “I love being home,” in a caption of a photo of himself cracking a smile while enjoying a boat ride across the lake.

A few distinct features of Muir’s historic home have taken up real estate on his Instagram profile, as well, including the charming wraparound porch that hugs the Skaneateles Lake property, which made an appearance in a 2022 post he shared for his sister’s birthday, where he made a note to give a shoutout to “porches.”

He purchased the 2,280-square-foot abode for $4.2 million in 2013, the same year he became the host of “World News Tonight,” following in Diane Sawyer’s footsteps.

Located on West Fourth Street, the three-bedroom, three-bathroom structure was built in 1877 by Alexander M. McKean, and Muir put it on the market for $7.5 million in April 2025.

“Inside, the original details of this 15 foot wide house have been lovingly restored,” the listing explained. “The renovation maintains and respects the character of this remarkable home, while bringing it completely up-to-date, upgrading electricity, plumbing, and gas service but keeping and restoring original details including hardware, flooring, fixtures, and historic plaster medallions and moldings throughout.”

Perhaps the most stunning feature of the townhouse was the primary bedroom, which spanned the entire fourth level of the building. With a bed area that faced over quiet gardens and a full wall of closets, the suite also included a spacious office and a windowed bathroom with a vintage claw-foot tub.

The home lingered on the market for a few weeks before it was removed and relisted, but nearly six months later, it was sold for $6.85 million.

#5628. How Kyle Whissel built eXp’s top real estate team

The San Diego-based CEO recruits up to 15 agents a month, has a dress code and gives his trainer authority to cut newcomers.

Kyle Whissel has a standing instruction for his “60-day” bootcamp trainers: they should be willing to cut people.

His team brings in 10 to 15 new agents a month, puts them through approximately 60 hours of training over two weeks, and gives the trainer a goal of removing two people from each class.

It’s a striking approach from the leader of eXp Realty’s highest-volume U.S. team in San Diego, California. Whissel is CEO of the Whissel Beer Group, formed in 2025 when his Whissel Realty Group merged with Daniel Beer’s Beer Home Team.

According to Whissel, the team made $875 million in sales volume across 1,042 transaction sides last year (it was the first team in San Diego to break 1,000). The median price in San Diego — which is where he likes to focus his attention  (“we love that median price,” he said) — is around $1 million, he told Inman.

They’ve done that by hiring — and retaining — the right people. “We’ll give people an opportunity to prove themselves … but we’ve grown far more by cutting people than simply by hiring more people,” Whissel told Inman‘s Taylor Anderson during an interview at eXpcon in Salt Lake City earlier this month.

The company’s saying: “Expectations without enforcement are simply suggestions.”

Whissel’s recruiting process starts with a conventional, short interview, but he views the company’s two-week training period as a far better measure of whether someone belongs on the team.

Spending 60 hours in training gives leadership a chance to observe how that person behaves, learns and responds to expectations. Role-playing and scripting exercises also reveal whether new agents have the communication skills needed to work with clients.

The process continues after training, too. New agents are assigned mentors, and Whissel said those mentors are empowered to recommend removing someone who fails to meet team standards.

“If you’re going to be disrespectful to our team, I’ll be damned if I’m going to give you a client because you’re probably going to be disrespectful to them too,” he said.

Whissel also has activity and production expectations for agents already on the team. They include participating in role-playing sessions and attending meetings, along with meeting production targets.

Whissel’s hiring philosophy reaches back to his own first job, scooping popcorn at a movie theater, where he would compete with others to see who could serve the most customers. He looks for that same competitiveness in prospective agents, even if their previous accomplishments have little to do with real estate.

An applicant who participated in a college sorority, for example, might be asked whether they held a leadership position. Whissel said he wants to understand whether someone has a history of taking initiative.

In August 2025, Inman reported the merger of Whissel Realty Group and Beer Home Team, two of eXp’s highest-producing organizations. The combined company launched with approximately 160 agents and more than 60 staff members across five offices.

He said the first six months involved understanding the two organizations’ systems and getting them aligned. Whissel now believes it could take 18 months to fully integrate the companies.

“We’re going to be almost flat year-over-year,” he said, referring to the team’s expected 2026 performance, “but we’re setting up for a really, really big 2027,” he said. “You’ve gotta take a step back to take two steps forward.”

He remains optimistic about 2027, when he expects the operational investments to begin contributing to stronger growth.

Agents need to understand assumable mortgages, he said. “If you are working with a seller … and you’re not asking questions to figure out ‘does this seller have an assumable mortgage?’ (If it’s FHA, VA or USDA, those are assumable), I’m gonna beat you, because I am asking those questions.”

To find out whether a mortgage is assumable, agents simply need to get the closing disclosure from the seller. “It’s simple,” he said.

#5627. Casino Mogul Steve Wynn Sells His $70 Million Central Park Condo as Manhattan Luxury Market Heats Up

Casino billionaire Steve Wynn has finally unloaded his Central Park duplex penthouse, making it the top luxury sale of a record-breaking week in Manhattan.

The mogul's prewar condo at 50 Central Park South—first listed in 2022 for $90 million, the most expensive in the country at the time—eventually saw its price drop to $70 million.

Even at this steep discount, it still took two years for the condo to find a taker. The duplex went into contract last week with Serena Boardman of Sotheby's International Realty as the listing agent (co-exclusive with Deborah Grubman of Corcoran).

The sale means the casino magnate failed to turn a profit on the 10,875-square-foot condo. But given that, according to Forbes, Wynn is worth $4.3 billion, he likely isn't sweating it too much.

The Billionaires Row duplex takes up the 30th and 31st floors within the 36-story Ritz-Carlton Residences, formerly the Hotel St. Moritz, which opened in 1930. The top 12 floors are the private homes.

The penthouse, formerly owned by real estate developer Christopher M. Jeffries, comes with an esteemed pedigree.

It was Jeffries' Millennium Partners that purchased the Emory Roth–designed building in 1999 and reimagined it along with the Ritz-Carlton Hotel Co. Jeffries was once married to Princess Yasmin Aga Khan, the only child of Prince Aly Khan and movie legend Rita Hayworth.

Yet the real selling point of the duplex is its sweeping Central Park views. With floors that aren't too high, from the vantage of the 45-foot long terrace, it feels as if one is sitting in the famed park's trees—a "bird's-eye perspective," as the listing puts it. Another terrace along the western wall stretches 28 feet.

With three bedrooms, four full baths, and two half-baths, the prewar unit features 10 grandly arched windows, a marble staircase, 15-foot coffered ceilings, and a living room that used to be the St. Moritz ballroom.

Modern touches include a chef's kitchen; a breakfast room with its own terrace; a primary bedroom with Central Park views, en suite bathroom, gym, and dressing room; a staff room with laundry; and a library.

As the condo sits atop the flagship Ritz-Carlton hotel, it comes with access to the amenities of the global luxury name, including the La Prairie spa and health club, a business center, the Contour Bar and Lounge, in-room dining services, and housekeeping services.

The unit has $31,362 in monthly dues on top of $15,500 in taxes.

As for why a property offering such grandeur may have taken so long to move, luxury broker Michael Reisor with Compass-affiliated Reisor.Team, who is familiar with the building, says, "Properties like this are wonderful but specific. There's a more limited buyer pool."

Despite the park views and architectural significance, it's still a century-old building, and buyers at this price range have their pick.

However, "when buyers at this level want prewar charm and detail, there is only one way to get it authentically, and that is to buy of that era," he says. "Are there people in droves wanting to pay at this level for prewar? No, but there are people who do. It's usually a more sophisticated buyer.

"They want that, 'This is classic New York.'"

The final price isn't yet known, but Reisor says, "We can assume it was right around [the ask price], if not right on."

The buyer hasn't been revealed, and listing agent Boardman did not return a call for comment.

One unique aspect of the 50 Central Park prewar is that it is a condo, not a co-op. Prewar buildings—built between the late 1880s and 1939—are typically co-ops.

In general, condos outsell co-ops each week—and after two weeks of the gap between them being slim, for the week ending Nov. 8, condos were far ahead, 34 contracts versus 7. Co-ops tend to be cheaper, with an average ask of $8.6 million last week versus $10.5 million for condos, according to Olshan Realty.

Another unusual feature of the sprawling duplex is that it has only three bedrooms. Often condos at this scale have expanded to four or more. Last week's top sale, a $31 million penthouse condo at 111 Murray St. in Tribeca, had five bedrooms.

"It's more of a psychological sticking point than an actual need," Reisor says of a high-end buyer's desire for plentiful bedrooms. "They think, 'At a certain price, I should be overflowing with bedrooms.' Even if they never need them."

Whoever snapped up the trophy unit likely wanted to be in that particular building, which is low-density, has only 11 private residences inside of a global luxury brand, and comes with a glamorous history and illustrious architect.

"It could be someone high-profile," Reisor speculates of the mystery buyer. "Someone high-profile would want something like this."

The Wynn sale was one of a slew of high-end contracts last week, with 45 signed, a big leap of 11 over the week before, and the biggest luxury sales week for the entire year. Of that, an astonishing 14 sales were priced over $10 million.

The New York City pied-à-terre tax doesn't seem to be squeezing the top end of the market. Reisor says last week's surge of luxury (over $4 million) buys can be attributed to the midterm elections.

"We always see a freeze-up before elections," he says. "The enemy to any financial market, including the housing market, is uncertainty. The biggest thing in play is that the election happened; it's over."

Additionally, he thinks that the "blue wave" was a positive for the high-end market, speculating that President Donald Trump's somewhat chastened stance on immigration is good news for monied buyers.

"This is especially relevant to New York City because of international buyers," he says, theorizing that affluent foreign buyers are wondering, "Will this be more friendly to me as an international purchaser?"

The second-highest contract of the week was a triplex penthouse with an asking price of $25.36 million. The condo, EA at 95 Madison Ave., is also in a 1912 prewar building. Although smaller at 8,355 square feet, the condo came with six bedrooms.

Formerly the Emmet Building, the Flatiron building is a quick stroll to Madison Square Park. Its Gothic facade is made from limestone and marble, reflecting the "architectural Golden Age," says the listing, which was held by Vicki Zhi Saali of Global Real Estate Ventures Group.

#5626. 12 housing bills that could shape affordability after the midterms

Concerns over housing supply and affordability have reached a fever pitch and become a major issue for voters in this year’s midterms.

With the midterm elections just days away, housing affordability remains a pressing issue for voters — and a growing legislative priority for lawmakers in Washington.

Congress has spent much of the past two years considering proposals aimed at lowering housing costs, helping first-time buyers, unlocking existing inventory and encouraging new construction. But despite growing bipartisan interest in housing policy, many of those proposals remain stalled in committee as voters prepare to decide which party will control Congress.

Lawmakers scored a significant bipartisan victory in July with the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a sweeping package aimed at boosting housing supply and addressing barriers to development. Yet much of the broader housing agenda remains unfinished, including proposals to expand homebuyer assistance, increase affordable housing investment and raise the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Some bills have continued attracting additional congressional support in recent weeks, but none of the proposals highlighted in September has advanced since. With both chambers largely out of session until after Election Day on Nov. 3, further legislative action will likely have to wait until lawmakers return to Washington.

Inman revisited the most consequential housing bills that could help shape the federal government’s approach to supply, affordability and homeownership in the next Congress.

What it does: The bipartisan legislation would double the capital gains exclusion on the sale of a primary residence, from $250,000 to $500,000 for individuals and from $500,000 to $1 million for married couples, and automatically adjust those limits over time to account for inflation. Why it matters: Supporters argue that the limits, which have remained unchanged since 1997, discourage longtime owners with substantial equity from selling and effectively lock inventory off the market. NAR has made the proposal a major 2026 priority and is currently framing it as one of the fastest ways to increase existing-home supply. Status: The House version remains before Ways and Means and the Senate bill before Finance, and neither has advanced beyond referral. Support has continued growing, however, with 159 House cosponsors and 25 Senate cosponsors as of late October, including lawmakers from both parties. With Congress largely out of session until after the election, inclusion in a broader tax package during the lame-duck session or next Congress remains one possible path forward.

What it does: This legislation would establish a refundable federal tax credit equal to 10 percent of a first home’s purchase price, capped at $15,000. Eligibility and the size of the credit would be subject to income and local home-price limits.

Why it matters: Unlike proposals intended to increase supply over time, the bill would directly reduce the cost of purchasing a first home for qualifying households. The tradeoff is that giving buyers more purchasing power does not add more homes to the market, and in a supply-constrained market, it can also put upward pressure on prices.

Status: Both versions were introduced in July 2025 and remain before the House Ways and Means and Senate Finance committees, respectively. Neither chamber has taken action beyond committee referral.

What it does: Introduced by Rep. Maxine Waters, D-Calif., the bill would increase the mandatory share of Federal Home Loan Bank earnings devoted to the system’s Affordable Housing Program. The Consumer Federation of America estimates the change would generate roughly $300 million in additional annual funding for affordable housing development, down payment assistance and home repair programs, without requiring additional taxpayer funding.

Why it matters: The 11 Federal Home Loan Banks provide liquidity to more than 6,500 member institutions, including banks, credit unions and community development financial institutions. Housing advocates have argued that the system should devote more of its earnings to its public mission. In a broader reform proposal, the Coalition for Federal Home Loan Bank Reform has called for doubling the mandatory Affordable Housing Program contribution from 10 percent to 20 percent, which it estimates would add about $600 million annually for affordable housing.

Status: The House Financial Services Committee considered H.R. 10325 on Sept. 16, but a motion to report the amended bill favorably failed 21–28. That leaves the measure facing a significant setback in the House, even as housing and consumer groups continue pushing for broader FHLBank reform.

What it does: Designed to make it easier to pull together a down payment, this bill would raise the amount first-time buyers can withdraw from an IRA without paying the usual 10 percent early-withdrawal penalty from $10,000 to $50,000.

Why it matters: The proposal targets a major barrier for many prospective first-time buyers: saving enough cash for a home’s down payment and covering closing costs. It would expand access to buyers’ existing retirement savings rather than create a new federal subsidy. NAR lists the bill among its current legislative priorities.

Status: The House version remains before Ways and Means, while the Senate companion, introduced by Sens. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., and Todd Young, R-Ind., is before Finance. Neither has advanced beyond committee, though the Senate bill’s bipartisan sponsorship distinguishes it from some other first-time buyer proposals.

What it does: Seeking to make homebuilding and rehabilitation more feasible in distressed neighborhoods, this legislation would create a federal tax credit to support the construction and rehabilitation of owner-occupied homes where development costs exceed what finished properties can command on the market. The credit is designed to help close that gap and make projects financially viable.

Why it matters: The credit is intended to make starter-home projects possible in communities where builders currently cannot make the numbers work, with a particular focus on for-sale housing rather than rental development.

Status: The House bill remains before Ways and Means and the Senate version before Finance. In May, the bipartisan sponsors released planned revisions, including more flexibility for state housing finance agencies and a shorter four-year authorization, that they intend to carry into the next version of the bill, whether in a year-end package or the next Congress.

What it does: This proposal would establish a federal investment tax credit covering 20 percent of qualifying costs to convert nonresidential buildings into housing, increasing to 30 percent in certain areas where development is particularly challenging. At least 20 percent of the resulting units would need to remain affordable to households earning no more than 80 percent of area median income for 30 years.

Why it matters: The bill targets two persistent real estate problems at once — underutilized commercial buildings and the shortage of housing. Office-to-residential conversions have attracted substantial interest, but challenging layouts, financing hurdles and construction costs can make projects difficult to pencil out. A tax credit is intended to help close that feasibility gap. NAR also lists this bill among its 2026 legislative priorities.

Status: Introduced in March 2025, the bipartisan bill has attracted 57 cosponsors, including lawmakers from both parties, but remains before the House Ways and Means Committee without advancing beyond referral.

What it does: Focused on expanding and modernizing the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, the proposal includes a broad series of changes involving tenant eligibility, project financing and credit administration.

Why it matters: LIHTC is a central federal financing tool that helps drive the construction of affordable rental housing across the country. Congress already adopted two pieces of the broader proposal in 2025, permanently increasing annual Housing Credit authority by 12 percent and lowering the bond-financing threshold from 50 percent to 25 percent. According to the National Council of State Housing Agencies, roughly two dozen other provisions remain unenacted.

Status: The House bill remains before Ways and Means and the Senate version before Finance, with both measures drawing broad bipartisan support. Advocates continue pushing the remaining provisions either through the standalone bills or as part of future tax legislation.

What it does: The bill would update federal rules for mortgage revenue bonds and mortgage credit certificates used by state housing finance agencies, including increasing limits on certain home improvement loans and changing refinancing and recapture provisions.

Why it matters: Those programs can help lower- and moderate-income households access lower-cost mortgage financing, giving this technical tax legislation a direct connection to homeownership affordability.

Status: The House version, introduced in February 2026, remains before Ways and Means, while the Senate bill remains before Finance. The Senate measure was discussed during an Oct. 21, 2025, Senate Banking housing subcommittee hearing, but neither version has advanced beyond committee.

What it does: Seeking to open underused land owned by churches and other religious organizations to new housing development, this bill would preempt certain state and local laws that block affordable housing on those properties.

Why it matters: Religious institutions collectively control substantial amounts of land, including parcels in expensive housing markets where zoning can constrain redevelopment. The bill is notable because it tackles supply by asserting federal authority over certain local land-use restrictions, rather than relying primarily on grants or tax incentives.

Status: Introduced by Reps. Scott Peters, D-Calif., and Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., in September 2025, the bipartisan legislation remains before the House Financial Services Committee. Rep. Emilia Strong Sykes, D-Ohio, joined as a cosponsor in October, but the bill has not advanced beyond committee referral.

What it does: This measure would amend the Fair Housing Act to prohibit discrimination based on a person’s source of income, veteran status or military status.

Why it matters: The change would expand federal fair-housing protections for veterans, service members and renters who rely on housing vouchers or other lawful sources of income. It could also create new federal compliance obligations for landlords, property managers and real estate professionals.

Status: Both versions remain in committee, with the House bill before Judiciary and the Senate measure before Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs. The House proposal has continued attracting support, reaching 23 cosponsors following the addition of Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, on Oct. 22. Neither chamber has advanced the legislation beyond referral.

What it does: Rather than establishing a tax credit or housing-production program, the Saving the American Dream Act would require HUD, Treasury, Agriculture, Veterans Affairs and the Federal Housing Finance Agency to coordinate housing research and market data and submit a joint report to Congress identifying opportunities to improve housing affordability.

Why it matters: Federal housing policy is currently divided among HUD, Treasury and other agencies. Supporters of the effort argue that greater coordination could reduce conflicting policies and give Washington a more coherent strategy for addressing affordability.

Status: Introduced in September 2025, the bipartisan bill remains before the House Financial Services Committee and the Veterans’ Affairs Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity. It has attracted 40 cosponsors, including two who joined on Oct. 1, but has not advanced beyond committee referral.

What it does: Introduced by Rep. Norma Torres, D-Calif., on Oct. 22, the legislation would establish a new HUD grant program to help states streamline financing and administrative processes for affordable housing development. The proposal would authorize $90 million annually from fiscal 2027 through 2029, including funding to consolidate state financing programs, simplify applications for builders and improve access to development assistance.

Why it matters: Affordable housing developers often navigate multiple state agencies, financing programs and administrative requirements to move projects forward. By simplifying those processes, the proposal aims to reduce administrative barriers that can delay projects and increase development costs. States that meet the bill’s initial requirements could also use funding to streamline zoning, permitting and Low-Income Housing Tax Credit administration.

Status: Torres introduced the bill without cosponsors on Oct. 22, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee. It has not advanced beyond committee referral.

NAR’s current legislative agenda is centered heavily on housing supply, with the trade group estimating the country is short 4.7 million homes. Following the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July, NAR has continued pressing lawmakers on housing supply, with its latest advocacy materials putting particular emphasis on unlocking existing inventory through the More Homes on the Market Act and proposed changes to the capital gains exclusion for longtime homeowners.

The organization is also pushing lawmakers to fully fund several HUD programs, including fair housing enforcement and housing counseling services, while calling for long-term reauthorization of the National Flood Insurance Program. NAR says the flood program supports roughly 500,000 home sales each year and argues that lapses or uncertainty around coverage can disrupt transactions in flood-prone communities.

The flood insurance program’s current authorization expires Dec. 11, the same day a temporary spending measure funding federal agencies, including HUD, is set to expire. The deadlines leave Congress facing another round of funding and insurance negotiations during its post-election lame-duck session.

Passage of ROAD has not ended NAR’s work on the legislation itself. Many of the law’s new grants and housing programs still depend on future congressional appropriations and HUD rulemaking, including incentives for local housing production, zoning and permitting reforms, commercial-to-residential conversions and home-repair programs. NAR is now encouraging states and local governments to prepare for those programs, while pressing Congress to provide the funding needed to put them into effect.

Implementation of the law is also underway. On Oct. 22, the Treasury Department proposed regulations clarifying restrictions on large institutional investors purchasing single-family homes. Under the law, beginning Jan. 7, 2027, investors controlling at least 350 single-family homes will generally be prohibited from purchasing additional properties, subject to exceptions for activities including build-to-rent and renovate-to-rent programs.

For qualifying programs designed to help renters become homeowners, the proposal also establishes a framework for a 30-day first-look period and a right of first refusal before investors sell the properties to other buyers.

Reporter’s note: This story was originally published on Sept. 24, 2026, and has been updated to reflect the latest available information.

Additional note: AI tools were utilized in reviewing and verifying current federal housing bills, legislative priorities and related reporting for this story. All substantive details were checked against congressional records, primary-source materials and prior reporting before publication.

#5625. Diagrid’s Dapr 1.19 lightens AI agent workflows and drops a control-plane service

Agent infrastructure startup Diagrid Inc. today released Dapr 1.19 with changes that cut the overhead of the durable workflows behind long-running artificial intelligence agents.

Operators of the open-source runtime can also drop one of its control-plane services. Until 1.19, Dapr’s workflow engine shipped the entire execution history to the worker on every step.

Each one adds to that history. On a job that runs for hours or fans out into dozens of parallel tasks, the payload keeps growing, and Diagrid said that pushed up latency and memory use. Now a worker keeps what it already holds and gets only new events.

That makes the data sent per step independent of how long a workflow has been running. Workers still replay the full history locally. The smaller transfers go only to workers that advertise support for them, which in 1.19 means those built on Dapr’s Java and Python software development kits.

Mark Fussell, Diagrid’s co-founder and chief product officer, said an agent “that runs all afternoon and splits into 50 tasks can’t haul its entire history across the network on every step.”

A second workflow change, an opt-in preview feature called WorkflowsFastPath, stops pushing every workflow event through a durable scheduler reminder. Wake-ups and local activities are handled in place. The reminder path stays as a backstop for recovery, and in Diagrid’s engine benchmarks median step latency fell from 553 milliseconds to 153 milliseconds with the feature on.

Two services have made up Dapr’s control plane until now, and a new mode in 1.19 retires Placement, which distributes the actor placement table. The surviving Scheduler service handles jobs, reminders and workflow scheduling, and it already tracks cluster membership and pushes state to sidecars the same way Placement does.

Yaron Schneider, a co-creator of Dapr who is also Diagrid’s co-founder and chief technology officer, said the pair “matured as two services doing overlapping work.” With the mode on, the Scheduler takes over actor placement and the standalone Placement service is no longer deployed. That spares operators a stateful service and the Raft consensus cluster behind it. Reminders get faster too, because the Scheduler knows which sidecar owns each actor.

Scaling events are also less disruptive. A host joining or leaving used to pause placement across the entire namespace while Dapr re-sent its placement table. In the new mode, only the affected actor types are locked and updated, and the rest keep serving traffic.

New alpha building blocks in 1.19 are aimed at developers of AI applications. A Vector building block offers a portable application programming interface for storing and querying embeddings through similarity search, with Meilisearch as its first supported component.

Binary Store streams large files such as model outputs in chunks so they never have to sit in memory whole. Its first components cover Amazon S3 and the object stores from Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle.

Developers working in .NET get Actors.Next, a new actor SDK that generates proxies and registration code at compile time, which cuts runtime overhead and lets actor apps compile with Native AOT.

Dapr 1.19 is available now. WorkflowsFastPath ships turned off, and the Scheduler placement mode is enabled through a Helm setting once every sidecar runs 1.19, with no sidecar restart needed to switch it on or off. Teams running Dapr on Kubernetes can manage the upgrade through Diagrid’s Dapr Ops Dashboard, and the company said the tool typically supports new releases within 24 hours.

#5624. Joanna Gaines Says an ‘Upset’ Buyer Lost Interest in Magnolia’s $7 Million Mansion Renovation Because She Preferred the ‘Before’ Photos

Joanna Gaines has had a successful career, thanks to her signature design aesthetic, but a recent real estate snafu served as a brutal reminder that not everyone has the same taste.

During an appearance on Kylie Kelce’s podcast, “Not Gonna Lie,” the “Fixer Upper” star revealed that her most involved renovation yet lost a buyer who much preferred the “before” photos.

Joanna and her husband, Chip Gaines, recently tackled the transformation of a 15,000-square-foot mansion in their hometown of Waco, TX. The process was documented in the upcoming Magnolia Network show “Fixer Upper: Chip Bought a Mansion,” and it appears the project was quite the struggle.

While the Gaineses are a solid team, Chip actually purchased the sprawling estate without Joanna, a decision she called a “bold move.” Although the mom of five vouched the property would “never be a fixer,” she changed her mind after the property lingered on the market without much interest for more than three years.

The 1990s-built palace is in an incredible location, set on a 5.7-acre lot boasting striking views of Lake Waco. But the outdated ‘90s interiors needed a serious face-lift, and when Chip and Joanna set out to work their magic on the abode, they realized it needed more work than they had anticipated.

The process was grueling, but to add insult to injury, an interaction with an interested buyer made it seem like it was all for nothing.

“If you look online, the pictures you see is of the ‘before,’” Joanna said. The listing, held by Amanda Nesbitt of Magnolia Realty, keeps the “after” images a secret to avoid spoiling the show.

In a twist of fate, the prospective buyer had fallen in love with the outdated photos in the listing and was disappointed to learn that Chip and Joanna had stripped the home of its former McMansion glory.

Joanna recalled that on “the day of the reveal,” the real estate agents called to let the Gaineses know that a “qualified buyer” had “fallen in love” with the estate and wanted to put an offer in. The HGTV personality offered to give the buyer a walk through the home to chat about the changes they had made, only to realize that the renovation was a deal breaker.

“She said, ‘Well, what did they do?’ She was like, ‘I liked the pictures that I saw,’” Joanna said.

Unfortunately, it wasn’t enough to retain the buyer, who decided not to come for the viewing at all.

“The lady was so upset,” Joanna recalled. “She was like, ‘I don’t understand why she removed all the red and gold.’”

“It’s like, Chip was right,” she continued. “He could have sold this thing as is. We didn’t have to touch it. I’m like, ‘This is a joke.' I finally did it. I revealed it, and now we have a buyer and she’s upset that I fixed it up.”

The six-bedroom, 11-bathroom mansion is still on the market, asking $7.39 million. Although the new furnishings are still under wraps, viewers can get a look when the series premieres on Dec. 27 on Magnolia Network and HGTV.

The missed opportunity wasn’t the only revelation Joanna shared on the podcast episode. She also divulged that lately, she and Chip have been discussing expanding the family.

“When I had Crew at 40, I said, ‘Chip, I want him to have more siblings,’” she said. “I really thought I’d have nine children. I’m that lady. Look at my hair. Don’t I look like a lady that would have nine kids? And he was not open to it. Guess who’s open to it now? At 48?”

Joanna went on to share that her husband is “telling everyone” that she’s pregnant, even though she is not. From their adult children to a crowd of 2,000 people at a recent speaking engagement, Chip has continued to share the false news in an attempt to “speak it out into the universe.”

“So that whole audience thinks I’m pregnant. I don’t know what’s happening, but I’m not,” she confirmed.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5623. Open Real Estate: We’re almost there, but not quite

OPINION: The Open Real Estate options give sellers just two choices: market or participant view. Darryl Davis makes the case for a third door.

Picture a homeowner at the kitchen table. She likes you. She trusts you. And she says something agents hear every week: “I want you to sell my house. Just you. I don’t want a parade of strangers walking through my bedroom with agents I have never met. But I don’t want to hide it either. Advertise it. Get the word out. I want the best price.”

That is not a strange request. Some homeowners would happily give up a few dollars on the sale price for less stress, more convenience, and the peace of working with one agent and one office. And right now, the newest system in real estate has no way to say yes to it.

On October 26, Keller Williams, AGNT (the parent of eXp and NextHome), HomeServices of America and Real REMAX Group launched Open Real Estate (ORE). Four competitors came together to stop listings from disappearing into company silos. They deserve real credit. But read the FAQ, and you will see the system gives a seller only two doors.

Now go back to our homeowner. Door one sends strangers through her bedroom. Door two gives her one agent but forbids anyone to advertise her house, the last thing she asked for. She wants one agent and full marketing. ORE makes her pick one.

That is not seller choice. That is a choice between two things she did not ask for.

Here is the option that is missing, and it is simple.

I can already hear the objection. “Darryl, isn’t this just a pocket listing with a nicer name?”

No. A pocket listing is hidden. A Coming Soon tease builds buzz while keeping other agents out, and nobody, not even the listing agent, can show it. The true exclusive is the opposite of both. The house is actively marketed to the public, and every member company knows it is available. The only thing exclusive is who walks through her front door.

Think of a restaurant that only takes reservations. Everybody sees the menu and knows where it is. You call first, and the owner decides who gets a table. Nobody calls that a secret restaurant.

Let’s say it out loud. In a true exclusive, the listing agent may well sell the house to their own buyer and get paid on both sides. For some sellers, that is exactly why they choose it. They understand that one cook in the kitchen managing the whole process beats two, especially when the second one is an untrained buyer’s agent.

ORE already has what it needs to offer this, and technology can make the fiduciary piece stronger than ever.

CCP had the right intentions. NAR wanted to stop listings from disappearing. But it was the wrong strategy, and it did the opposite. Once a listing is publicly marketed, it must go into the MLS within one business day.

Keep it quiet, though, and it falls under the office exclusive exemption. That does not tell agents to share. It tells them to stop advertising and keep the listing inside their own company. The brokerage itself became the pocket.

A rule meant to bring listings into the open pushed many further underground. As I wrote earlier this year, a Redfin analysis found pocket listings rose 67 percent after CCP passed. NAR leaves enforcement to local MLSs, and in a lot of markets, they have quietly stopped enforcing it or issuing penalties. A rule on the books but not enforced protects no one. It only confuses the agents trying to follow it.

For newer agents: Before CCP, a seller could hire one brokerage to market and show her home exclusively. But those exclusives usually stayed out of the MLS, so other agents often never knew the house existed. The true exclusive keeps what sellers liked about the old way and adds what was always missing: every agent knowing the house is for sale. That is the replacement.

Let’s give our homeowner the third door: one agent, full marketing and a way for the right buyer to find her. That is real seller choice.

Until a model like this is in place, we are still hurting buyers and sellers. Period.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Darryl Davis is the CEO of Darryl Davis Seminars. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

#5622. Jamie Foxx’s Halloween Festival Draws Police to His California Home After Reported Stabbing

Police were called to Jamie Foxx's California home after a reported stabbing at his annual Halloween bash.

On Nov. 7, the Ventura County Sheriff's Office responded to a call at the sprawling mansion during the Hollywood star's party, dubbed Skvlk Fest.

As first reported by TMZ, a man was stabbed in the neck and had a superficial wound, which paramedics treated at the scene.

According to the outlet, one man was arrested in connection with the assault with a deadly weapon.

A video of the aftermath of the incident that began circulating on Nov. 8 showed that multiple people were put in handcuffs by police while everyone else ran out of the home.

The outlet reported that the home had several signs that indicated guests could not enter with  “real or fake weapons,” even if they were props for their costumes.

Skvlk Fest is the Halloween festival hosted by Foxx's daughter Anelise, 18, and featured carnival rides and performances from Tyga, Ty Dolla $ign, Sexyy Red, and more.

The actor shares his 18-year-old daughter with his ex Kristin Grannis. He is also father to Corinne, 32, whom he shares with his ex Connie Kline.

Although the event was meant to take place on Oct. 31, it was postponed due to heavy rains on Halloween.

This isn't the first time the event was disrupted by violence. Just last year, an attendee threw a glass bottle at rapper GloRilla.

The rapper had been performing when the bottle came flying. Foxx took the microphone and quickly came to her defense.

“Why would you do something like that?Why would you throw something at the stage, man? This is for free. Y’all don’t deserve this s--t. That’s f---ed up, bro. I’m so disappointed. I love y’all but hate whoever the f--- that was. That ain’t cool, bro. You throw some s--t at my house? That ain’t cool," he said.

Foxx resides in a 17,000-square-foot property, which is situated on 40 acres and located in Thousand Oaks, CA.

The home comes with 10 bedrooms, 12 bathrooms, a resort-style pool, sports courts, and a recording space.

#5621. Americans cling to homeownership as affordability gap widens

New ACS data shows incomes up 3.9 percent, but buyers still need $110,700 to comfortably afford a median-priced home.

Americans are clinging to the dream of homeownership — even though their incomes are barely enough to sustain it.

The U.S. Census Bureau released its 2025 American Community Survey 1-Year data on Thursday, which includes statistics on 40-plus topics, including housing. The national homeownership rate held steady at 65.3 percent, only 0.1 percentage points below the 5-year high of 65.4 percent. The majority of homeowners carry a mortgage (59 percent), with the real median mortgage payment increasing 2.4 percent year over year to $1,598.

Total housing costs, which may include expenses like homeowners association (HOA) fees, maintenance and repairs, increased 3.5 percent year over year from $2,090 to $2,163. Households now spend 21.9 percent of income on these costs, up 0.5 percentage points and just 8.1 points below the widely recognized 30 percent affordability threshold.

Median household incomes are edging up (+1.2 percent yoy after inflation), but Realtor.com Senior Economist Hannah Jones said it’s not enough to keep up with median home value growth.

“New 2025 American Community Survey data show median household income rose 3.9 percent to $84,780, with incomes up nominally in 49 of 50 states,” she said in an emailed statement. “But housing remained out of reach for many households. With a median listing price near $424,000 in 2025, mortgage rates averaging 6.6 percent, a 20 percent down payment, and taxes and insurance at roughly 1.7 percent of home value, a buyer needed about $110,700 to afford a median-priced home, roughly $26,000 more than the typical household earned.”

“Closing that gap would have required incomes to be 30.5 percent higher, prices about $99,000 lower or mortgage rates near 3.5 percent,” she added. “That affordability challenge has persisted, even as the year started with a promise.”

Jones said the market was primed in homebuyers’ favor at the beginning of the year, with sub-6 percent mortgage rates. However, macroeconomic and geopolitical conflicts have pushed mortgage rates up — now in the 7.30 percent range — leaving most homebuyers unable to take advantage of better inventory levels and falling list prices.

“Even assuming incomes have grown in line with recent wage gains of 3 percent to 4 percent since 2025, the typical household income would still be roughly $28,000 short,” she said. “Demand has cooled in response to higher rates, and pending sales fell 4.1 percent year over year in September, the steepest annual drop since March 2025, even as inventory approached pre-pandemic levels and prices softened.”

Realtor.com has released several reports on how homebuyers can attempt to make the math work, even as rates fluctuate. They can improve their credit scores, increase their down payments, shop lenders and build a budget buffer to help them absorb a 0.50 percent rate increase or decrease.

As for what lies ahead this year, homebuyers aren’t expected to receive mortgage rate relief.

The Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate steady (at 3.75 to 4 percent) at its Oct. 28 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting. The federal funds rate affects how banks and financial institutions set rates, including mortgage rates, but a change doesn’t guarantee mortgage rates will move in tandem.

The 10-Year Treasury Yield has the greatest impact on mortgage rates as lenders add a spread — or percentage markup — on top of it. The spread reflects the effects of monetary and fiscal policies, economic growth, inflation, higher origination costs and the gap between mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and Treasury yields.

“Whether the Fed hikes or holds this month, homebuyers shouldn’t expect a big change in mortgage rates,” First American Senior Economist Sam Williamson told Inman on Wednesday after the Fed’s FOMC meeting. “With another hike widely expected in December and further increases possible next year, borrowing costs are likely to remain elevated, keeping many buyers and sellers on the sidelines. But not everyone has the luxury of waiting. New jobs, growing families and other life events will keep some buyers moving forward, even as higher rates delay moves that can wait.”

Jones said mortgage rates will remain “the swing factor” and will shape next year’s American Community Survey results.

“For rates to trend lower, inflation has to cool, and the latest data shows it is moving the wrong way,” she said. “Annual inflation rose to 3.7 percent in September as energy prices surged amid the conflict in the Middle East, and core inflation edged up to 2.6 percent.”

“With the Fed focused on bringing inflation back under control while protecting the labor market, a significant drop in mortgage rates is unlikely in the near term,” she added. “For buyers on the fence, though, today’s mix of more inventory, more price cuts and more room to negotiate is the best they’ve had in years.”

#5620. Broadcom open-sources its Kubernetes VM manager

Broadcom Inc. is contributing an open-source project for managing virtual machines with Kubernetes to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, part of an effort to simplify operations across increasingly diverse enterprise computing environments.

The company announced today that its VM application programming interface project has been accepted into the CNCF Sandbox, the entry point for early-stage cloud-native projects. VM API  provides a vendor-neutral framework for provisioning and managing virtual machines using the same APIs that Kubernetes employs to orchestrate modular and portable software containers.

Broadcom also announced an initiative to standardize application behavior across Kubernetes distributions and expanded support for third-party software on VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service.

The announcements, made at KubeCon North America in Salt Lake City, reflect the growing need for infrastructure that can support traditional applications alongside modern containerized and artificial intelligence workloads.

Although Kubernetes has become the dominant platform for container orchestration, virtual machines remain central to enterprise computing. A Linux Foundation survey of 492 practitioners scheduled to be released today found that VMs account for 53% of production applications, with most respondents expecting that proportion to remain stable. Among organizations expanding their VM deployments, 34% cited AI and agentic workloads as contributing factors.

Broadcom’s VM API project addresses the operational complexity of managing VMs and containers separately. It uses Kubernetes’ declarative management model to create and manage virtual machines across different infrastructure providers while preserving capabilities such as hardware isolation and specialized input/output performance.

“We want to do the same thing now for virtual machines,” said Prashanth Shenoy, Broadcom’s chief marketing officer and vice president of marketing for cloud platform, infrastructure and solutions, referring to Kubernetes’ existing Cluster API initiative.

The goal is to provide consistent management across environments without requiring organizations to abandon their existing virtualization investments.

“Ultimately, our goal is to make virtual machines first-class citizens of a Kubernetes environment without sacrificing what makes them distinct and valuable for our customers,” Shenoy said.

The project could also simplify operations for administrators accustomed to working with Kubernetes rather than maintaining separate management tools for virtualized and containerized infrastructure.

Broadcom’s second initiative addresses a different interoperability problem: inconsistent application behavior across Kubernetes distributions.

The company is co-chairing a newly established Workload Conformance Working Group to develop common expectations for how applications operate across Kubernetes environments.

Existing conformance programs verify that Kubernetes distributions support standard APIs, but that doesn’t guarantee applications will behave identically across platforms. Differences in infrastructure capabilities, configuration and operational practices can introduce incompatibilities.

“Just because two Kubernetes environments are conformant doesn’t necessarily mean that the application will behave consistently across both,” Shenoy said.

The proposed workload conformance standard would help software vendors reduce the need to certify applications separately for individual Kubernetes distributions while giving enterprises greater confidence in application portability.

Broadcom also announced more than 20 newly validated partner solutions for VKS, the Kubernetes runtime integrated into VMware Cloud Foundation.

The validations span observability, security, data management, AI, application delivery, networking and storage. They are intended to help organizations deploy Kubernetes workloads using familiar third-party tools without requiring extensive integration or changes to existing operational practices.

Broadcom said its broader VKS ecosystem now includes more than 90 independent software vendors participating in testing and validation.

#5619. ‘Breaking Bad’ Star Dean Norris Lists $3.2 Million California Estate—After His Wife Files for Divorce

Dean Norris is looking for a buyer for his 11-acre Temecula, CA, estate, listing the hilltop property for $3,199,000—after his wife, Bridget Norris, filed for divorce.

The “Breaking Bad” actor is bidding farewell to the property he and his estranged wife bought for $1.7 million in 2024.

According to Page Six, the property first came on the market in September, roughly a year and a half after Bridget filed for divorce in Riverside County.

The property, which is listed with Sherrie Snyder of Allison James Estates & Homes, is described as a "timeless architecturally designed estate with explosive commanding views from one of the most desirable area's of De Luz."

The palatial compound sits on 11.37 acres and totals 7,315 square feet of living space across the main residence and guesthouse.

Together, the two homes have nine bedrooms, seven full bathrooms, and two half-bathrooms. The current asking price is about $1.47 million above what the couple paid.

At roughly 6,067 square feet, the main house contains seven of the estate’s nine bedrooms, with six on the first floor.

Both the living room and the family room boast cozy fireplaces. A third fireplace is in the primary suite, which features exposed ceiling beams and a walk-in closet.

"At the heart of the home, the spectacular family room offers an impressive setting appointed with a fireplace & custom built-ins," reads the listing.

The kitchen is set up for large crowds, with an eight-burner Wolf range, three ovens, and a walk-in pantry. There’s seating at the center island and space for a table in the adjoining dining area, in addition to a formal dining room.

But the real jewel of the property is the primary suite, which comes with "a fireplace, exposed wood beam ceiling, walk-in closet & luxury bath."

Overnight guests have a residence of their own on the property, which has the remaining two bedrooms.

"The park-like setting acreage is perfect for entertaining from all aspects, featuring an infinity edge pool with a walk-in beach entry, spa, waterfall, fire pit, fountain, outdoor shower, gazebo, dog kennel, lush mature landscape & tree's, outdoor kitchen with BBQ, 2 power burners, sink, ice bin & dining counter," reads the description.

"For the Equines there is a 4 stall breezeway barn with a hay loft, wash room, tack room, storage, two paddocks & a half bath. The family fruit orchard, garden bed's & chicken coop's add to the properties character & country lifestyle," the listing adds.

The estate was listed as active when the divorce drew public attention in November. According to court documents, Bridget filed for divorce on Feb. 14, 2025, and gave Jan. 15, 2025, as the date of separation.

The couple tied the knot in October 2001 and share five children. Dean, best known for playing DEA agent Hank Schrader on “Breaking Bad,” responded to the filing in May 2025. The divorce remains pending.

In her filing, Bridget cited irreconcilable differences and requested spousal support. She also asked to share legal and physical custody of their two youngest children and sought a court determination on the division of marital property.

The listing puts one of the couple’s Temecula properties in the spotlight at a time when another part of their life in the city is also in flux.

The business behind their Swing Inn Cafe has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection. The couple bought the Swing Inn Cafe in 2022, TMZ reported. According to bankruptcy documents reviewed by the outlet, the restaurant business reported approximately $147,000 in assets and more than $1.8 million in liabilities.

Its gross revenue fell from about $6.8 million in 2024 to $5.9 million in 2025.

Bridget later asked the bankruptcy court to let the business fund payroll. She warned in the filing that staff could leave if they went unpaid, putting the cafe’s ability to stay open at risk. The bankruptcy case is still ongoing.

#5618. Amid ‘tough market,’ Rocket revenues are up

Rocket’s Q3 earnings, explained: Revenue, market share, Redfin metrics and the questions agents should be asking about the integrated model.

Detroit-based Rocket Companies on Thursday announced its third-quarter 2026 earnings, and despite being in what CEO Varun Krishna said “might be the toughest mortgage market in 30 years,” revenues increased.

The company generated net revenue of $3.28 billion and adjusted revenue of $2.57 billion; net income was $709 million and adjusted net income was $419 million. The company’s Q3 adjusted EBITDA was $748 million (a 29 percent margin, up from 28 percent from last quarter).

Rocket also reported $11.4 billion in liquidity (a record), including $2.7 billion in cash and cash equivalents.

“Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter over quarter and year over year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” Krishna said in a statement. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage, and invested heavily in technology.”

The company’s third-quarter net income compares with a $124 million loss in the same period of 2025.

“The market is literally testing every single lender,” Krishna said during the company’s earnings call Thursday. “If you have a strong business model, it’s gonna shine through, but if you have a flaw, it’s gonna get exposed.”

He pointed to Redfin as a source of new mortgage clients. “Redfin is the doorway to Rocket,” Krishna said. According to the company, the number of Redfin visitors who started a purchase mortgage from a listing rose 50 percent year over year. Cumulative unique listings displayed through Rocket’s partnership with Compass reached nearly 40,000, up from about 25,000 in the prior quarter.

Brian Brown, Rocket’s president, chief financial officer and treasurer, said the fourth quarter will come in well below the third, with refinance volume falling as much as 50 percent. Rocket expects adjusted revenue between $2.1 billion and $2.3 billion for the period. “The fourth quarter will be harder still,” Brown said. “We’re ready for it.”

In Q2 2026 earnings, Rocket Companies reported $2.78 billion in revenue for a $229 million profit, up from $34 million year over year. Company executives credited its broker partners with more than $2 billion in net rate lock volume through its Compass partnership, a three-year collaboration undertaken in February.

In March, Rocket and Redfin joined Compass International Holdings in writing an open letter to multiple listing service leaders, urging them to support phased listing distribution and stop fining agents for what they called “seller-directed marketing plans.”

Rocket Companies now encompasses Rocket Mortgage, the U.S.’s largest lender, which includes Mr. Cooper, the country’s largest mortgage servicer, acquired just over a year ago; Redfin’s brokerage and home search portal; Rocket Close, its title and closing company; and Rocket Money and Rocket Loans, its consumer finance brands.

Christy Murdock and Lucy Cohen Blatter contributed to this story.
