#5617. Court Report: Tuccori Settlements on Hold as Judge Requests Further Logistics

Editor’s note: The COURT REPORT is RISMedia’s weekly look at current and upcoming lawsuits, investigations and other legal developments around real estate.

Tuccori settlement on hold after judge request

The approval of settlement agreements with more than 20 real estate companies in a major antitrust lawsuit filed by recent homebuyers challenging commission practices in the residential real estate market has been put on hold by a judge following a request for more information.

The settlements in the Tuccori v. At World Properties commission lawsuit were preliminarily approved back in May, but final approval has been put on hold as Judge Lindsay C. Jenkins has put in a request for additional information on five topics.

Firstly, Jenkins asked for clarification on a concern that was previously raised at a hearing: The valuation of claims filed, namely that “resolving 1/8 of all claims for 1/8 of what you paid to resolve the other 7/8 of all claims does not imply you valued the 1/8 and 7/8 equally on a per claim basis.”

Other requests include how each settler’s “ability to pay and transaction volume influenced their proposed settlement,” further information for the court to be able to arrive at the “net expected value of continued litigation,” benchmarks for “substantive adequacy from other indirect purchaser class actions,” and lastly, an estimation of per claimant and per class member recovery.

The National Association of Realtors®, one of the settlers in the case, said in a statement that it “continues to believe the Tuccori settlement is fair, reasonable, and in the best interests of the class.”

“The settlement offers meaningful protections across the industry, providing a broad release for REALTOR® members, REALTOR® associations, MLSs, and those brokerages that meet the settlement’s eligibility requirements,” the statement read. “NAR remains committed to fostering fair, transparent, and pro-consumer real estate markets while providing resources and value to our REALTOR® members nationwide.”

NAR added that the judge’s request is “a routine part of the class action settlement approval process, consistent with the judge’s role in evaluating the fairness of the settlement.”

“NAR is committed to abiding by the judge’s request to provide the Court with information in a timely and efficient manner, including working with the other parties, to demonstrate the settlement is fair and reasonable,” the statement concluded.

Briefs on the topics are due by Dec. 14, after which time the court will say if it needs further responses.

Fair housing lawsuit against Bank of America dismissed

A racial-discrimination lawsuit filed against Bank of America and a Virginia-based appraiser has been dismissed.

The suit was filed by Darchelle Braxton, a Black woman who last summer attempted to secure a loan for home improvements on an investment property. She claimed in her filing that an initial appraisal ordered by Bank of America valued her property at $135,000, but a subsequent second appraisal valued it more than 50% higher, at $208,000.

The appraiser—Velox Valuations—filed a motion to dismiss, refuting Braxton’s claims that it provided a “shockingly low” valuation on her property due to alleged “material errors, omissions, and inconsistencies,” which stemmed from racial bias. Such errors included allegedly using an incorrect map reference, using an incorrect neighborhood valuation, only using two comparable properties, inconsistent descriptions of the property’s condition, and more.

The suit was dismissed with prejudice, meaning it cannot be refiled.

With the many legal battles the portal has faced as of late, Zillow CEO Jeremy Wacksman said lawsuits are “not impacting our business” during its Q3 2026 earnings call.

CFO and COO Jeremy Hofmann added that legal costs are “normalized” going forward as the company hunkers down for what is expected to be a tough environment for real estate.

“It’s not obvious to us how things are necessarily going to improve,” Hofmann said.

The portal is currently still facing a proposed class-action lawsuit from a real estate agent who claims Zillow’s “monopoly power” inflates fees and commissions. A judge ruled in September that the lawsuit could move forward.

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5616. These Sun Belt States Are Falling Behind on Home Permitting, Study Finds

In an era of strained housing affordability, new-home construction is one of the keys to easing the housing shortage. And some states are building faster than others.

South Carolina, Idaho, and North Carolina lead the nation in permitting new homes, according to data from the Lied Center for Real Estate at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. On the other hand, the more affordable Midwest was stagnant. UNLV looked at data from the U.S. Census Bureau in the first eight months of this year compared to 2025.

Meanwhile, in the Sun Belt, which has been a bright spot in housing production the past few years, some states are falling behind, a new study finds. UNLV found slowing permitting activity in Texas, Arizona, Utah, and Oklahoma.

"The supply side will determine what housing or rent prices people will face in 18 to 24 months," study co-author Nicholas Irwin said. "And through political action, community members can encourage more development and put pressure on elected leaders to become accountable for rising housing prices."

New permits nationally fell in September—5.2% month over month and 7.4% year over year to an annualized 1.22 million units. Builders in some of these markets are relying on concessions to attract more buyers, but there's no question their confidence is shaken in such a difficult housing market.

For the first nine months of the year, overall new-home sales are 2.9% below where they were in 2025, Realtor.com® senior economist Joel Berner says.

Permits have been the "lone bright spot" in a lot of difficult data, Berner adds.

Housing affordability was top of mind in many swing states this year, and Democrats and Republicans both said they favor reforms that make it easier to build homes. State laws this year could lead to permitting of more homes, especially accessory dwelling units.

UNLV based its study on permits per resident. In total, cities issued 968,187 housing permits nationwide, or abut 2.83 per 1,000 residents. That's essentially flat from the same time in 2025, but it's a 4.1% drop from the same time in 2023.

South Carolina topped the study, permitting 6.07 units per 1,000 residents, a 5% increase from where it was one year ago. Idaho followed at 6.4 units per 1,000 residents, and North Carolina came in third at 5.77 units per 1,000 residents.

Those three states also top a recent Realtor.com report on top new-construction markets.

"These states combine fast-growing economies with favorable new-construction environments to bring homebuyers a larger share of new builds on the market," Berner says.

While Florida, Texas, and Arizona are still in the top 10 states by number of permits, they've slowed the pace of permitting. Rhode Island, New York, and Massachusetts are near the bottom on number of permits, but they've seen notable jumps in how many homes they permit.

Overall, 26 states and the District of Columbia permitted more homes compared to the same time in 2025. The other 24 states permitted less. The biggest drops came in Nevada, whose permit-to-resident ratio is down 29%, and Vermont and Connecticut, which both dropped 18%.

Nevada, which permitted 12,662 units in 2025 and 8,986 this year, joins North Dakota in permitting fewer homes than its projected household growth. That could spell trouble for affordability long-term.

About 64% of the permitted units are single-family, and 3.5% were 2- to 4-unit homes. The remaining 32% of homes are multifamily of 5 or more units.

Much of the housing data this year tells a story of a difficult market for homebuilders, with little relief in sight. This year, Mortgage Bankers Association Chief Economist Mike Fratantoni predicted mortgage rates would remain around 7.3% for the rest of the year and hover above 7% through 2027.

And National Association of Realtors® Chief Economist Lawrence Yun predicted the existing-home sales volume would rise just 4% from last year, having revised that downward this year.

Homebuilders are using incentives to entice buyers, and yet there are more existing homes on the market to compete with newly built ones. Berner explains that's true in the Midwest, often a center of affordability, where demand for homes is softer. Growing cost of land and labor is also making it harder for builders to compete for buyers.

But homebuilders still seeking permits for many units also says something. A permit doesn't mean a home starts construction immediately; it signals future intent.

"Builders are facing diminished buyer demand and high input costs, causing them to slow down when it comes to beginning and finishing projects. But permitting them has held relatively steady," Berner says. "We take this as a sign that builders expect conditions to turn around in the near future, and they want to be ready to capitalize when they do."

The UNLV study points to how affordability has worsened in many areas since 2018, and building new homes is key to improving it.

“Alleviating challenges related to the housing crisis really comes down to a city’s ability to actually build housing," Shawn McCoy, the report's other co-author said. "People need to be able to afford their home, but if they can’t find a home to rent or buy at all, there’s going to be a problem."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5615. I analyzed 1,133 Instagram posts with Meta’s new AI

Meta Muse for Small Business connects to your Instagram analytics. Here are five prompts to analyze your past posts before asking AI to create more.

Meta quietly released something at the end of September that I think a lot of real estate agents are going to want to play with.

It’s called Meta Muse for Small Business, and while there are plenty of AI tools that can help you brainstorm a Reel or write a caption, what is massive about Muse is that it can connect directly to your Instagram professional account analytics, along with your Facebook Pages, Meta ad accounts and other business tools.

I connected mine and started playing with it, but instead of asking it to make more content, which is how I use AI most of the time, I wanted to see what would happen if I used it to understand all the content I had already made.

Eventually, we analyzed 1,133 of my Instagram posts. It helped me understand why my rolling views had fallen from roughly 4 million to 2.46 million, showed me that at least 27 of my 98 newest followers were real estate professionals, and identified patterns in the topics and formats that have historically performed best for me.

That was when I realized I had probably been using AI backward. If you have been consistently creating content for a few years, you already have your own data set of what works and what doesn’t, so before asking AI for another 10 Reel ideas, there may be more value in asking it to help you understand what your audience has already told you.

Here are five prompts I’m using to do that.

“Analyze my Instagram performance over the past 90 days. Don’t give me content recommendations yet. First tell me where the biggest weakness is between reach, engagement, profile visits, follower growth and conversion, and show me the data that led you to that conclusion.”

A few months ago, my Instagram analytics showed roughly 4 million views in a 30-day window, and more recently that number had fallen to about 2.46 million, so naturally my first reaction was that something wasn’t working.

The story was a little different once I dug into the data. Some of my biggest posts, including videos with more than 1 million views, had simply aged out of the rolling reporting period. I would love to tell you I publish a million-view video every week, and I’m working on it, but I don’t.

My views were down, but roughly 84 percent were still coming from non-followers, and my content had reached more than 1.4 million accounts. The point wasn’t to ignore the decline; it was to understand what was causing it before changing a strategy that might not actually be broken.

“Analyze my most recent followers, and group them into the most common audience types you can identify. Don’t assume who my target audience is. Tell me what the data shows.”

We pulled roughly 100 of my newest followers, and of the 98 we could analyze, at least 27 had Realtor, real estate, broker or realty directly in their name or username.

Initially, I wondered whether that was a problem because I sell houses and still want consumers seeing my content, but last year we closed roughly $12 million in sales volume from referrals, and relationships with other agents have also created speaking opportunities, partnerships and other revenue. Trying to get rid of an audience already producing real business made very little sense.

Instead, I’m leaning into it while becoming more intentional about building consumer-focused lead pillars through my local Dana Point Daddy page and YouTube.

I’m also still making consumer-focused and humorous content on my main account because my past clients, database, sphere, friends and family are seeing and engaging with it. We’re still marketing directly to our database, hosting client events and doing the things that generate real estate business outside social media.

Your unexpected audience might be completely different from mine, but you probably shouldn’t decide whether the audience you’re building is good or bad until you know who is in it and what that audience is worth to your business.

“Analyze my highest-performing posts from the last year and group them by topic, format and hook. Tell me what patterns repeat among my winners and which patterns I seem to be underusing.”

I spend an embarrassing amount of time studying other creators, saving their posts and trying to understand why something went viral, while apparently not spending nearly enough time studying the years of content I already had telling me what my own audience responds to.

We analyzed 447 of my carousel and single graphic posts and isolated 103 that used headline-style hooks. The winners repeatedly included income statistics that create sticker shock, local rankings people want to agree or disagree with, surprising changes in the Southern California housing market and California housing policies translated into something useful for homeowners.

This October, Inman turns its focus to AI and its rapid rise in real estate. During Artificial Intelligence Month, we’re digging into the startups shaking things up and the established players folding AI into their offerings.

I don’t need to make variations of those posts forever, but I can look for new topics that share the DNA of things my own audience has already told me it wants instead of constantly trying to recreate somebody else’s viral post.

“Compare how frequently I publish each content format with how those formats actually perform. Where is my time allocation inconsistent with my results?”

At the time of the analysis, I had published 66 times over 28 days, and Reels were the format I was publishing most frequently even though they weren’t my best-performing format. Carousels were.

I’m not going to stop making Reels because different content has different jobs, but if I’m deciding where to spend another hour this week, I should probably know whether the format consuming most of my time is producing my best results.

“Based only on the patterns you identified in my historically best-performing content, give me 10 new content ideas. For each one, tell me which past pattern it is based on and why you think it fits my audience.”

This is where the first four prompts become useful instead of just interesting because I can ask any AI tool for 10 content ideas and it will happily give them to me, but without context it is essentially making an educated guess.

Once it understands what my audience has historically responded to, I can ask a much better question: What should I make next based on what has already worked for me?

I’m still going to experiment, tell personal stories and make something weird because I think it’s funny, but now my own history gets a vote.

Meta Muse for Small Business has only been out for about a month, so I am sure I’m barely scratching the surface of what I can do with it, but this experiment has already changed the way I’m using AI.

If you’ve been consistently posting for a few years, you may already have hundreds or thousands of experiments sitting inside your Instagram, so before asking AI for another hook, caption or content idea, ask it to help you understand those experiments first.

For me, the most interesting thing AI has done for my content lately isn’t helping me create more of it. It’s helping me make better decisions about what I create next.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#5614. Mark Zuckerberg Meta AI Predicts ‘Will Crypto Recover in November’

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin (BTC) is trading near $75,800–$76,000 and Ethereum (ETH) is around $2,230–$2,235 as of November 8, 2026. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI predicts, ‘Will crypto recover in November? ‘, which is the question on many traders’ lips heading into a big week across the markets.

Bitcoin sits roughly 40% below its October 2025 peak of about $126,000, while Ethereum remains well off its own highs. The market is asking whether crypto can stage a meaningful recovery this month. After the post-midterm bounce, both assets have consolidated.

Bitcoin has held the mid-$70,000s after testing higher levels earlier in the recovery, while Ethereum continues to lag, trading with a relatively weak ETH/BTC ratio near 0.0295.

This is typical in the early stages of a potential recovery, when Bitcoin usually leads, which is why all eyes should be on BTC USD over the coming week.

Bitcoin has formed a series of higher lows since the mid-year troughs and is defending the $74,800–$75,500 zone. A weekly close back above $81,000–$82,000 would strengthen the case for a durable base.

A break below $74,000 would reopen downside risk toward the low $70,000s. Ethereum remains softer. It is struggling to reclaim key moving averages and needs a sustained move through $2,400–$2,500 to show relative strength returning.

Until the ETH/BTC ratio turns higher, a full “altcoin season” style recovery remains unlikely, but a shift in market conditions can quickly change sentiment.

CRYPTO THIS WEEKNovember 9–15, 2026A busy week across crypto markets, policy, institutions and blockchain infrastructure. Inflation, exchange and ecosystem updates will shape the week.THE HIGHLIGHTS:✧ China October inflation data arrives November 9.✧ US CPI is out… pic.twitter.com/26z29H08Aa

The most immediate event is the October CPI report on Tuesday, November 10. Consensus expects a cooling in the monthly rate (around +0.2–0.3% headline). A softer-than-expected print would ease rate-hike fears, support risk assets, and give Bitcoin and Ethereum room to push higher into the second half of the month.

A hotter reading would reinforce the “higher-for-longer” narrative, pressure yields higher, and likely stall or reverse the recent rebound.

Soft inflation and resilient but not overheating growth data would be constructive. Sticky inflation or stronger-than-expected economic prints that raise December rate-hike odds would act as a headwind. Spot Bitcoin ETF flows remain the marginal driver.

Recent weekly outflows have weighed on price, so a return to consistent net inflows would be an important confirmation of recovering institutional demand.

Stablecoin growth and on-chain activity continue to favor Ethereum over the longer term, but near-term price action is still dominated by macro and Bitcoin leadership.

A modest recovery is possible if the November 10 CPI comes in soft and ETF flows stabilize. In that scenario, Bitcoin could retest the $82,000–$85,000 area and Ethereum could push back toward $2,400–$2,500 by month-end.

A hotter inflation print or continued ETF outflows would likely keep the market range-bound or push prices back toward recent lows. A full-blown bull-market breakout to new all-time highs is unlikely in November.

The more realistic path is a grinding recovery that builds through the end of 2026 and into 2027, assuming inflation continues to cool and institutional demand returns.

For now, the November CPI print is the single most important near-term catalyst that will decide whether the post-midterm bounce has legs or fades.

#5613. Red Hat adds agentic AI operations, stronger security in OpenShift 5 and RHEL updates

Red Hat Inc. today announced a major update to its OpenShift Kubernetes-based application development platform that adds artificial intelligence-powered troubleshooting, stronger security controls and simplified upgrades as the company seeks to make its hybrid cloud infrastructure easier to manage.

The company also announced new versions of Red Hat Enterprise Linux with enhanced protection against software tampering, AI-assisted system administration and post-quantum cryptography.

The releases, unveiled at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City, reflect Red Hat’s continuing initiatives to embed AI into enterprise infrastructure management while strengthening security across increasingly distributed environments.

Red Hat OpenShift 5, the first major version upgrade in seven years, extends the platform’s ability to manage containers, virtual machines and AI workloads within a common environment. It also broadens the OpenShift Lightspeed generative AI assistant into an agent capable of investigating operational problems and recommending corrective actions.

“It’s infusing intelligence into the platform with agent-based troubleshooting through a simple interface with Lightspeed and natural language,” said Chris Wright, Red Hat’s chief technology officer and senior vice president of global engineering.

The updated Lightspeed interface allows administrators to generate visualizations of system performance using natural-language requests. For example, an administrator can ask for central processing unit utilization over the previous week, add memory consumption and overlay application errors. The resulting charts can be saved to dashboards that update continuously.

More significantly, OpenShift 5 introduces agentic troubleshooting that automatically investigates cluster events. When problems occur, the system can examine related information, reason through possible causes and propose remediation steps. Administrators retain control over whether the recommended actions are executed.

The platform also includes an AI-driven upgrade planner that examines application dependencies, Kubernetes application programming interfaces and optional operators to identify potential compatibility problems before updates begin.

“It is easy to upgrade Kubernetes,” said Mike Barrett, Red Hat’s vice president and general manager of hybrid cloud platforms. “What is difficult is navigating all the things you’re running on top of Kubernetes.”

Security enhancements include hardened multitenancy, more extensive network isolation, automated certificate management and post-quantum cryptography for control-plane communications. The capabilities are aimed in part at sovereign cloud providers and regulated organizations that must maintain strict separation between tenants and demonstrate compliance with security requirements.

OpenShift 5 also supports automated graphics processing unit resource allocation across AI inference and traditional enterprise workloads, potentially improving utilization of that expensive computing infrastructure.

Unlike previous major platform transitions, OpenShift 5 can be installed as an in-place update from OpenShift 4, avoiding the need to reinstall software or migrate workloads, Red Hat said. A revised lifecycle approach provides greater predictability for customers operating long-lived enterprise applications and virtualized infrastructure.

“We are no longer asking you to reinstall or migrate to use more of our product,” Barrett said. “This is a simple upgrade.”

The company is emphasizing virtualization as an increasingly important part of its business. Barrett said OpenShift Virtualization has grown to an $800 million business as customers seek alternatives to traditional virtualization platforms.

It said NASA’s laboratory migrated approximately 2,400 virtual machines to OpenShift Virtualization, while Gates Corp. moved more than 1,300 virtual machines and reported a 50% increase in available compute capacity.

The forthcoming Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.3 and 9.9 releases extend the company’s security strategy to the operating system.

A principal addition in RHEL 10.3 is support for sealed images, which use customer-controlled cryptographic keys to verify operating system integrity from the bootloader through the kernel and root file system. The technology is designed to prevent unauthorized modifications and block compromised software components from running.

Red Hat is also introducing a Model Context Protocol server that allows compatible AI assistants to investigate live Linux systems while maintaining access controls. Integration with Performance Co-Pilot, an open-source toolkit for monitoring, recording, analyzing, and controlling infrastructure, enables agents to examine historical performance information alongside current system conditions to identify the causes of operational problems.

A self-managed version of the RHEL command-line assistant, available in developer preview, lets organizations run AI inference locally. The capability is intended for disconnected, air-gapped and regulated environments where sending operational information outside the organization may be prohibited.

The releases also introduce post-quantum cryptography support for applications built using the Go programming language, including integration of the post-quantum Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism encryption algorithm with the language’s Transport Layer Security implementation. Additional enhancements include updated developer toolchains and support for newer processor architectures.

Red Hat separately announced Developer Hub 2.1, an update to its enterprise developer portal that gives AI coding agents governed access to organizational information, approved software components and standardized development workflows. Through MCP integration, agents can discover existing services, follow established development procedures and perform authorized actions using enterprise tooling.

The update also introduces expanded AI asset cataloging, a context-aware assistant and a longer support lifecycle, increasing the release support window from six to 10 months. Developer Hub 2.1 is generally available, as is OpenShift 5, while the new RHEL versions are expected in the coming weeks.

#5611. Why Now Is the Time to Prepare Senior Homes for the Spring Market

For seniors preparing to sell a home they’ve lived in for decades, fall may be the ideal time to start downsizing before spring brings a new wave of buyers. When the weather starts to cool and the leaves start to fall from the trees, it can feel like a natural time to reset, to refresh a living space and prepare for the next life chapter.

As families shift holiday decorations, reorganize storage and prepare for the end of the year, it can also be a natural opportunity to begin sorting through a lifetime of furniture, keepsakes and belongings before a home goes on the market.

Nan Hayes, VP of Business Development at Caring Transitions, a company specializing in transforming the way seniors and their families transition through life’s stages, talks about the various aspects of preparing now for homeselling later.

Why is fall a good time to begin downsizing before a spring sale?

Fall can be a good time to adjust old habits and set new goals. As the season changes, it creates a natural opportunity to take stock of our homes and begin letting go of things we no longer need.

For homeowners considering a spring home sale, fall is a good time to begin downsizing and decluttering. Starting months before listing provides time to address repairs, sort through belongings and make decisions without the added pressure of an active home sale. As a bonus, a more organized home can also make holiday entertaining easier.

Homeowners can choose to sort, donate, sell, gift or dispose of excess belongings themselves, or bring in professionals to handle some of the more time-consuming tasks. Either way, starting early can help ensure the home is ready when it is time to list.

For real estate agents, the journey from lead to listing can take several months. Timelines become longer when homeowners are waiting for more favorable market conditions, completing home preparations or waiting on another life event, such as end of the school year, or the birth of a child.

For older adults who are downsizing into a senior living community or other care setting, the process may take even longer. Selling a family home in later life can be a major task. Many times, the home holds a lot of memories as well as a lot of ‘stuff.’ Beginning early gives families time to plan the transition and make thoughtful decisions along the way.

How can decades of belongings affect a home’s perceived space?

Even a spacious home can feel smaller when closets, cabinets, garages and rooms are filled with belongings.

Reducing excess items before listing helps buyers focus on the home rather than its contents. With fewer distractions, buyers can better understand the storage space, room sizes and possibilities the property offers.

Removing excess belongings and highly personal items can also help buyers imagine themselves living in the home. The space feels more open, and the features of the property become easier to see.

Why can waiting until a home is listed create unnecessary delays?

Once a home is listed, the clock starts ticking. If the home is not yet market-ready, the remaining tasks make the home less appealing than others on the market, and can interfere with showings, or complicate the sale and closing process.

Rushing through all the tasks at the very end isn’t a good solution either. If sorting, organizing, packing, donating, selling belongings, repairing the home, and moving all have to happen at once, the home seller can quickly become overwhelmed, and they may stop the entire process.

Starting early separates the emotional work of downsizing from the time-sensitive work of selling.

How can agents approach emotionally difficult downsizing conversations?

When clients are overwhelmed by years of possessions, unsure where to begin, or suffering from decision fatigue, they need a clear plan and calm communication that stems from a place of empathy rather than urgency.

Instead of saying: “You really need to get rid of all this!” Try: “You don’t have to figure this out all at once. Let’s start with what you would like to take with you, and then we’ll come up with a plan for everything else.”

This shifts the conversation away from what the client feels they have to give up or get rid of, so they can instead focus on what comes next. For many homeowners, belongings represent decades of memories, family milestones, and important moments. Recognizing that emotional connection can make difficult conversations easier and help clients feel supported rather than rushed.

Agents do not have to solve every part of the transition themselves. They can provide direction, connect clients with reliable relocation resources, and help break a large project into manageable steps.

How can families use the holidays to start sorting, organizing, and letting go?

The holidays may provide a natural opportunity to start on home projects because families are already spending time together. Rather than turning every family gathering into a major downsizing event, use the time to share memories, make a few decisions, and start conversations about the future.

Families might look through photographs, collections or keepsakes together. Consider digitizing large collections so they can be shared with family members. Share the stories behind meaningful belongings or write those stories down.

Invite children and grandchildren to choose items that are meaningful to them. Tackle one closet, cabinet, collection, or small area together. Identify which belongings might be donated, gifted, sold, or included in an estate sale or online auction.

Contact professional downsizing, relocation, estate sale, and auction resources early to request estimates and reserve time before spring schedules begin to fill. The goal is not to spend the holidays cleaning out the house or emptying every room. It is simply to start a conversation, make a plan, complete a few manageable tasks that can help build momentum. In short, a little progress now can mean fewer decisions and less pressure when it is time to list the home.

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

Routine maintenance, sensible storage, suitable flood protection and a clear emergency plan can help homeowners prepare more effectively. The right approach depends on the property, its surroundings and the conditions it may face. Read more.

#5610. A Halloween tale: Spooky events and a haunted house sale

Author and trainer Bernice Ross shares a spooky tale of unusual home happenings and a sale process plagued by tragedy.

When you’re in the real estate business, sooner or later there will be a house that someone says is haunted. The story below is true. Were these events just coincidence, or were they something else?

When I was working on my doctorate, my closest friend and study partner was living in a new house in Orange County. She was in the antique business. Her home was like a showcase, every last inch of it beautifully decorated. When I met her, she was in the process of getting a divorce.

Although her house was a little over a year old, it already had the makings of a strange history. While the house was being built, a little girl was sexually assaulted in it. A few months after she and her husband moved in, he became manic-depressive.

Over the next few months, he had numerous confrontations with the police. He refused to take his meds. Unbeknownst to his wife, he placed a warranty deed on the property to access part of the equity. He then took off to Hawaii, where he was reportedly living in the bush outside the Honolulu airport.

We would normally study together at her house about twice per month. The lights would flicker periodically. If we went out for dinner, it was common for pieces of the furniture to be moved away from the wall.

Since my friend had changed the locks and placed a security system on the house, there was no one who had access to move the furniture. There was also a window in the family room overlooking the canyon that would vibrate for no apparent reason. You could put your hand on the window and tell it to stop vibrating, and it did.

After spending the afternoon preparing for our upcoming qualifying exams, we decided to go out to dinner to take a break. When we returned, the lights were flickering, and a number of pieces of furniture were moved again.

As we sat back down to hit the books again, there was a loud rustling in the garage where she refinished her antiques. Her German shepherd, a very mellow dog who never barked, started barking and scratching crazily at the door to the garage.

Although this didn’t disturb my friend, I made sure the dog was between me and whatever was in the garage. As soon as she opened the door, the dog broke away from me and raced into the garage. The dog raced to the other side of the garage, sat down and acted as if nothing had happened.

After consuming a carton of chocolate ice cream to soothe our jangled nerves, we decided to watch a movie — The Ghost of Flight 401. This probably wasn’t the smartest movie choice, but that was the best of the evening’s shows back in the days of seven TV channels and no cable.

As I was getting ready to leave, we were standing by the front door adjacent to the stairway. Her stairs had beautiful wrought iron work topped with a heavy oak banister.

As we were standing there talking, the banister and the wrought iron started to vibrate. Everything else in the house was still. I turned and asked her, “Do you see what I see?” She did.

We were both mesmerized because nothing else was moving. This went on for about five minutes, and then it stopped. At that point, I was out of there, and there was no way I was going back.

My friend wanted out of the house. Needless to say, there were numerous challenges that had to be addressed before she could legally sell the property. California law allowed her to list the property, but both she and her husband had to sign the grant deed to close the transaction.

The lender who held the warranty deed was demanding payment as per the terms of the note. Normally, their option would have been to foreclose. The challenge was that the police reports documented the fact that the husband was probably not legally competent at the time he signed the deed.

Since he was nowhere to be found, my friend and the lender petitioned the court to order the sale as part of the divorce proceedings. The court granted her request.

The house was listed and finally went under contract. The buyer was a deputy sheriff. Two days after opening escrow on the property, the escrow officer had a heart attack and died. The title officer handling the file also had a heart attack but recovered.

About four weeks into the transaction, the deputy sheriff’s right arm became mysteriously paralyzed. He saw several specialists, but no one could find a cause for the problem. He was forced to take disability leave from his job. This meant he didn’t have sufficient income to qualify for the loan. The transaction was canceled. Within a few days after he canceled, the paralysis disappeared.

After almost a year, the house finally sold. The buyer was a psychiatrist.

Fortunately, this transaction took place prior to California passing its disclosure laws. I have to wonder how you would make those disclosures today. Much of what happened could be coincidence. I still don’t have an explanation for the moved furniture, the strange window and, most of all, the vibrating staircase. Perhaps it’s just as well that I don’t.

Bernice Ross is president and CEO of BrokerageUP and RealEstateCoach.com, the founder of Profit.RealEstate and a national speaker, author and trainer with over 1,500 published articles.

#5609. ‘Haunted as a matter of law’: How real estate agents handle stigmatized listings in 2026

Stigmatized homes have long sold at a steep discount. Agents and attorneys say an unaffordable, low-inventory 2026 market may be shrinking it.

Many may assume that the rule of thumb on stigmatized homes is simple: A murder, suicide or infamous ghost story knocks a big chunk off the price. Real estate agents who’ve sold these homes say it’s more complicated, and today’s unaffordable, short-on-inventory market may be shrinking the discount.

A “stigmatized” property can mean many things. It can be a home tied to a violent crime, a suicide, a notorious former owner or an alleged haunting.

Would you live in the Amityville Horror house, where Ronald DeFeo Jr. killed six members of his family in 1974?

Or what about the Menendez mansion in Beverly Hills, where Lyle and Erik Menendez killed their parents, José and Kitty, in 1989, a case that has stayed in the headlines for more than three decades?

These gruesome crimes may not always change the bedroom count or the square footage. But they can change who’s willing to buy, and for how much.

Ahead of Halloween, Inman asked real estate agents and attorneys how they handle stigmatized listings in 2026.

Their answers suggest the discount is real but uneven. It often depends less on the stigma itself than on how many buyers it drives away. And in a market with increasingly few affordable options, fewer buyers may be walking away.

The best-known estimate for stigmatized listings comes from real estate economist Randall Bell, who has put the typical “murder-house” discount at 10 to 25 percent. Bell has also said he’s seen some stigmatized homes sell at full value — usually smaller, more affordable homes — while others sit unsold for a long time.

Bell is an expert on real estate damage, earning the nickname “Master of Disaster,” and he runs the advisory firm Landmark Research. He has consulted on some of the most notorious crime-linked properties in history, from the Rancho Santa Fe mansions where the bodies of 39 Heaven’s Gate cult members were found to the home of Sandy Hook shooter Adam Lanza.

While Bell’s estimates are frequently cited, academic research suggests the price discount effect on stigmatized properties may fade over time.

A 2020 study of Tokyo apartment buildings by economist Taisuke Sadayuki found that a homicide in one unit initially cut rents on other units in the same building by about 10 percent, with the effect disappearing after roughly seven to eight years.

Survey data suggests buyers may also be less squeamish than agents assume. In a 2023 Zillow survey, 67 percent of prospective buyers said they could be persuaded to buy a “haunted” house with the right features, location or price.

When Inman covered stigmatized homes more than a decade ago, we framed them as bargains. The market has changed a lot since then.

Rebecca Chambliss, an agent with Carmody Real Estate in the Santa Monica, California, area, recently sold a home in a gated community where the previous owner had died by suicide only a few months before it was listed. All of the neighbors knew.

Chambliss disclosed the death to serious buyers who were discussing an offer. In her experience, buyers don’t spread out along a spectrum of tolerance. They split into two groups.

“Some people will never buy a home where a suicide or other non-natural death occurred no matter what, and then there are people who it doesn’t bother,” Chambliss told Inman. “There aren’t people in between.”

One interested buyer made an unexpected offer. When Chambliss disclosed the death, he demanded to know exactly where in the house it happened and how. Chambliss had chosen not to learn those details herself and told him as much. He wouldn’t move forward without them and withdrew the offer.

The home did eventually sell at a discount because of the suicide, Chambliss said. The buyer understood that he’d have to disclose the death if he ever sold. He relisted it about a year later, asking $1 million more than he paid, and the home still hasn’t sold.

Chambliss also brought in an energy clearer before marketing the home. It’s a reminder that for some agents, handling a stigmatized listing takes more than paperwork.

The discount doesn’t always stay with the property. Sometimes a savvy investor who knows about it collects it.

Jonathan Carcone, principal of 4 Brothers Buy Houses and a licensed agent in Washington state, bought a home in Poulsbo, Washington, with local ghost stories attached.

He said the home was listed at $640,000, while comparable homes were selling for about $650,000. Carcone said the listing didn’t mention ghost stories, but neighbors told him about them.

Carcone used the ghost stories in negotiations and bought the house for $585,000, about 9 percent below list and roughly 10 percent below comps.

Carcone’s company buys, renovates and sells dozens of houses every year, including “challenging properties.” After renovating the house in Poulsbo, he sold it for $660,000 about two months later.

“The ghost stories had no influence on the sale, and we made a good profit,” Carcone told Inman.

He said Washington law doesn’t require agents to disclose a home’s reputation, including ghost stories, so he didn’t. No buyer asked about it during showings, either. So, in this case, Carcone used the stigma to his advantage.

Because the resale price reflects a renovation, it isn’t a clean before-and-after comparison. Still, the pattern is worth noting. The seller absorbed a 10 percent discount for the stigma, and the next buyer paid none.

What agents must disclose for stigmatized properties varies widely by state.

California sets a three-year line. Under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, sellers and agents aren’t required to disclose a death that occurred on the property more than three years before a buyer’s offer. They also can’t be sued for staying silent. Whether it must be disclosed depends on whether it’s material, and the common practice is to disclose to be safe.

Answering a direct question is a separate matter. The law doesn’t protect anyone who lies when asked.

“The main point of contention between sellers and buyers is whether answering questions truthfully violates the seller’s wishes,” Nick Heimlich, founder and attorney of San Jose, California-based Nick Heimlich Law, told Inman. “Under California Civil Code, a seller’s agent cannot refuse to answer questions about the property’s history.”

Texas Property Code Section 5.008(c) says a seller or seller’s agent has no duty to disclose a death on the property from natural causes, suicide or an accident unrelated to the property’s condition. But not homicide, which may still be a material fact that must be disclosed.

Tennessee goes further. Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-5-207 lists a homicide, felony or suicide on the property among the things sellers don’t have to disclose. It also covers any act or occurrence that didn’t affect the property’s physical structure.

Ghost stories bring their own risk. In the famous case of Stambovsky v. Ackley (1991), a New York appellate court let a buyer back out of buying an allegedly haunted home in Nyack, New York.

The seller had publicized the ghost stories herself in Reader’s Digest and the local press, then didn’t tell the out-of-town buyer. In effect, the court held that because she’d told everyone else the house was haunted, it was haunted as a matter of law.

Donald Leeth, managing partner at Leeth & Gaglione, has spent 27 years as a criminal defense attorney and former prosecutor in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, and the Poconos. During that time, he’s encountered many homes where crimes took place. He advises disclosing rather than gambling on the legal minimum.

“It’s always best to be honest up front so you’re not dealing with misrepresentation claims once your transaction has closed,” Leeth said.

The more interesting question for 2026 is whether affordability is eroding the discount stigmatized listings usually have.

Median prices for new and existing homes now both top $400,000, according to Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. Existing-home prices have climbed 54 percent nationwide since 2020 and sit at nearly five times median income, well above the 3-to-1 ratio that held in the 1990s.

Leeth thinks the affordability crisis is negating the discount effect on stigmatized listings.

“Many buyers won’t care if there’s an infamous story behind a house because they simply don’t have other options,” he said. “Stigma isn’t as much of a factor as it once was because the price will determine what someone buys.”

That fits with Chambliss’s two-camp theory. If the buyers who’ll never consider a stigmatized home stay out no matter what, the discount depends on how many buyers are left in the other camp. In a tight, low-inventory market, more buyers are in that camp, and they may have fewer alternatives.

Heimlich said the type of event still matters. Buyers might shrug at a home that sat empty for a long time, he said, but something like a murder “can severely influence the property value.”

Still, he added, it likely depends on the market. And if stigma leads to a bargain, that helps, too.

“Some buyers may be willing to invest in stigmatized real estate if it falls within an affordable price range,” Heimlich said.

For agents, the practical takeaway is that a stigmatized listing’s real challenge is finding the buyers who don’t care, not pricing in a fixed discount, and disclosing in a way that doesn’t create legal exposure after closing.

Sometimes the stigma bothers the buyer’s friends and family more than the buyer themselves.

Years ago, Chambliss, the California-based agent, sold a home where a murder had taken place in the front yard. The buyer was a young single father whose Italian immigrant parents were involved in the buying process and may have been helping with the purchase. Chambliss took him outside and told him what had happened there.

He became very concerned, then immediately asked, “Do you have to tell my parents?”

His whole body relaxed, and he laughed. Then he said, “OK, I have no issue with it. But my parents would never let me buy this house if they knew.”

He bought the house, and Chambliss assumed he never told them.

#5608. Hardware-testing and engineering startup Nominal raises $240M at $3B valuation

Artificial intelligence-powered hardware-testing and engineering software startup Nominal Inc. today announced it has raised $240 million in new funding led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and Insight Partners.

The investment triples the company’s valuation to $3 billion, up from $1 billion cemented in March after it raised $80 million in a Series B-2 funding round. Additional major investors in the Series C round included Lux Capital, Sequoia, General Catalyst, Founders Fund, Avenir, Salesforce Ventures, M13 and Lockheed Martin Ventures.

Nominal assists engineers with hardware development by supporting testing and development. Engineers must piece together data from disconnected testing systems to understand how a machine performed under realistic conditions and understand what needs fixing.

The platform brings that information together, automates testing, and uses AI to help analyze the results. This shortens the cycle between testing and design, enabling faster improvements and iterations.

The challenge in the field isn’t collecting more data; there are plenty of ways to get that from simulation, sensors, video, and more. Hardware tests generate streams of sensor readings, logs, video and simulation results that all need to be analyzed together to create a whole picture of what happened. The company’s AI agent, Nominal Analyst, investigates that data and performs analysis based on the underlying evidence.

“Hardware engineering is getting its AI moment, with real operational value that goes far beyond making existing workflows faster,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Cameron McCord. “The companies building the world’s most advanced machines have decades of hard-won knowledge in their organizations.”

The company said it built its AI Intelligence Platform to bring together all the systems needed for testing and design assistance. It has multiple layers, including connections to engineering applications, the agent infrastructure, the data and finally the physical world through sensors.

Examples of what Nominal’s AI product works with alongside engineers include aircraft, rocket engines, autonomous vehicles, drones and energy systems. Engineering data and documentation associated with the hardware fed to the agents help during the development process to investigate performance, compare tests and check results against requirements.

The company said the challenge is putting engineers’ knowledge to work and connecting it to data so engineers can take on harder problems than wiring up tests. The objective is to let them sit down, smooth out challenges and address what looked impossible before.

“Engineers stay in command, with purpose-built AI helping them do their best work,” added McCord.

Nominal works with the tools engineers already bring, including application programming interfaces, Model Context Protocol and SQL for database queries. Developers can also directly access the platform to connect tools, build custom applications, and create their own workflows and agents.

The company said more than 80 commercial and government organizations use its platform, including five of the seven biggest defense contractors. Nominal’s customers include defense technology company Anduril Industries Inc., military shipbuilder Huntington Ingalls Industries Inc., known as HII, and high-speed aircraft developer Hermeus Corp.

#5607. Commission settlement accounts hold $711M as claim payouts await (EXCLUSIVE)

New disclosures show that the settlement fund accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026.

That’s how much money was held in accounts associated with the sweeping real estate commission antitrust settlements as of Sept. 30, according to newly filed federal court documents offering a fresh look at the money from the nationwide agreements.

The disclosures, filed Thursday in federal court in Missouri, show that the accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026, while roughly $5.8 million was transferred out during the same period.

The filings also come amid an ongoing court-ordered audit of settlement administrator JND Legal Administration, which reported earlier this year that it had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions.

The financial accounting follows a series of appellate rulings upholding the commission settlements, although questions remain about when eligible homesellers will receive payments.

According to a declaration signed Oct. 13 by Isaac Lim, a senior vice president and senior risk officer at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, and filed by plaintiffs Oct. 29, the settlement accounts had a combined balance of $711,251,720.86 as of Sept. 30.

The funds were transferred from Huntington Bank to Morgan Stanley on Oct. 23, 2025, at class counsel’s direction.

Lim reported that $17,705,101.82 in interest was paid into the accounts between January and September 2026, while $5,780,467.43 was transferred out during the same period. The declaration does not identify the purpose of those transfers or establish whether any money has been distributed directly to eligible homesellers.

According to the filing, the money is invested in a BlackRock institutional money market fund yielding about 3.63 percent annually, Morgan Stanley’s preferred savings program paying 4 percent or a combination of both. The yields are estimates and subject to change.

The reported balance represents funds held in the identified Morgan Stanley accounts, rather than necessarily the full amount collected through the broader commission settlements. The declaration does not provide a complete accounting of earlier distributions, expenses or outstanding settlement contributions.

In a June declaration, Jennifer Keough, CEO of JND Legal Administration, said the company had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions. In June 2025, more than 2.5 million claims had already been submitted, while JND had invoiced approximately $32.8 million for its administrative work.

Keough said JND’s original assignment expanded into six separate notification campaigns involving more than 138 million emails and 44 million postcards. Four of those direct-mail campaigns cost about $18.7 million in postage alone, which JND characterized as a pass-through expense.

In May, Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Bough ordered JND to stop receiving payments while the court considered appointing a special master to audit the company’s past and future bills.

On July 27, the judge appointed Chris Hellums and Randall Sansom as special masters.

Hellums was tasked with overseeing the audit and helping establish future administration arrangements, while Sansom, a certified public accountant, was directed to audit JND’s billing and expenses dating back to the beginning of its work.

The order requires JND to provide detailed financial records, including employee timesheets, vendor invoices, billing records and information about rebates, credits or other financial incentives.

JND opposed the need for an independent audit, arguing in a June filing that the process would be expensive and burdensome and that its work had been performed appropriately. The company said it would cooperate if the audit proceeded, but requested confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive pricing information.

JND also said its responsibilities had expanded substantially at class counsel’s direction and that it had advanced nearly $3 million in out-of-pocket costs on behalf of the class.

The dispute escalated in August when JND sought to disqualify Hellums, alleging he had demonstrated bias against the company through his involvement in a separate antitrust settlement proceeding.

Bough denied the motion Aug. 26, finding that JND, as a nonparty, could not seek disqualification under the applicable rules. He added that even if JND could bring the challenge, it had failed to establish sufficient grounds to question Hellums’ impartiality.

The ruling also examined a question Hellums had raised in the Blue Cross Blue Shield case about potential vendor rebates and credits, which Bough said JND never answered in its email exchange with him and only partly addressed at the Aug. 20 hearing. Keough acknowledged at the hearing that separate vendor agreements govern how rebates and credits are calculated.

JND has maintained in sworn declarations that it has received no rebates, credits or other financial benefits from banks or vendors in connection with the commission settlements.

In its latest accounting, JND reported $155,932 in additional administrative invoices covering July through September, bringing the outstanding balance shown on its October invoice to $494,249.

Keough said JND continues submitting invoices and performing administrative work despite not currently receiving payments.

JND did not respond to Inman’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Despite a series of appellate rulings upholding the real estate commission settlements, it remains unclear when eligible homesellers can expect to receive payments.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit unanimously upheld the landmark Sitzer | Burnett settlement, rejecting seven appeals challenging its scope, fairness and accompanying industry practice changes.

The court subsequently affirmed another $110.6 million in brokerage settlements in the related Gibson litigation on Sept. 1, bringing the total collected for the class to about $1.02 billion, according to the appellate opinion.

After rejecting three additional objector appeals on Sept. 15 and denying rehearing petitions from objectors Robert Friedman and Monty March on Sept. 24, the 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the main Sitzer | Burnett appeals Oct. 2, concluding those proceedings before the appeals court. Objectors may still seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the Gibson appeals Oct. 14.

Despite those developments, the latest financial disclosures do not establish when eligible homesellers will receive distributions or precisely how much of the $711 million held in Morgan Stanley accounts is available for payment.

Eric Dirks, an attorney with the Kansas City-based Williams Dirks Dameron, one of the plaintiffs’ co-lead counsel firms, did not respond to Inman’s request for comment regarding the account balance, interest earnings and anticipated distribution timeline.

#5606. VA Loans Can Open the Door to Homeownership 4 Years Sooner

When Thomas Couling, a young Air Force veteran, tried to buy his first home in the late 1970s, conventional lenders turned him away.

He had recently left the military, and his $11,287 annual salary as a rookie police officer in Michigan was barely enough to support his wife and newborn child.

"I could not afford to buy a home with that kind of wage," he tells Realtor.com®.

But a VA-backed mortgage gave him an opportunity that conventional financing couldn't. With help from his uncle, a contractor, and money borrowed from relatives to cover upfront costs, Thomas built his first home.

More than three decades later, his son, Coast Guard veteran Matt Couling, would turn to the same benefit to overcome a different obstacle: He had enough income to buy a home, but not enough savings for a substantial down payment.

Their experiences illustrate the findings of a new analysis from Realtor.com, which examines how Veterans Affairs loans can reduce the financial barriers to buying a home.

"At first glance, a 0% down VA loan costs about $20 more per month compared with a similar conforming loan requiring 10% down," explains Jiayi Xu, Realtor.com senior economist and author of the report. "But it saves $41,925 upfront, which cuts the time to homeownership by around four years."

Those savings are perhaps the biggest benefit of the VA loan program, because they address the biggest hurdles to homeownership head-on.

Roughly 11% of renter households under 40 have sufficient income to afford a median-priced home but lack the savings for a 10% down payment, according to the Realtor.com analysis of Federal Reserve consumer finance data.

Meanwhile, the median age of first-time homebuyers remains at a record 40, and their share of home purchases sits at just 22%, according to the National Association of Realtors®' latest report.

And those who are breaking in are relying on family help more than ever before. One-quarter (25%) of first-time buyers received gifts or loans from family and friends toward their down payment, according to NAR.

But many would-be buyers can’t count on that kind of family support—just like Matt couldn’t when he purchased his first home near Portland, ME, in 2011.

"The zero money down aspect of the VA loan is really what allowed me to buy my first house," he says.

Over the past year, 75.7% of VA-financed home purchases required no down payment whatsoever, while 86.1% involved down payments below 10%. By comparison, just 41.1% of home purchases financed with conforming mortgages had down payments below 10%.

But the benefits of VA loans don’t stop there. Between October 2025 and September 2026, the average rate on 30-year fixed VA purchase loans was 5.81%, compared with 6.22% for conforming loans.

When both borrowers put 10% down on a median-priced home, the analysis finds that the VA borrower would save approximately $261 monthly, or more than $3,100 annually.

The program also offers borrowers with less-established credit greater flexibility. Nearly one-quarter (24.3%) of recent VA borrowers had fair credit scores, compared with just 4.8% of conforming borrowers.

After about eight years in his first home, Thomas sold it and used the proceeds to help finance another house in the Michigan countryside, where he raised his family.

"Probably without the VA loan, we would have had to rent for several years," he says. Also, they likely wouldn't have accumulated the money needed for their next purchase.

He's speaking to perhaps the biggest long-term advantage that homeownership offers: Each additional year gives owners more time to pay down mortgage debt and potentially benefit from rising property values.

So the earlier you get in, the more room you have to benefit.

Earlier research from Realtor.com found that households buying their first home between ages 28 and 32 had approximately 22.5% more net worth by age 50—equivalent to $119,000—than comparable households that waited until their 40s.

Matt would also discover the value of having access to the benefit at another pivotal moment in his life.

After retiring from the Coast Guard and experiencing a significant financial setback, he wanted to establish a permanent home for his children in Celebration, FL, where he was working for Disney. But the local housing market presented another obstacle.

"While I had recovered some savings at the time, I didn't have sufficient savings to put 20% down on a million-dollar house," he says.

So he used his VA benefit for a second time and was able to purchase the home without exhausting the savings he had rebuilt.

He describes it as far more than a financial investment.

"The availability of the VA loan made buying a house something that I could do, a gift I could give to my children that I otherwise would not have been able to do," he says.

But military service can present its own challenges to becoming a homeowner, even with access to favorable financing.

Active-duty military personnel have substantially lower homeownership rates than the general population, despite higher incomes and educational attainment, according to a 2024 Urban Institute study. Researchers identified frequent moves and younger ages as the two largest contributing factors.

Matt, who retired as a Coast Guard command master chief, says military life often encourages service members to think about their finances in much shorter increments.

"You're basically living two or three years at a time," he says, citing deployments, duty stations, and promotions shaping financial planning.

That short-term focus can make it harder to plan for a home purchase, particularly when service members don't know how long they'll remain in one location.

Awareness is another issue: 68% of current and former service members were unsure or incorrect about whether VA loans required a down payment, according to 2026 survey commissioned by mortgage lender NewDay USA.

Thomas knew about VA mortgages when he left the Air Force, but there was one advantage he didn't discover until years later: The benefit can be used more than once.

"I thought it was a one and done deal," he says.

The Department of Veterans Affairs reiterated in September that eligible borrowers can use the benefit repeatedly, provided they meet applicable lending and occupancy requirements.

Thomas says he would have considered using the benefit again when buying his second home, had he known it was an option. His son, meanwhile, has now used it three times.

"I didn't have 10 years of planning behind that," Matt recalls of his first purchase. "The VA loan allowed me to do that."

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5605. Housing on the ballot: What to watch in the Nov. 3 midterms

Realtor associations in Florida, California and Massachusetts have lined up behind statewide housing measures on the Nov. 3 ballot, led by $18 million from Florida Realtors for a property tax cut.

Those are among six midterm housing ballot measures at the state level in four U.S. states, the most in a single election year since at least 2006, according to Ballotpedia, not counting property tax measures like Florida’s.

Thirty-six states will also elect governors, and candidates in California, Texas and Florida have released housing plans that range from a statewide housing emergency to ending school property taxes on homesteads.

In federal races, housing has surfaced as part of a broader argument about cost of living. Among Americans who plan to vote, 85 percent say housing affordability is at least somewhat important in choosing candidates, but 64 percent don’t know where their congressional candidates stand on housing, according to a Clever Real Estate survey.

Inman’s editorial staff will be watching California, Texas and Florida most closely next Tuesday. Each has a large real estate market and pairs a governor’s race with policy that would affect transactions, property taxes or construction.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra would declare a housing state of emergency on his first day, penalize cities that ignore housing element commitments, back local rent control within the statewide framework and seek disclosure of bulk investor purchases. Republican Steve Hilton would cap government fees and mandates on a new home at $50,000 and freeze new housing rules for five years.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott says his plan would cut the cost of a new home by more than $16,000 through faster inspections and pre-approved designs, and he wants to end school property taxes on homesteads. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa would restrict corporate purchases of single-family homes and pursue an end to residential property taxes.

In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds wants local governments to remove zoning restraints and supports Amendment 3. Democrat David Jolly opposes the amendment and says the state’s Live Local Act has not delivered affordable housing.

Housing is also a campaign issue in governor races in Colorado, Michigan, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. In Colorado, Democrat Phil Weiser has proposed 40,000 more owner-occupied homes by 2035, and Republican Victor Marx would cut state regulations and red tape. In Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson has pitched affordability proposals, and Republican John James says local codes add more than $100,000 to developers’ costs.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat seeking a second term, supports Question 7, a zoning change that could lead to the construction of more single-family homes. In Rhode Island, Democrat Helena Foulkes proposes a $1 billion plan for 20,000 homes over eight years, funded by a millionaire tax; independent Ken Block says the fund would produce no more than 375 units.

Florida Realtors had contributed $18 million to the Vote Yes on 3 committee as of late September, funding the campaign in full, WLRN reported. Amendment 3 would raise the state’s homestead property tax exemption.

“Affordability is on the forefront for every Floridian, and they need meaningful relief,” Florida Realtors President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said in a statement.

The California Association of Realtors supports Prop. 37, which would fund second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, and Prop. 45, which would speed permitting and shorten environmental review. The Massachusetts Association of Realtors supports Question 7.

At the federal level, NAR’s political action committee directed more candidate contributions and independent expenditures to Texas than to any other state through February, according to FEC filings Inman reporters reviewed. NAHB’s BUILD-PAC backs what the group calls pro-housing, pro-business candidates for Congress.

The National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals backed the ROAD to Housing Act in a March letter to Senate leaders, citing its provisions on zoning reform and by-right development.

Florida’s Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and lower the cap on annual assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent. It needs 60 percent of the vote.

California voters will decide Prop. 1, an $11.25 billion housing bond; Prop. 37, up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages covering up to 17 percent of a new home’s price; and Prop. 45, which would set permitting deadlines and shorten environmental review.

In Massachusetts, Question 7 would require cities and towns to allow a single-family home on residentially zoned lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and public water and sewer.

Below the statewide level, voters will weigh more than 50 housing-related measures, according to a Shelterforce scan. Inman reporters will track the local questions most likely to touch agents’ markets, including property tax relief for older homeowners, transfer tax changes in San Francisco and Oakland and housing bonds in Charlotte and Raleigh.

Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July. None of the 12 housing bills Inman reporter AJ LaTrace is tracking have advanced since September, including a bipartisan proposal to double the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Bills that don’t pass before the current Congressional session ends in January would need to be reintroduced. When lawmakers return after the election, they face a Dec. 11 deadline to fund federal agencies, including HUD, and to reauthorize the National Flood Insurance Program.

Inman reporters will follow how the results shape development, including data center development, which has become a campaign issue in Tennessee. The state has about 60 operating data centers and 15 to 20 more proposed, according to WSMV, and the major-party nominees for governor differ on how to handle them. Republican nominee Sen. Marsha Blackburn has said local communities should decide, and Democrat Jerri Green has called for a moratorium.

Most governors elected Nov. 3 will take office in January as state legislatures convene. That same month, the ROAD to Housing Act’s limits on large investors buying additional single-family homes take effect, and Florida’s higher homestead exemption would follow in 2027 if voters approve it.

“BHHS EWM Realty is an established brokerage with a reputation for excellence, and we couldn’t be more excited to help bring their digital presence to the next level,” RELIANCEai COO Nick Villanti added. “The company’s new platform is purpose-built for the South Florida luxury market and designed to showcase world-class properties, empower agents and deliver the kind of elevated experience that BHHS EWM Realty clients have come to expect.”

#5603. On theCUBE Pod: Blue wave sends AI stock plunging

The very blue results of last week’s midterms have sent technology investors into a tailspin.

With many successful candidates running on platforms opposing data centers and calling for greater restrictions on artificial intelligence, investors anticipate a slowdown in AI spending. Tech stocks fell, with a collective loss of $2.5 trillion in market cap, and the Nasdaq dropped more than 5.5%.

“Yesterday was a bloodbath,” said John Furrier (pictured), executive analyst for theCUBE Research. “It was brutal here and the tech stocks got pounded. 41 states had data centers on the ballot. They all lost or won, depending how you look at it. Now it’s so mainstream, it’s a political football. So you’re starting to see the reality of AI. It’s hitting everybody. Everyone is impacted.”

On the latest episode of theCUBE Pod, Furrier and Dave Vellante (pictured, right), chief analyst for theCUBE Research, discussed the fallout from the midterms and whether or not AI companies will really suffer in the long term. They also explored who will own the “system of intelligence” that will govern enterprise AI.

After the “bloodbath” last week, the question remains: Can enterprise AI pay for the boom? Despite the shockwaves from the midterms, theCUBE’s researchers are predicting a longer path toward monetization. A recent analysis identified 2029 as the highest-risk year for the AI bubble.

“There’s a clock in terms of the data center monetization and financing and how long it takes to build data centers,” Vellante said. “We know anybody who can sell GPUs is making money but the enterprises aren’t yet self-funding. I had said that by 2026, this year, you’re going to start to see clear evidence of monetization in the enterprise. I think you see it, but you’re seeing it within tech companies.”

Tech companies are applying AI more effectively, according to Vellante, which should not come as a surprise. He thinks the tech titans are in a solid position while neoclouds are taking on a greater share of risk by pioneering a new software model, although not all of them will make it in the long term.

A GPU-based AI economy will shift in the next several years, Furrier believes, which could lead to surprising winners and losers.

“Supermicro [Inc.], good numbers, [Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Arista Networks, Marvell Technology Inc.],” he noted. “My take is this: the infrastructure is evolving beyond GPU-centric computing. Networking, optics, memory, storage, power efficiency. System-level architecture is becoming the strategic advantage, and those bottlenecks are being solved by the companies I just mentioned. You saw the news that Marvell closed a $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum.”

The stock market plunge shows that not everyone is going to make it through the AI era’s eventual slowdown. Public opinion on data centers is mixed, to say the least, so companies will need to establish a foothold in the developing system of AI intelligence to remain competitive.

“Neoclouds like CoreWeave are going to make it through,” Vellante said. “They’re the first movers and they’ve got some quality advantages but they’re going to go through some pain. Hyperscalers are like an ATM. They could dial it down at any point in time … but right now it’s all about growth, it’s about footprint, it’s about market share.”

Who owns the “system of intelligence”? This layer, which will bridge the gap between intelligent agents and the data systems they depend on, appears to still be in play. Palantir Technologies Inc. has the ontology that could give it the edge, while Snowflake Inc. and Databricks Inc. are still developing the operational systems — though Vellante sees the latter as having one of the best strategies.

“You need determinism to own that system of intelligence,” Vellante said. “So I think it’s wide open. Right now, I think Ali Ghodsi [chief executive officer of Databricks] has the best vision. He’s going after the client surface, he’s going after the system of intelligence, he’s going after the governance catalog, he’s going after the agent action layer, and he’s partnering … with all the frontier model vendors. Whether or not they can pull it off, we’ll see.”

Frontier models are the “wild card,” as Vellante puts it, but at the moment, all the tech companies are trying to get a slice of the pie. Despite the recent market shakeups, Furrier sees AI-native enterprises as the ultimate result of this current period of growth.

“The AI-native enterprise or businesses is going to be the model,” Furrier said. “Everybody wins in that one. Compute providers, hyperscalers, the data platforms that are on the right side, and the application companies, which are basically going to be agentic. That’s going to be the winners on the profit concentration. The control point … it’s not going to be the models, it’s going to be data and context, and the agents will be the proof point.”
