#5602. A Tuskegee Airman’s Legacy of Generational Wealth—and His Granddaughter’s Mission to Expand It

Julia Lashay Israel bought her first home at 19, never considering it a remarkable achievement.

Only decades later did she begin tracing that sense of possibility to a VA mortgage her grandfather, one of the original Tuskegee Airmen, secured after World War II.

"We never talked about the house. We always talked about the Tuskegee Airmen," Israel tells Realtor.com®.

Her family's experience stands apart from that of many Black Americans. Just 44.4% of Black households owned their homes in the third quarter of 2026, compared with 75.1% of non-Hispanic white households, according to Realtor.com research.

Israel, now a real estate broker and educator, has spent years teaching agents about the discriminatory housing policies that helped create that divide—and how their own practices can perpetuate it.

Ahead of Veterans Day, she shared her grandfather's story at the National Association of Realtors® NXT conference in New Orleans, illustrating what access to homeownership could make possible for generations of a family.

Israel's grandfather Sgt. Morrissey Whitley was just 20 when he entered the military aviation training program in Tuskegee, AL, in 1942—eventually serving in intelligence as a draftsman for the 332nd Fighter Group, according to Israel.

Just a year earlier, the U.S. Army Air Corps had begun admitting Black men after decades of exclusion, following pressure from civil rights organizations.

But the training program remained segregated, and the Tuskegee Airmen faced hostility, unequal treatment, and military officials who questioned whether Black servicemen were capable of flying combat missions.

Despite those systemic obstacles, the Tuskegee Airmen distinguished themselves in combat, helping challenge the racist assumptions that had excluded Black Americans from military aviation.

Whitley made sure his descendants understood their achievements, too.

When Israel told him an elementary school teacher had claimed Black Americans hadn't served in WWII, he assembled a folder of evidence for her to take to class.

But the racial barriers facing Black servicemen didn't end when they returned home.

And in the housing market, those divisions were reinforced by redlining, which restricted where Black families could obtain mortgages—and, ultimately, where they could build wealth.

In 1940, just 22.8% of Black households owned their homes, compared with 45.6% of white households, according to historical U.S. Census Bureau data.

And even while the GI Bill subsequently helped millions of returning veterans purchase homes through government-backed mortgages, lenders often refused to finance properties in predominantly Black neighborhoods.

On top of that, racially restrictive covenants excluded Black buyers from many white neighborhoods.

As a result, just 5.1% of VA-guaranteed loans in an early federal mortgage sample went to Black borrowers, according to a 2026 study published in Nature.

Whitley was among those who secured financing, purchasing a home in Gary, IN, after moving his family from Chicago, according to Israel—a move that she believes was made necessary because of discriminatory lending practices.

"You can't use your VA loan in Chicago," she says. "You have to live where Black people are redlined to live."

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Israel developed a course teaching real estate agents about the history of housing discrimination—including redlining, restrictive covenants, and the industry's role in perpetuating segregation.

She later taught it through Keller Williams' social equity task force, established after George Floyd's killing in 2020. Her training has since reached more than 40,000 agents, according to NAR.

What surprised Israel was how many agents were unfamiliar with that history—or how their own decisions could perpetuate its consequences.

"There's been different buyers, different sellers," she says of the persistence of residential segregation. "The only common denominator is the Realtor®."

Israel has witnessed discrimination firsthand.

"I've had people not sit in closings with us because we were Black," she says, recalling a Minnesota home closing in the mid-2000s.

Black applicants were 7.8 percentage points more likely than white applicants to be denied mortgages, even after accounting for financial characteristics and lender differences, according to a 2026 Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis study.

Israel also worries about agents discouraging buyers from pursuing certain financing programs or directing them toward particular neighborhoods without considering the long-term consequences.

Her courses emphasize the importance of understanding those barriers and earning buyers' trust, particularly when they're navigating a process nobody in their family has experienced before.

During 13 years working primarily with first-time buyers, many of them Black single women, she encountered clients who were hesitant to sign agreements or trust the professionals guiding them.

"A lot of times they are the first, and so if you're the first person who's ever done it, yeah, that's pretty scary," she says.

Israel grew up with a very different understanding of homeownership.

"My grandparents always had a house. My parents always had a house," she says.

In fact, she remembers envying classmates who lived in apartment complexes, where they could play together after school.

Her own children inherited that familiarity. Israel recalls her young son accompanying his grandmother to look at a rental apartment and repeatedly asking, "When's the closing?"

He couldn't understand why someone would pay to live in a home they didn't own.

It wasn't until Israel began working in real estate that she recognized how her family's experience differed from that of many neighbors and fellow churchgoers who rented their homes.

That early exposure can have lasting consequences. Children who grew up entirely in homeowner households were 18.4 percentage points more likely to become homeowners themselves by age 35 than those raised entirely in renter households, according to Realtor.com research.

Housing-related financial advantages can also persist across generations independently of what children earn themselves. Less than half of the persistence in housing capital across generations is explained by children's earnings, according to a 2025 U.S. Census Bureau study examining more than 3.4 million families.

Those advantages have been distributed unequally. Median white family wealth stood at approximately $332,100 in 2025, compared with just $36,800 for Black families, according to a Tax Policy Center analysis of Federal Reserve data.

Israel's own family never had substantial financial resources growing up, despite their history of homeownership.

"We never had a lot of money, but we always had a lot of sense," she recalls.

And when her granddaughter was born, Israel began reconsidering how far the opportunity her grandfather secured had carried the family.

"He didn't leave us any money, but he left us, like, a legacy," she says.

It was that realization that prompted Israel to begin incorporating Whitley's experience into her educational work.

"It's really not about quartz countertops or, you know, the cute fence," she says of the work real estate agents do. "It really is that we're planting seeds for families."

Her own grandfather had planted one more than eight decades earlier. And now, another generation of his descendants is benefiting from the opportunities that followed.

"This little baby is a trust fund baby, and she'll never know that it was because her great-great-grandfather had an opportunity that other people didn't have that set the path of this legacy for her," Israel says.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5600. Las Vegas Inventory Hits Record High as Buyer Demand Sinks—but One Surprising Segment Defies the Slump

Housing inventory in Las Vegas surged to an all-time high in October as high mortgage rates priced out everyday buyers, yet the luxury tier of the local market continued to outperform.

Active listings in Nevada's largest metro jumped nearly 10% year over year, reaching 11,447 units—the highest level on record for Realtor.com® data going back to July 2016, according to the October housing market report.

Tania Jhayem, a real estate agent at Keller Williams The Marketplace's luxury division in Las Vegas, says that mortgage rates exceeding 7% and broader affordability headwinds have encouraged buyers to be far more selective.

"After several years of an extremely competitive housing market, we're seeing a shift toward more balanced conditions, where buyers have additional choices and sellers are adjusting to a different pace," Jhayem tells Realtor.com.

New listings—a measure of fresh homes hitting the market—plunged 10.5% compared to last year, further underscoring a wider market cooldown.

Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel notes that new listings accounted for less than a quarter of the overall inventory in October compared to 30.4% a year ago. The result is an inventory that is growing increasingly stale.

The typical for-sale home in Las Vegas lingered on the market for 59 days last month, two days longer than during the same period in 2025.

While the selection for sale may not be the freshest this fall—with half of the available homes sitting on the market for nearly two months—the buildup offers buyers a key advantage: time.

"Buyers who previously felt priced out or pressured into quick decisions now have more opportunities to explore their options," says Jhayem. "For sellers, proper pricing, presentation, and marketing have become increasingly important. Ultimately, we're seeing a market where both buyers and sellers are becoming more deliberate in their decisions."

Homes lingering on the market present well-prepared shoppers with opportunities to negotiate favorable terms, including price cuts, closing-cost assistance, repairs, or mortgage rate buydowns.

This fall, house hunters can also take their time to evaluate properties, review comparable sales, and make informed decisions without the intense pressure seen in recent years.

Yet, a prolonged listing history does not always spell a bargain: Some homes require major updates, have features that appeal to a small pool of would-be buyers, or are simply mispriced.

The record-setting inventory buildup was not an overnight development. Data analysis reveals that active listings in Las vegas have climbed steadily since January.

"That's a massive part of what's going on in markets like Vegas—not just in October but over the last several months as rates have risen and erased the financing advantage that buyers had enjoyed for much of this year compared to last," notes Krimmel.

The median asking price in Las Vegas registered at $459,900 in October, down 2.6% year over year but still nearly $45,000 higher than the national price. Meanwhile, contract signings were down by more than 25% year over year, outpacing the 17% decline recorded nationally.

Despite the slowdown, sellers are keeping their cool: Roughly 24% of all listings in Vegas saw price reductions, down 1.4 percentage points from last year. Mirroring the broader national trend, the dip suggests that sellers are in no rush to hand out concessions just to offload properties.

"Many of the homeowners choosing to sell today are doing so because of important life transitions rather than simply reacting to market conditions," says the Vegas agent. "We're seeing reasons to sell that include job relocations, growing families, retirees looking to downsize, estate settlements, and homeowners seeking properties that better fit their current lifestyles."

Jhayem points out that one of the important differences between today's market and previous downturns is that many local homeowners have built substantial equity, which provides greater flexibility and allows sellers to make more strategic decisions about when and how to sell.

"Homeowners with favorable mortgage rates and no immediate need to move may choose to stay put, while those ready for their next chapter are continuing to move forward," she adds.

While the broader Las Vegas housing market cooled, the upper tier heated up.

The entry threshold for the top 10% of the metro's housing market reached $1.2 million in October, up 2.2% from a year ago, marking the 10th-biggest price growth among the 43 largest metros, according to the latest Realtor.com luxury housing report.

According to Krimmel, this divergence stems from two market dynamics: robust demand from wealthy, well-capitalized buyers who are less sensitive to high mortgage rates, and the resilience of the luxury tier buoyed by sellers who can afford to wait for their target sale price.

"While the general market is maybe kind of softening, the ultraluxury market ... there's no breaks in store for it," Natalia Harris, global real estate adviser with Las Vegas Sotheby's International Realty, tells Realtor.com.

Harris points out that so far in 2026, there have been 23 properties in Vegas that were sold for over $10 million, with two more under contract. This is up from the 18 that were sold in that price range all of last year.

The adviser attributes this trend in part to Nevada's tax-friendly climate and pro-business policies, which continue to draw a steady stream of what she jokingly calls "refugees" from higher-taxation markets in California and Washington.

The other part of the equation, according to Harris, is the evolution of Las Vegas from a weekend gambling getaway destination into a prestigious sports and entertainment capital.

Jhayem agrees, stressing that year to year, Las Vegas continues to demonstrate its appeal as a luxury hub drawing deep-pocketed buyers relocating for lifestyle upgrades, tax considerations, and long-term investment goals.

"Our city offers an exceptional combination of luxury living, entertainment, dining, outdoor recreation, and relative value compared with many other major metropolitan areas," she says.

While rising luxury asking-price thresholds are an encouraging indication of the market's positioning, high-end properties are still taking longer to sell compared to average homes.

In October, the median days on the market for a luxury listing reached 73, a full week slower than a year ago. According to Jhayem, the longer wait time comes down to high net worth buyers being increasingly selective and placing a greater emphasis on quality, location, and value.

"Overall, I see Las Vegas transitioning toward a more balanced, opportunity-driven market," concludes the agent. "Buyers have greater choice and negotiating power, while sellers who approach the market strategically can still achieve successful outcomes. Today's market is less about urgency and more about making informed decisions."

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5597. Cisco research: Trust, not technology, is now the speed limit on enterprise AI

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

For several years, the conversation about enterprise artificial intelligence has focused on capability: which model is smartest and which GPU is fastest. That made sense when technology was the constraint.

It isn’t anymore. AI can now do far more than most organizations will allow, and the gap is trust.

That’s the core finding of “Permission to Scale: The Critical Role of Trust in Successful AI Adoption,” new research released today at Cisco Systems Inc.’s Cisco Live APJC in Melbourne. Authored by independent researcher Brad Howarth, the study draws on data from 25 Australian organizations.

At Cisco Live APJC, Cisco hosted a press panel to discuss the report. The panel, moderated by Howarth, featured a number of corporate leaders from companies that participated in the report, including Carl Solder, chief technology officer of Cisco ANZ (far left); Anna Tosky, chief people officer at Elmo Software (second from left); Chris Locke, CTO at Flight Center Travel Group (third from left); Naz Wilson, group culture and enablement manager at Funlab (third from right); and Lucio Ribeiro, chief AI officer at TBWA Australia (second from right).

Though a sample size of 25 is small, the results align with conversations I’ve had with corporate leadership. I appreciated the panel’s mix of technologies, human resources and cultural leadership. I also valued the mix of roles, as the biggest barrier to scaling AI isn’t technical but people-related.

Australia makes an interesting test case. According to University of Melbourne and KPMG research cited in the report, half of Australians use AI regularly, but only 36% trust it, and just 30% believe its benefits outweigh its risks. That’s the lowest among 47 countries surveyed. If you can build trust in AI in Australia, that work will scale globally. In the press release, Stefan Leitl, vice president and general manager of Cisco Australia and New Zealand, discussed the benefits of winning over this region: “It’s a playbook that travels well beyond Australia.”

Solder noted that among the six pillars in Cisco’s AI Readiness Index, chief information officers and CTOs gravitate toward what they know, namely infrastructure and data, and leave culture for others. He described a customer that invested in infrastructure, governance, data and information technology skills but “didn’t focus on the culture. And they found that there was a big pushback from their employees and customers on using the toolsets they’ve invested in.”

This is something I’ve seen repeatedly: Companies spend millions on AI platforms only to see utilization remain tepid. Howarth discussed an adoption “flywheel” in which successful use creates evidence, evidence builds trust and trust enables broader use. Companies sit around waiting for trust before deploying, and the evidence of trust must be something measurable.

Trust in AI needs to be established with realistic parameters. Many people reject AI after a single mistake, even though in most cases the error rate is much lower than that of people. This mirrors what the automotive industry went through when a Tesla accident would trigger a media storm. The reality is that Tesla’s Autopilot system experiences one crash for about every 7 million miles, compared with human drivers, who average about one crash every 1 million miles.

Perfection isn’t a realistic goal, but being faster and more accurate than others is. Users should understand this going into any kind of trial or proof of concept, as the expectation of perfection can erode trust.

Chris Locke offered a great example of an executive leading by example. The company’s 77-year-old founder, Graham “Skroo” Turner, uses AI every day. “He’s a big Anthropic Claude user,” Locke said. “This is also a guy who once said the internet wouldn’t catch on back in 2000. He may have gotten that one wrong, but he’s betting on AI catching on, so I think he gives us permission to play.”

Ribeiro outlined a more structured approach, describing trust as an equation built on four elements: ownership, competence, consistency and transparency. He was matter-of-fact about why asking a nervous workforce whether it wants AI doesn’t yield an accurate answer. “You never ask a barber if you need a haircut, as the answer is always yes.”

His alternative was honesty. Companies can’t promise to protect every job, but they can promise to make employees “the most prepared, trained, trusted person” if AI disrupts their role.

Funlab, where 79% of the workforce is 21 or younger, relies on peer learning. Its “AI Super Squad” convenes representatives from every department every four weeks. Wilson said early sessions simply clarified which tools were safe, because many employees’ real limitation was “just not knowing whether I am allowed to do certain things or not.”

The report’s central concept is calibrated trust. People need to know when to rely on AI, when to verify its outputs, and when a human must decide. Blindly trusting these systems and their outputs is a significant risk.

During the Q&A, I asked how companies protect against over-trust, especially in high-intensity jobs where people just take the answer and move on. Tosky was candid. “The AI slop. It’s real,” she said. “You ask the employee a question, prompt the AI system and then they send a report without looking at it, and it’s completely wrong. It’s 10 pages you now have to read.”

Elmo keeps a human in the loop on nearly everything, and she argued that the fix starts with redesigning the work. “It’s very unsexy, but start with the process itself, instead of just going, ‘OK, let’s throw a bunch of agents at it.'”

The report recommends that IT leaders adopt a specific practice: Stop treating log-ins as a proxy for trust, and track how often people challenge or override AI outputs. Usage shows people are clicking. Override rates show they’re thinking.

I also raised a contact center concern. AI automates the mundane tasks that served as cognitive breaks for agents, leaving them with nonstop, high-intensity work and higher churn. Tosky called it “AI brain fry” and suggested rethinking metrics and breaks. Wilson added that if AI absorbs routine work, employees lose the repetition that builds context and expertise. That’s a talent pipeline problem few companies are considering.

AI that drafts content is one thing; agents that act are another. Locke said Flight Centre now has agents handling a small subset of airline ticketing that was previously outsourced offshore, with security engaged from day one. He used AI to book his Uber to the event, but a return flight to Europe? “Not yet.”

Fewer than half of respondents are very or extremely confident that their foundations are ready for more autonomous AI, and more than half say their infrastructure needs upgrading. Cisco’s 2026 Relentless Defense report found that only 36% of Australian organizations apply consistent controls to AI agents and nonhuman identities. In the report, Lendi Group CTO Devesh Maheshwari described the target as “bounded autonomy, where the agent can act on your behalf but cannot go beyond the boundaries you have established.”

This is where Cisco can help its enterprise customers. Solder argues that trust must be enforced at the network and security layers. “Built into the network and security underneath, control stops being the brake and becomes the permission to move faster,” he said. Cisco is betting that its networking, security and Splunk portfolio will become the trust layer for agentic AI, and the report provides a business rationale for that bet.

As I stated above, the research is qualitative and aligns with what I hear from CIOs globally. My advice for IT leaders:

The AI winners won’t necessarily have the best models. They’ll have employees, boards and customers who trust the systems enough to let them do more. As Solder put it, “The leaders in our research aren’t scaling AI first. They’re scaling trust.”

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5596. ‘Home Is Where You Spend’: How Your Neighborhood Shapes Your Buying Habits

Your home isn't just where you live; it's also where you spend the majority of your money, a new study from financial technology platform Bilt has found.

Bilt partnered with 451 Research and S&P Global on the 2026 State of the Neighborhood survey, aimed at exploring consumer spending habits as it doubles down on American business with the launch of Bilt Neighborhood OS and the expansion of its membership platform.

Bilt Neighborhood OS is an AI operating system and commerce network designed to unlock America's $6.6 trillion neighborhood commerce opportunity to help businesses grow without replacing their existing systems, the company says.

In the consumer spending survey, around two-thirds of the 6,951 survey participants conducted at least 80% of their "everyday spending" within 15 miles of their homes, and 92% of those surveyed planned on spending the same or more at local businesses in the coming months.

That's not surprising, given the results of a recent Re/Max survey, which found that 29% of prospective homeowners valued proximity to grocery stores and shopping, while 20% said they valued having restaurants and cafes nearby.

More than half of all survey respondents said future neighborhood development, including new housing or retail development, was "very important" to how they chose where to buy a home.

The results of the Bilt survey spell good news for small businesses in popular residential areas, suggesting that physical stores close to dense residential neighborhoods may continue to thrive in the age of online shopping.

"The disconnect between what people talk about versus where people actually spend is quite significant," Ankur Jain, founder and CEO of Bilt, tells Realtor.com®. "When you you look at the stats, all online shopping in the U.S. is $1.3 trillion a year. But offline, small- and medium-business local retail and food spending is $6.6 trillion."

On a quarterly basis, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, that broke down to $340.2 billion in online spending in the second quarter, making up 17.1% of total consumer spending.

Bilt's study found that 70% of food and grocery spending is still made in person.

Consumers spent an average of $375 on in-person grocery shopping each month. They spent an additional $175 on in-person dining and takeout and another $175 on in-person general shopping. Study participants reported spending an average of $50 each on entertainment and recreation; health and personal care; and transportation.

Sixty-six percent of survey respondents said they were were actively looking to support local businesses over big-box and online retailers and were willing to spend more to support them.

A recent report on consumer spending habits around the holidays from research firm Epsilon found that Gen Z in particular values in-store options for gift shopping. And while online shopping is still, overall, the preferred method for gift shopping, the study found that consumers across all generatios are doing the majority of their food and decoration shopping in person. Furthermore, they spent about an equal amount of their holiday clothing budgets online and in store.

One possible reason for the continued primacy of in-person shopping is consumers' paradoxical relationship with artificial intelligence marketing.

Research from McKinsey found that AI continues to drive sales and that AI usage in completing purchases climbed 70% year over year. However, younger, more tech-native shoppers "tend to be more skeptical of AI on average," the report found. (Sixty-seven percent of American Gen Z AI users trust AI chat and search tools versus the global average of 73%.)

The study was conducted in advance of Bilt launching its new offerings. Alongside Bilt Neighborhood OS, the Bilt Membership Platform is an expansion of the company's existing membership and loyalty technology. The company says it will enable organizations to launch their own branded membership programs via white-labeling or extend existing loyalty programs into the neighborhood.

"We are betting pretty big on the neighborhood versus online commerce," Jain says. "There is a huge gap between what the media and the Silicon Valley world talk about versus how real Americans are living. People talk about AI as 'How are we going to do online commerce AI and replace coding and jobs and all this stuff.'

"The truth is, the biggest beneficiaries of AI can be the local mom and pop businesses who don't have the ability to hire 2,000 people to go compete with, like, a Walmart or Amazon online.

"Everything is tied together. The more you can invest in the neighborhood, the more value you create in the housing. The more housing you have, the more you can invest in the neighborhood," he adds.

Bilt also announced a coalition of partners spanning payments, point-of-sale technology, reservations, and commerce platforms. Partners include Altamarea Group, AM Parking, Bungalow Hospitality Management, ByNext, FlyBox, Lettuce Entertain You, Lowe’s, Prince Street Hospitality Group, The Dinex Group, Thumbtack, among others.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5595. What real estate agents should watch on Election Day, per NAHB

NAHB’s Ken Wingert on housing and the midterms, from state ballot measures and the ROAD to Housing Act to tariffs, labor and mortgage rates.

Housing may not be on many ballots by name on Nov. 3, but it’s running through nearly every race.

With the midterms set for Tuesday, candidates from both parties are pitching voters on affordability. Lawmakers are campaigning on the recently passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, states from California to Massachusetts are voting on measures meant to make building easier, and homebuilders are grappling with tariffs and immigration enforcement that have driven up costs and thinned out job-site crews.

Inman spoke with Ken Wingert, chief advocacy officer at the National Association of Home Builders, about the races and ballot measures NAHB is watching, whether data centers are really competing with housing for land, and what agents should keep an eye on as votes are counted.

Inman: What are two or three outcomes to the midterms you think matter most for housing — on the federal- level and state-level?

Ken Wingert: The overall theme is that this is turning out to be, once again, an affordability election, and housing is at the top of that pain point … because we don’t have enough of it. So regardless of who controls Congress or who wins the governor’s race in any given state, I think housing will be near or at the top of the agenda going into 2027. That gives us, and other groups you’re probably talking to, a lot of opportunity to advocate for more housing supply.

On specific issues, people are starting to understand that supply matters. You’re seeing ballot initiatives in a number of states aimed at making it easier for builders to build and cutting some of that red tape. Members of Congress are running on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Congress is still debating permitting reform that may pass in the lame-duck session or get kicked to the next Congress.

From a congressional standpoint, if Democrats win at least one chamber, there will probably be more pushback and oversight on issues like tariffs and immigration, which have made it harder for builders to build more housing, or at least more expensive.

Are there specific races that NAHB is watching closely, at the state, federal or local level?

We’re not quite NAR size, but we’re involved in a lot. At the federal level, I think we’ll see how big a wave is, if one materializes, and whether it takes out some folks who have been very helpful on housing over the years.

Financial Services Chairman French Hill will be fine, I think, but he’s in a tighter race than expected. Mike Hill, chairman of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, faces the same challenge. In Michigan, Bill Huizenga is a former Realtor and builder. Sherrod Brown, former chair of the Banking Committee, is potentially coming back to the Senate from Ohio. A lot of folks are watching that race.

But really, at the state level: California has a couple of ballot initiatives, one in particular we’ve been involved with on changes to CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act. The legislature had made some changes, and this would codify them in state law. In Massachusetts, we’re supporting a ballot initiative that would reduce minimum lot sizes, meaning how big your lot has to be to build on it. And there are a bunch of funding ballot initiatives around the country. All of those aim to increase supply, so we’re keyed in on those state-level races.

I’ve seen candidates from both parties campaigning on the recently passed ROAD to Housing Act. Does that kind of policy achievement resonate with voters, or does a general affordability pitch resonate more?

Both parties are campaigning on the fact that Congress passed major housing legislation with overwhelming bipartisan support. Beyond affordability, another theme in this election is that people want less divisiveness and more collaboration to solve problems. ROAD to Housing was a great example of both parties giving up a few things to get a bill they wanted.

I don’t know that the average voter is digging into a bill with 60 titles, but they understand that Congress recognized a housing supply problem and is at least trying to fix it. If I’m running for Congress, that’s something I’m going to go out and tell people.

Have you noticed more local candidates running explicitly on pro-housing or YIMBY platforms? Any examples?

Our state and local associations make their own endorsements and funding decisions, so, honestly, I’m too far removed to say whether a certain state rep in Texas is doing X.

One interesting part of this election is that the NIMBY focus has shifted from housing to data centers. The recognition that we need more housing has shifted more in the YIMBY direction. That’s a dynamic we’re not encouraging, because data centers are a separate issue, but it’s been interesting.

Talking to our locals, more folks at the city council and county level, where the rubber really meets the road on development, are talking about the need to build more affordable and workforce housing.

We’ve seen in our own polling a real desire, and real angst, from younger voters who feel they can’t afford a home, and from their parents, who are also worried their kids can’t afford a home, may be living with them for a long time, and want them to stay in their state and area and raise their families there. That underlying affordability challenge is driving a lot of the rhetoric and, quite frankly, a lot of the ads. They may not mention housing specifically, but it’s embedded in broader affordability concerns.

You mentioned data centers. I’ve written a couple of stories about data centers competing with housing development for the same land. Is that something NAHB has seen? Is it a real phenomenon?

I think it’s a little overblown, at least right now. A lot of the areas where they’re looking to build data centers aren’t necessarily areas where you would build housing. So there may be some competition over land, but it’s not as big an issue as people may think.

The larger issue is competition for labor. Residential construction always competes with commercial construction for talent and labor, whether it’s somebody building an office building or a house. That competition is real, but it also means more investment in workforce training and more attention to the trades.

We’ve seen many large tech companies announce they’ll fund apprenticeship and training programs because they also need those workers. So there may be some trickle-down help for homebuilding. But it’s still too soon to see real impact, beyond utilities and similar things.

Speaking of labor, I’ve seen quite a few stories about how immigration policy and enforcement have affected construction labor. Has NAHB seen that, what’s your stance, and how have you worked with lawmakers on it?

We’ve definitely heard a lot about it, especially in the last few months. It’s been primarily in Southern states, but not exclusively.

The big concern from members is that the way enforcement is being carried out, whether at the local level, by ICE or some combination, is scaring off all Hispanic workers, regardless of immigration status or citizenship. They’re coming onto job sites, rounding everyone up and detaining folks for hours, repeatedly showing up or pulling people over in a van on the way to a job site. That’s made it very hard to retain workers or get them to show up, because there’s a fear factor in the Hispanic community about even U.S. citizens and green card holders getting roped in with folks who may not be here legally.

That’s caused delays on job sites and made it hard to find labor, period, because there’s no immediate replacement. That’s why we’re so focused on workforce training.

I think it’ll be a factor in places like Texas and Florida, and in the electoral outcome. You’re already seeing Hispanic turnout larger than historic levels. Some polling shows that even folks who supported the president on immigration, who maybe voted for him based on closing the border and enforcement, feel the enforcement has gone too far. It’ll be interesting to see what the exit polls show.

Inman’s core audience is real estate agents. What should agents pay the most attention to in these midterms? Does it depend on their local market, or is there something general to watch?

Disclosure: I used to work for NAR, too, so I understand where they’re coming from. I don’t know if there’s one particular issue, or whether it’s about the House or Senate flipping. It’s the overall voter mindset. If Congress changes control, or a governorship flips one way or the other, does it have an immediate impact? Does it change the [Trump] administration’s course? Those are all open questions.

Ultimately, voters hope inflation can be tamed, and interest rates obviously drive much of this for agents. Resolving the situation in Iran, and maybe dialing back some tariff policies, could affect the inflation numbers driving interest rates. If we can get rates back down, certainly below 7 percent and into the mid-6s, that will unlock a lot of demand that’s still out there but has moved to the sidelines over the last six months.

It’s hard to see how those things will change, no matter the outcome. They all feel very up in the air.

Yeah, but there’s a certain psyche to it. We saw this after the 2024 election. Everyone’s so wrapped up in politics now that people go into a weird holding pattern for the last month or two before an election. They say, “I’m going to wait until after the election and see, and then make a major decision.”

Uncertainty is a factor, and depending on your political outlook, you may be much happier on Nov. 4, or you may not be. But at least it resolves one more question mark for the next two years before we start a presidential cycle.

I hope that, whatever the outcome, having the election behind us will ease angst for potential buyers and sellers, calm the overall market, and get it moving again.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#5594. California Voters Reject ‘Billionaires Tax’ Amid Fears of an Exodus of Wealth from the State

California voters have rejected a proposed wealth tax, which could have meant a one-time influx of billions for the state but threatened to trigger an exodus of billionaires in the state.

The ballot measure, one of several housing issues Californians considered, is projected by the Associated Press to narrowly fail, with 53% voting against the measure with most votes counted a week after Election Day. Proposition 40 would have created a one-time 5% wealth tax on individuals with a net worth above $1 billion.

The Service Employees International Union–United Healthcare Workers West, which backed the measure, said it could have offset federal funding cuts. It estimated the one time tax could have brought in $100 billion in one-time revenue.

But the measure could have affected about 200 people, and billionaires in the state have put significant money toward fighting it. The California Budget & Policy Center estimates they hold a combined $2 trillion in wealth. Proposition 40 excludes real property holdings from determining an individual's net worth.

State leaders say tax could trigger some of those wealthy people to flee the state and take their spending with them. The National Taxpayers Union Foundation estimates California could collect $40 billion from the tax. But it could lose $25 billion in other taxes if wealthy people leave.

Governor Gavin Newsom opposed the measure. "This will be defeated, there's no question in my mind," Newsom told the New York Times, as it reported that several wealthy people had begun moving assets out of the state.

Palantir and PayPal co-founder Peter Thiel and Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin all have reportedly moved some assets to Florida. Voters in that state approved a measure on Tuesday that would reform its property tax system, potentially setting it up to be yet more attractive.

However, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg had pledged to remain in California, where he has spent more than $112 million assembling a megacompound in Palo Alto. Earlier this year, Zuckerberg reached an agreement with Meta board to remain in California regardless of the outcome of Prop 40. He would have faced a potential tax bill of some $12.5 billion if the measure had passed.

Taxes raised by Prop 40 would have gone to health care, education, or food assistance. But the state legislature would have had discretion to determine how those funds are used.

The California Association of Realtors President Tamara Suminski said at an elections forum last month that it opposed the measure. CAR is concerned about the potential loss of tax revenue and the state's economic competitiveness, she said.

"Prop 40 is just a bad idea," Jennifer Barrera, President & CEO, California Chamber of Commerce, said at the event. "Billionaires are the individuals who have the ability to move quickly, they have the ability to live outside the state, they don't have to be in California. And yet they pay a tremendous amount of revenue to our general fund if they're living here."

Two other items on the ballot, Proposition 41 and 42 both aim to block or counter Proposition 40, but their language could have much broader implications, Barrera said.

But even if Proposition 40 were to pass, it would invite years of litigation, said Joe Bishop‐​Henchman, executive vice president at National Taxpayers Union Foundation. Prop 40 applies to all of a California-domiciled billionaire's holdings across the globe, inviting Constitutional challenges.

And then there's the matter of actually calculating net worth. Wealthy individuals hold assets that can be hard to value, such as patents, artwork, and stakes in private companies. So, would likely take years of expensive legal process to determine how much to tax them.

"The Franchise Tax Board currently has no infrastructure for valuing these types of assets," Bishop‐​Henchman said. "Valuing these kinds of assets will entail years of costly litigation on both ends and establishment of an extensive and costly administrative apparatus for an ostensibly 'one-time' tax."

Californians meanwhile also voted on a set of other measures. Voters passed Proposition 1 to authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in bonds to support housing affordability programs. Co-chairs of its organizing campaign Chione Flegal and Ray Pearl called the win "a resounding show of support for affordable housing."

Voters also approved Proposition 37, which creates a $25 billion loan program for middle-income buyers to purchase new homes. Realtor.com economist Joel Berner said this could be a boon for new home sales. But he cautioned it might not touch the more expensive parts of the state.

"The complicating factor here is that the major California metro areas are short on newly built homes below $1.5 million, and the ballot measure does nothing to address the supply of these homes, only bolstering demand for them," Berner said.

"Proposition 37 has the potential to help prospective California homebuyers, but only if they can find new homes to buy," he said.

The California Association of Realtors, a major supporter of Proposition 37, cheered the result.

“This measure will help create more housing, provide low-cost down payment options and give teachers, nurses, firefighters and other hardworking Californians a better opportunity to own a home in the communities they serve," Suminski said. "We look forward to working with stakeholders to bring Proposition 37 to life and deliver on its promise for California families.”

But, voters rejected the controversial Proposition 45. It would have set timelines on environmental reviews for some projects under the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA.

California earned an F grade on the Realtor.com® State-by-State Housing Report Card. It tracks how effectively each state balances affordability and new construction.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5593. Why real estate agents wanted Barbara Corcoran for ICNY ’27

Barbara Corcoran (l) onstage at Inman Connect San Francisco 2015, Holly Meyer Lucas (r) onstage at Inman Connect San Diego 2026 |

As our team at Inman began planning Inman Connect New York this January, we asked real estate agents a fairly straightforward question: “In this market, who do you want to hear from most right now?”

The overwhelming response was Barbara Corcoran.

I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about that answer, because I think it tells us something interesting about the current state of real estate, the people who work in it and what they’re looking for from our industry’s leaders.

For context, before becoming Inman’s CMO, I spent years building a $100 million-plus producing real estate team in South Florida. I’ve personally sold more than 1,000 homes, ranging from properties under $20,000 to deals north of $20 million.

I’ve represented distressed sellers, helped families through extraordinarily difficult circumstances and negotiated transactions where getting to the closing table meant everything to the people involved. I’ve also mentored, trained and managed hundreds of agents through slow markets, busy markets and everything the last decade has thrown at us.

My point: I’ve carried the bag, and I understand my real estate agent brethren.

So, all summer when agents told me how much they are struggling (in what should be peak homebuying season), I took that seriously. For the past several months, I’ve heard from some of the most successful agents in the country who were going months without closing a transaction. These are experienced professionals who have built substantial businesses and survived multiple market cycles, suddenly finding themselves in unfamiliar territory.

Meanwhile, the industry around them is in a rather extraordinary state of upheaval. Major brokerages are consolidating, brokerages and MLSs are suing one another, the debate over private listings continues to divide the industry, and NAR is working to rebuild trust following several tumultuous years.

And somewhere in the middle of all this, agents are trying to sell houses while being told to post more on social media, stay hydrated and use more AI.

Our industry has some consequential decisions ahead of it, and the people making those decisions deserve to be questioned. Inman’s newsroom has an important responsibility to cover these issues, and our events should provide a place for the people involved to explain their positions.

But there’s another conversation agents want to have, and I think their overwhelming request for Barbara tells us exactly what it is.

They want to hear from someone who has been in their shoes, knows how to get scrappy in a down market to sell real estate, and can offer an experienced perspective without having to defend a corporate agenda.

One of my favorite anecdotes about Barbara is one that she shares often and seems to take enormous pride in — how gritty she was in her early life. Her LinkedIn bio opens with: “Barbara Corcoran’s credits include straight D’s in high school and college and 20 jobs by the time she turned 23.”

Tell me that doesn’t win the heart of a real estate agent. Our industry has a remarkable way of attracting people who struggled to find their place elsewhere.

Some weren’t great students. Others bounced around between jobs before finding real estate. I’ve met extraordinarily successful agents who can negotiate their way through an impossible transaction, recognize an opportunity before anyone else and build a relationship with practically anyone, and yet were kicked out of school when they were younger. (Looking at you, James Harris!)

Barbara herself has spoken openly about her struggles in school and dyslexia and how the challenges she experienced influenced the way she approached business. (I’ve got a completely unscientific theory about how I think many of America’s top-producing real estate agents who claim they struggled in school but are elite at selling are all actually just dyslexic, but I’ll save that for another time.)

Real estate agents find Barbara’s story particularly inspiring because real estate has always been an industry where people can build extraordinary careers around abilities that aren’t necessarily rewarded in a classroom, and Barbara took those abilities and turned a $1,000 loan into one of the most recognizable real estate brokerages in the country. She is one of us, and she made it out on the other side a literal Shark. And agents love her for it.

To boot, she built The Corcoran Group in New York City, where competition was fierce and standing out required creativity — something agents covet and understand deeply. Long before agents were being told to become content creators, Barbara understood how to make herself and her business interesting to the public. She launched market reports, generated publicity and became a recognizable authority on New York real estate.

She understood personal brand marketing before most of our industry knew what to call it.

She sold her brokerage in 2001 and went on to build another career as an entrepreneur, investor and television personality. And now, after all of that, there she is sitting in a chair on Shark Tank, evaluating other entrepreneurs and deciding which businesses deserve her money.

Barbara understands something that most successful real estate agents figure out, and the new ones need to hear: A willingness to take risks, build relationships and solve problems can take you a very long way in this business.

And she’s spent enough time carrying the bag to know how to find business when everyone else is convinced there isn’t any. Her perspective on this is particularly valuable for agents to hear, if we consider the voices dominating our industry’s conversations right now.

The real estate conversations are dominated by brokerage executives defending their business models, MLS leaders explaining their policies and industry organizations navigating enormous changes; senators are filing FTC complaints against industry leaders, too. It’s overwhelming, and yet, none of it helps Susie Realtor or Mike Agent close a home this quarter.

There are important questions being debated about how homes should be marketed, who controls listing information, and how real estate professionals will operate in the years ahead, and while I do believe all of those discussions deserve a place on highly influential stages such as Inman Connect New York, agents also desperately need to hear from voices right now who don’t have a dog in the fight, who can hunker down on a mic and say, “OK, listen up, this is exactly what I would do right now if I were in your shoes.”

Barbara Corcoran is the real estate fairy godmother who is uniquely positioned to say that, without an obvious bias, something to sell the audience or any other ulterior motive. That dynamic really appeals to agents right now, who are growing tired of the industry’s constant infighting.

A real estate agent trying to figure out how to get their listing sold after sitting for 90-plus days, so they can get their client the win and feed their own family, is less concerned with which brokerage executive launches their AI tool most effectively and who is winning the latest argument about private listings.

Agents need a change of scenery right now, and Barbara knows how to generate business, find the buyer and create buzz around listings that have been sitting for weeks.

She’s also famously candid, and I suspect she will have plenty to say about what is happening in our industry.

My takeaway from the overwhelming request for Barbara is that agents are craving an independent voice of reason. Someone who understands the realities of selling real estate and can speak from experience.

And when our community made that request, we listened.

I want to give credit to Inman CEO Tom Bohn for taking the feedback seriously and making Barbara a priority for New York. One of the things I’ve appreciated about working with Tom is his willingness to listen to the real estate professionals who make up our community with fresh perspectives, while also prioritizing the industry leadership who are critical to our ecosystem as an industry.

We have an opportunity to put some of the smartest people in the business on our stages. I think we should pay particular attention when the people in our audience tell us whose perspective they value.

So, we got Barbara, and she’s going to tell our audience exactly what she would do right now. And we can’t wait to hear it.

Join us at Inman Connect New York, Jan. 26–28, 2027, at the New York Hilton Midtown.

#5592. Your Voice Matters: RISMedia Launches New Letters to the Editor Feature

From premarketing and private listings, to data ownership and MLS antitrust lawsuits, to massive consolidation, AI advancements, brokerage model productivity, affordability and so much more, the real estate industry is evolving faster than ever and on many fronts all at once. As news breaks almost daily and we jump between covering the topic of the day and breaking down what it all means via insights from industry leaders, the views of boots-on-the-ground, everyday practitioners–those in the trenches whose lives these big decisions affect daily–can sometimes get lost in the shuffle.

As the headlines come and go, you may nod in agreement or vehemently disagree; you may be aware of something a reporter overlooked or of an important viewpoint that hasn’t surfaced yet. You might chat around the water cooler the next day, text a colleague or post your thoughts on social media or under an article in the comments section, only to have them disappear as quickly as the next round of posts come flooding in. Your voice matters and deserves to be elevated.

As a leading industry media organization charged with the important responsibility of keeping you informed on the issues that matter to your bottom line, we also view our space as your “town square” in a sense, a place your professional community turns to for fair and balanced coverage, and to read what’s on the minds of your peers and how they are responding to the news of the day. We recognized in our current choice of options for that platform, an opportunity for improvement.

With that in mind, RISMedia is asking our readers to continue conversations that begin in our news coverage, offering a new Letters to the Editor platform where working agents, brokers, executives and industry thought leaders can speak out. Our goal with this new feature is to allow real estate professionals at every level to share their perspectives, opinions, commentary and criticisms related to issues that matter to our industry—just your words and thoughts, no writing experience necessary and no pay-to-play.

The space, prominently accessible on our website navigation, was created for you to share thoughtful, original letters responding or relating to an issue, event or industry practice that was covered in our digital news over the previous few weeks.

Your viewpoints can provide a vital reality check on high-level reporting, where a national headline might only tell the story from the thousand-foot level, but your local market insights can offer invaluable perspectives that can enlighten your peers and possibly influence the industry’s top leaders or policy makers who look to trade media to weigh decision-making.

Oftentimes in our industry, the narrative is shaped by a small but vocal few at the top of the ranks while the challenges of today’s market–of which are many–and the daily grind of doing business right now–are carried out by the quiet majority of independent contractors at the heart of the business, doing their level best every day to move the market forward.

It’s never been a more dynamic time to be a real estate professional in the United States, and the stakes are too high on too many issues to stay silent. So the next time you pause on a headline, we hope you’ll take a moment to step into the town square and share your thoughts with your community. You can read the guidelines for submitting a Letter to the Editor and share your thoughts with us here.

Beth McGuire is RISMedia’s vice president of online editorial.

#5591. Alphabet’s Wing to invest $125M in new delivery drone factory

Wing Aviation LLC today announced plans to spend $125 million on the construction of a new delivery drone factory.

The initiative is part of a broader investment that also encompasses the Alphabet Inc. unit’s research and development teams in California. Additionally, Wing stated that it plans to invest in the communities where it operates. It currently offers deliveries in five U.S. cities and intends to bring its service to 14 more markets soon.

Wing is building its factory in Fort Worth, Texas. The 15,000-square-foot facility is expected to create up to 100 jobs. Wing says it will have capacity to make tens of thousands of delivery drones per year, which should significantly speed up its market expansion efforts.

The Alphabet unit’s drones reportedly have a wingspan of about 4.9 feet. They’re based on a frame made of styrofoam, a foam that mostly consists of trapped air, and carbon fibers. Styrofoam is lightweight and repels water, which comes handy when a drone is navigating challenging weather. The frame’s carbon fibers, in turn, boost its sturdiness.

The drone frame is equipped with 16 electric rotors that enable it to reach speeds of up to 60 miles per hour. Workers at stores that use Wing’s delivery service attach merchandise to its drones via a tether. After a drone takes off, it reels in the tether until the package comes into physical contact with its frame. When it reaches the customer’s house, the drone descends to an altitude of 20 feet and lowers the parcel.

Wing has built a software stack that automates much of the work involved in coordinating deliveries. It picks the most suitable drone for a given delivery run, plans its flight path and ensures that it won’t interfere with other drones. Human safety teams monitor for weather and air traffic changes that may make it necessary to adjust flight plans.

The unit plans to make its delivery service available to more than 40 million Americans by 2027. It’s pursuing the growth initiative in partnership with retailers such as Walmart Inc., which uses its drones to process e-commerce purchases. Last month, the latter company announced plans to make Wing deliveries available at more than 270 stores.

The Alphabet unit also intends to offer its service in Japan. Last month, it teamed up with Tokyo-based internet provider KDDI Corp. to make drone deliveries available to local consumers in 2027.

Although the drone delivery market is in an early stage, Wing already faces a significant amount of competition. In August, Amazon.com Inc. announced plans to make its Prime Air service available in nearly 500 U.S. markets by year’s end. More recently, drone delivery startup Zipline International Inc. raised $1.5 billion in funding at a $21.5 billion valuation.

#5590. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

Jimmy Burgess is the Chief Coaching Officer for HomeServices of America and President of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Get connected on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5589. Inflation Remains Hot in October and Strengthens Case for Another Fed Rate Hike

Inflation accelerated faster than anticipated in October, driven by surging costs for housing and food, which will bolster the case for another Federal Reserve interest rate hike next month.

On a monthly basis, overall prices rose 0.4%, according to the Consumer Price Index (CPI) data released released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) on Tuesday. That's down from the 0.6% monthly increase recorded in September but higher than the 0.2% gain forecasted by economists.

CPI measures the average costs consumers pay for a range of goods, including food, energy, commodities, and services.

Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy categories, rose 0.3%, also exceeding the anticipated 0.2% increase.

The BLS did not publish an official annual inflation rate because last year's government shutdown prevented the agency from collecting survey data for October 2025.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.
