#5588. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5587. IBM builds on hybrid cloud and governance to advance its enterprise AI operating model

Enterprises are moving beyond AI pilots, putting greater emphasis on governance, production readiness and measurable business outcomes.

Research from Deloitte highlights a significant gap between enterprise AI ambition and execution: 54% of organizations plan to move at least 40% of their AI initiatives into production within six months. Yet only 25% have done so today. IBM is betting on its strengths — mainframe hardware, hybrid computing assets and a legacy of strong governance — to gain a leg up on the rest of the market, according to theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante.

“In our opinion, IBM has found a differentiated path in enterprise AI by productizing workflow-level outcomes across a stack that, while sometimes confusing, customers generally trust,” he said. “Client Zero proof, a workload-first hybrid design, durable platforms reimagined for agents and a pragmatic quantum roadmap create a credible basis for sustained advantage.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of how enterprise AI has moved beyond the race for model supremacy, with major technology players now focused on enabling governed enterprise AI that delivers trust, reliability and predictable business outcomes. (* Disclosure below.)

IBM already has a substantial book of business around generative AI, with AI-related software sales and consulting engagements totaling more than $12.5 billion as of Q4 2025, up from $9.5 billion the previous quarter.

Through a series of investments, acquisitions and product launches, IBM is gathering assets for an enterprise AI operating model with four pillars: agent orchestration, trusted data, intelligent operations and governance.

Many of these capabilities were rolled out as part of a steady drumbeat of announcements leading up to IBM Think 2026 in May. In February, the company announced a partnership with Deepgram Inc. to integrate voice capabilities into watsonx Orchestrate, its enterprise platform for building, deploying and managing agents. Two months later, it made IBM Bob — an AI-assisted coding tool that helps developers plan, write, test, modernize and deploy code —  globally available.

In May 2026, IBM completed its acquisition of Confluent, the data streaming platform, to enhance watsonx.data. By integrating streaming and real-time data, IBM aims to make watsonx.data the trusted data foundation, providing AI agents with continuously updated context.

At Think 2026, the company repositioned Concert from a point product into an agentic IT operations platform designed to unify observability, optimization, security and automation across hybrid environments. The move positions Concert as the intelligent operations layer of IBM’s broader enterprise AI strategy.

The IBM Sovereign Core platform announced at Think 2026 is designed to address the final pillar: governance. It helps enterprises build and operate AI-ready sovereign environments by embedding governance, compliance and operational control directly into the underlying infrastructure.

June brought more AI-related announcements: IBM joined OpenAI’s Daybreak Cyber Partner Program, which aims to identify AI-driven cybersecurity threats. IBM has partnered with Google Cloud to help IBM consultants design, build and govern enterprise-grade agents on Google Cloud.

All these announcements paint a picture: IBM wants to be the one-stop shop for enterprise AI, and to do so, it is investing significantly in new capabilities while leaning on its reputation for trusted enterprise security and governance, according to theCUBE Research’s John Furrier.

“While others chase frontier models, IBM is betting on something harder: trusted AI in production,” he told theCUBE. “The question coming out of Think is simple — are they becoming the system of record for enterprise AI or just another layer in the stack?”

In a media briefing ahead of Think 2026, IBM Chief Executive Arvind Krishna pointed out that over 70% of all enterprise data remains locked up in on-premises systems. That makes hybrid cloud a critical component of IBM’s enterprise AI operating model, allowing enterprises to use corporate data for AI workloads without abandoning existing infrastructure.

Recent earnings reports appear to reinforce IBM’s bet on hybrid cloud in the AI era. Red Hat Inc., whose OpenShift Kubernetes platform underpins IBM’s hybrid cloud software portfolio, saw revenue increase 13% year over year. Meanwhile, revenue from IBM Z, the company’s mainframe platform, saw revenues grow 51% year over year, underscoring the continued importance of mainframes in IBM’s infrastructure business.

IBM is embedding AI technology directly into IBM Z mainframes to support demanding AI workloads, according to Ric Lewis, senior vice president of the Infrastructure Division at IBM.  This strategy has resonated with clients and led to 20%-30% program-to-program growth for almost a decade. Z mainframes, a key priority for enterprises looking to deploy AI while maintaining control over their data and systems, are also a pillar of IBM’s sovereignty strategy.

“Sovereignty is our home court. We do 70% of the world’s financial transactions,” Lewis told theCUBE. “The most important data that travels around the world is in our Z systems. Those are sovereign systems. They’re on-prem, they’re in environments, they’re in banks, they’re in financial institutions, they’re in insurance. Sovereign is our home court, and we know this space extremely well.”

IBM’s view of sovereignty centers on customer control: keeping critical data and AI workloads in environments customers own and govern, rather than depending entirely on third-party infrastructure. Javier Olaizola, global managing partner for hybrid cloud and data at IBM Consulting, explained that the topic is coming up earlier in client engagements.

“Sovereignty and exposure was coming in on slide 40 in a PowerPoint pitch,” he told theCUBE. “Now it’s coming up front: ‘How much is my exposure?’ That is coming up with a new set of conversations that we are having with clients.”

Sovereign Core is the company’s answer to those questions, according to Sripriya Srinivasan, general manager for Core and ALM software products at IBM. Its goal is to help companies maintain operational consistency even as AI regulations and geopolitics constantly shift. It also helps companies contend with massive AI agent sprawl.

“The proliferation of agents is real in enterprises. Everybody is starting to build agents,” Srinivasan told theCUBE. “How do you, as a [chief information officer], make sure that there’s a level of standardization, consistency, governance, orchestration? All of these are internal fears, not necessarily coming, just based on regulations.”

How does this all translate to real-world results? It’s useful to look back at Krishna’s comments from Think 2026, where he presented IBM’s point of view on what makes a successful enterprise AI strategy.

“The enterprises pulling ahead are not deploying more AI; they’re redesigning how their business operates,” Krishna said during a media briefing.

IBM sets its own example by viewing itself as Client Zero for its enterprise AI strategy, according to James Kavanaugh, senior vice president and chief financial officer of IBM.

“AI is now embedded across our business, from how we deliver services to our software portfolio to the capabilities we are adding to our infrastructure platforms and how we drive our own productivity,” he said.

IBM reports that more than 80,000 of its employees use IBM Bob, with users reporting more than a 45 percent increase in productivity. Additionally, IBM Consulting has deployed more than 4,000 digital workers across 450 active projects, including agents from watsonx, Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC.

To keep this digital workforce under control, the company relies on a management philosophy that treats AI agents like human workers, an idea that Krishna himself suggested, explained Mohamad Ali, senior vice president and head of IBM Consulting.

“Arvind called me, and we had a conversation about three years ago, and he said, ‘I want you to come over, and I want you to be a consulting business,’” he said in an interview with theCUBE. “‘What is digital labor? It’s a whole bunch of bits of software. I need you to come in, and I need you to build this set of software and do it in a way that it could be managed. You could think of this as HR management … but now you have to HR manage human workers and digital workers.’”

IBM customers are also putting elements of the enterprise AI operating model into practice. Global bank BNP Paribas SA has nearly 1,000 AI use cases underway across its operations, using a group-level framework with governance distributed across business units and functions.

“The strategy is to use AI, not to become AI — to use AI to better serve our customers and to give more value to them,” Jean-Michel Garcia, group chief technology officer at BNP Paribas, told theCUBE. “But also internally, for employees, to give them more capabilities to focus on the right set of tasks and to make them more efficient and more focused on what they do.”

#5585. CTM Research Finds One in Five Adults Say They Tried to Contact a Mental Health Provider and Never Heard Back

New research examines persistent barriers to behavioral health care, generational differences in AI adoption, and the importance of human connection

ODENTON, Md. and MILLERSVILLE, Md., Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- One in five U.S. adults who tried to contact a mental health or addiction treatment provider reported they never received a response, according to CTM's second annual behavioral health survey. The findings reveal persistent challenges in accessing care and explore how consumers' attitudes toward artificial intelligence are shaping the way they seek behavioral health support.

The findings come amid ongoing challenges in the behavioral health system and growing interest in AI as a tool for navigating care. According to the Health Resources and Services Administration, 137 million Americans live in a mental health professional shortage area, underscoring the challenges many communities face in accessing care.

CTM's research suggests that while people are exploring new options, getting connected to a person who can help remains central to the care journey. Three-quarters of respondents said they are comfortable speaking with a live person by phone about a mental health or addiction concern, up from 64% in 2025. Yet one in five respondents said they had tried to contact a mental health or addiction treatment provider and never heard back, a figure unchanged from last year.

"When someone reaches out for help, they shouldn't have to wonder whether anyone will respond," said Todd Fisher, co-founder and CEO of CTM. "In behavioral healthcare, technology should help providers connect with people more quickly and consistently, not create another hurdle. Whether reaching out by phone, text, or another channel, the goal is to help them reach trusted care that can understand their situation and guide them toward support."

The data underscores an opportunity for behavioral health providers to make the path to care more accessible by offering multiple ways to connect, improving follow-up, and using technology to support the people responsible for helping patients. As AI becomes more embedded into how patients find health information, providers must consider not only which tools they adopt, but how those tools help people move from an initial question to meaningful support.

The full report, The Changing Face of Mental Health Access, explores these findings and their implications for behavioral health providers navigating evolving consumer expectations. To access the report, visit https://tinyurl.com/3pyys555.

CTM commissioned kNOW Instant Insights to survey 1,000 U.S. adults ages 18 and older from August 31 to September 3, 2026. Year-over-year comparisons are included where survey questions and response options were consistent.

#5583. Trump stands by Nvidia boss Jensen Huang despite spy scandal, but FBI is investigating

The revelations this weekend that Nvidia Corp. boss Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with a woman who has been accused of working for Chinese intelligence have now ensnared U.S. President Donald Trump, raising further questions about national security.

At the same time, the Federal Bureau of Investigation said it’s looking into the affair, meaning it’s likely to get continuing attention in coming weeks or longer.

Nvidia said it has launched an investigation into Chief Executive Huang’s actions after he admitted to cheating on his wife with a woman known as Alice Huang (no relation), who serves as the CEO of a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed.

U.S. intelligence officials suspect Alice Huang has been feeding information about Huang and the chipmaker’s plans to the Chinese government. And though Trump was informed of the possible infiltration, he has continued working with Nvidia and Huang on domestic policy issues related to technology and artificial intelligence, which have become of vital importance to the U.S. economy.

Huang has spent the last two years cultivating a close relationship with Trump, gaining extraordinary access to America’s top decision-maker and influence over the country’s AI strategy. He has gone from being virtually unknown to the president to being a key member of a cadre of technology industry executives accompanying him on trips aboard Air Force One, including a visit to China in May.

He has come to be seen as a major ally of Trump, attending numerous White House events while repeatedly praising his policies. Notably, his company made a $25 million donation to the president’s gaudy ballroom project, becoming its top corporate contributor alongside Apple Inc.

Those efforts seem to have gone a long way toward getting Huang into the president’s good graces, and it seems to have paid off for the company. Last year, after months of lobbying from Huang and Nvidia, the Trump administration agreed that it could sell more advanced chips to China that were previously banned from being exported to the country.

Though that decision was widely known, it seems that the Trump administration has intervened in other ways to protect Nvidia’s interests. Earlier today, the New York Times reported that a Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed, which was suspected of smuggling banned chips into China, was abruptly canceled after receiving an email from Nvidia’s general counsel. Commerce official Jeff Kessler, who was nominated for the role by Trump, reportedly gave Nvidia permission to contact the investigation team and mention his name, which goes against standard protocol.

Investigators had grown suspicious that Megaspeed was essentially just a front for smuggling embargoed Nvidia chips into China, but the correspondence from Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter kicked off a kerfuffle that ultimately led to the investigation being transferred to the Department of Justice.

But Trump defended Huang late on Sunday, stating that the Nvidia boss is an “honorable guy” who has not committed any wrongdoing. The president had been briefed about the suspected Chinese intelligence operation as far back as October 2025, but decided not to do anything, according to the Times. “I haven’t heard that he’s done anything wrong,” Trump said. “He dealt with somebody, but, you know, so does everybody else.”

Trump continued to defend Huang on Monday when quizzed about the situation again, before revealing that the Federal Bureau of Investigation is also looking into his relationship with the suspected spy. “I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape,” he said at a White House briefing.

Despite the apparent protection afforded by Trump, Huang appears to be taking no chances. A report in Wired said today that the Nvidia boss has hired the services of a public relations firm called Heller that specializes in handling public scandals. Rise Heller, the firm’s founder, has developed a reputation for helping powerful men sidestep allegations of sexual misconduct and other personal controversies. She previously represented clients including the former Congressman Anthony Weiner, the writer Jeffrey Toobin and the chef Mario Batali, Wired reported.

Tech industry personalities have also leapt to Huang’s defense. Shaun Maguire, a partner at the venture capital firm Sequoia Capital said in a post on X that Huang is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation,” and stressed that although he did something “incredibly dumb,” he believes there was “no bad intention.” Tesla Inc. CEO Elon Musk later shared Maguire’s post, saying he agrees with all of it.

However, no intervention has managed to protect Nvidia’s stock, which slid more than 4% on Monday, wiping around $190 billion off of the company’s valuation.

Nvidia is scheduled to hold its next financial earnings call on Nov. 17, in which Huang is likely to face some very difficult questions — if he is on the call as has been customary.

#5582. NAR moves from survival to ‘showing receipts’ on member value

NAR leaders used the 2026 NXT board meeting to outline year 1 of the 2026 to 2028 strategic plan. Updates included outreach to 450+ MLSs, Tuccori settlement participation, MLS policy changes, advocacy wins and education platform upgrades.  AI Summary

A little over two years have passed since Nykia Wright was named permanent CEO of the National Association of Realtors (NAR). Her tenure as the CEO of the nation’s largest trade association began in a period of unprecedented turmoil for the over 100 year old organization.

During an address to NAR’s board of directors Monday morning at NAR’s 2026 NXT conference and board meeting, Wright attributed much of the association’s success in navigating this turmoil to 2025 NAR President Kevin Sears, who began his term early, in January 2024 after Tracy Kasper’s resignation.

“I wanted to remind us just how much leadership matters. The two years of Kevin Sears’s leadership was defined by leading us through never before experienced turbulence,” Wright, a HousingWire Woman of Influence, said. “Not just the turbulence of survival versus extinction, which is singularly difficult on its own, but also cultural turbulence. And under his leadership, we set the groundwork for what we were promising we were going to do if we were given the chance.”

For the past year, however, it was 2026 NAR President Kevin Brown, who was tasked with carrying out the plan, namely the first year of NAR’s 2026-2028 strategic plan.

“Kevin Brown’s leadership was defined by the showing of actual receipts. January 1st of this year represented the official starting of the clock for our three-year strategic plan that was authored by the membership. They asked, and he began to deliver,” Wright said.

Under Brown’s guidance this year, Wright said that this was the first year NAR made contact with all 450+ MLSs across the country. In addition to this, NAR settled the homebuyer commission lawsuits by opting into the Tuccori settlement, which is awaiting final approval, added 30 new co-sponsors to the More Homes on the Market bill and the trade group implemented zero-based budgeting.

“I want to thank Kevin Brown and his leadership team for every single week continuing to hold us accountable, continuing to cross-examine our thinking, and for using every opportunity when he traveled across the country to bring back new and fresh feedback as we needed to be considered as we strive to continue to add value for our members,” Wright said.

In taking the helm from Sears last fall, Brown said his primary focus was on getting Realtors “back to business” by helping members “navigate the issues that impact their day-to-day business like financing, inventory, insurance, zoning restrictions and other barriers to home and property ownership.”

This translated into tackling a variety of challenges. Building off the changes approved last year, under Brown’s leadership NAR continued its work focused on supporting and strengthening MLS, but without trying to “run the MLS ecosystem.”

“We’ve strengthened the MLS collaboration through outreach to nearly 500 MLS executives, forming a new MLS work group to address emerging issues, help modernize the policies and shape resources and help members better serve clients and collect feedback to understanding the on-the-ground impact from members and the industry through surveys, focus groups, and in-person meetings,” Brown said.

These efforts came to fruition this week when the association approved four MLS policy recommendations that increase MLSs’ options to claim copyright in listing content, expand local flexibility on data feeds, clarify permissible uses of MLS data and update qualifications for NAR’s MLS Committee.

Beyond this, Brown aid NAR is working with federal lawmakers and MLS leaders on things like modernizing the copyright registration process, as well as advocating to antitrust regulators that the MLS helps increase competition in the brokerage space.

Brown also highlighted NAR’s advocacy wins this year, which included the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act and the expanded use of newer credit scoring models by Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and the Federal Housing Administration (FHA).

Looking ahead, Brown said NAR remains focused on the implementation of the ROAD Act and working on gaining more support for the More Homes on the Market Act, which would update the capital gains tax exclusion on the sale of a primary residence.

The past year also saw NAR work to improve  its education for agents, building a “unified education experience.” This included modernizing education classes, improving the quality of instructors and creating an improved digital learning experience with a new learning management platform.

“NAR is enhancing the Center for Realtor Development so we can raise the professionalism of our industry through education and provide better programs and resources members can use to get to their next transaction faster with greater confidence,” Brown said.

Finally, Brown noted NAR’s efforts to deepen its relationships with its brokers, expanding broker engagement and “turning direct broker input into dedicated programming, peer connections and business resources.”

“NAR is connected with more than 15,000 brokers through state and local brokers for summits. And we’re on track for participating in more than 85 broker summits by the end of the year,” Brown said. “We also organized the inaugural broker innovation forum here at NXT based on the success of the broker policy forum at the Realtors Legislative Meeting. The first broker mastermind event drew more than 460 participants to discuss, strengthen the talent pipeline, modernizing the brokers using AI and broker tech essentials.”

Brown said that this was clearly the type of content brokers found helpful and that positively contributed to their business.

As he departed the presidency, Brown thanked NAR’s advocacy team for all of their work this year, as well as the leadership team, staff and Wright.

“It has been an honor to represent NAR and serve as your 2026 president because each day Realtors work hard to make a positive difference and change people’s lives for the better. I’m proud to be a Realtor and I hope you are too. Let’s keep working together so we can continue making a difference for our communities, our organization and our industry.”

#5581. Vodacom will seek partners to build AI data centers across Africa

Free daily briefing on global business news.

CEO Shameel Joosub names Egypt, Kenya and South Africa as bigger markets; half-year headline earnings rose 25.6%

Vodacom Group will seek partners for the construction of AI data centers across Africa, splitting the costs and drawing on outside know-how, CEO Shameel Joosub told Bloomberg. The Johannesburg-based company, majority-owned by Vodafone Group, made the comments as it reported half-year results.

Vodacom is co-investing with Elsewedy Electric and Cassava Technologies in an AI data center in Egypt, the company said in its results presentation. Joosub said in the interview that Vodacom will look at other markets, including South Africa and Kenya.

"Egypt, Kenya, South Africa are our bigger markets," Joosub said, according to Bloomberg. "It will be a big investment, and that is why we're bringing on partners."

The data centers, held in joint ventures, will draw their funding from both equity and debt, Joosub said. Vodacom will hold a stake in the facilities and probably handle most of the sales to customers, he said.

For the six months ended Sept. 30, Vodacom’s headline earnings attributable to equity holders rose 25.6% to R11.3 billion (about $646 million). Headline earnings per share rose 25.7% to 587 cents. Dividend per share rose 7.6% to 355 cents, and customers grew 11.8% to 250 million.

Service revenue rose 29.4% to R85.1 billion (about $4.9 billion), and EBITDA rose 40.0% to R42.7 billion (about $2.4 billion). Reported growth rates reflect the consolidation of Safaricom from the second quarter, the company said. On a pro-forma basis, service revenue rose 13.3% and EBITDA rose 18.0%.

Vodacom's stake in Safaricom rose to 55% from 35% effective June 30, 2026, and the transaction remains subject to appeal, the company said.

Africa represents under 1% of data-center capacity, while South Africa is home to most of the computing power on the continent, according to Bloomberg. Rival MTN Group has teamed up with an investment platform based in the Middle East to begin work on AI data centers in both Nigeria and South Africa.

Vodacom stock gained close to 5% in Tuesday trading on the Johannesburg exchange.

#5579. What View Homes’ rebrand says about Gandhi’s operating overhaul

View Homes is consolidating its regional brands into a single identity as CEO Natasha Gandhi works to standardize operating practices and data systems. The company is expanding in Colorado and assessing how Hunt’s new Strata platform could support land strategy.  AI Summary

Seven months into her effort to transform View Homes from a loose collection of regional builders into a cohesive enterprise, CEO Natasha Gandhi has drawn a line between the company’s past and its ambitions.

A newly unified brand makes that promise visible. Now Gandhi and her team must overdeliver on it.

View Homes announced Monday a new corporate brand identity, unifying its formerly distinct Aspen View, Desert View, Horizon View and View Homes operations under one name. The change spans five divisions across Colorado, New Mexico and Texas and marks a milestone in the operational transformation Gandhi began after becoming CEO in March 2026.

The announcement also comes one week after View’s parent, Hunt Companies, joined with global investment manager Wafra to launch Strata Land Partners, a new land-financing platform led by former Landsea Homes president Michael Forsum. Together, these developments offer a clearer view of Hunt’s expanding ambitions in U.S. residential construction and development.

In an exclusive interview with HousingWire TBD, Gandhi said the branding initiative is part of a broader effort to prepare View for growth, strengthen operating standards, and compete across more markets and homebuyer segments.

“We want to be a premium builder, and by premium, it’s not that we’re unaffordable,” Gandhi said. “It just means that we want to be the best in every price point that we’re out there, we want to be the best in every market that we build in.”

Hunt acquired full ownership of View Homes in 2025, inheriting an established 35-year-old homebuilding business whose regional operations had developed distinct identities, systems and operating practices.

When Gandhi arrived in March, she found an organization with strong local relationships and experienced teams, but lacking the consistent management processes, reporting systems, and enterprise infrastructure needed to support the growth Hunt envisioned.

As The Builder’s Daily reported in October, Gandhi’s initial work focused on leadership changes, clearer accountability, more disciplined sales concessions, selective land investment, and a comprehensive review of enterprise technology.

The new branding establishes four standards intended to apply across the organization: exceptional customer experience, people-first leadership, design-forward homes, and premium quality across price points.

“I felt like previously, we had different standards in different markets, but now with this new brand, it really sets the stage,” Gandhi said. “These four pillars are something that is now going to be operationally executed in all our markets.”

The challenge is to translate those commitments into consistent performance without compromising the local knowledge and customer relationships that have made View’s regional businesses successful.

For a multiregional homebuilder, Gandhi notes, that means more than consistent signage and marketing. It requires shared expectations for product quality, customer service, sales execution, and management accountability, supported by reliable information and operating systems.

Gandhi is candid that the transformation remains unfinished. “This is just the start of our growth journey,” she said. “I will tell you, we’re not there yet, but we’re on the path of getting there.”

The branding initiative has prompted further scrutiny of the operational capabilities needed to support the company’s ambitions to up its game. Gandhi acknowledged that View’s enterprise resource planning systems and website are not yet up to par.

A builder seeking to expand across markets needs timely, consistent information on sales, margins, construction costs, inventory, and land commitments. Without it, management cannot easily compare performance across divisions or make informed decisions about capital allocation.

Gandhi previously outlined a 12-to-18-month enterprise technology implementation, along with efforts to standardize sales concessions and improve the quality of operating data. Those initiatives remain important to the company’s ability to scale.

View has also raised the bar in its home merchandising across markets and is developing products designed to reach beyond its traditional entry-level customer base. The objective is to preserve affordability where that remains the market opportunity while broadening View’s appeal to move-up buyers and customers seeking greater design and product differentiation.

The transformation is unfolding amid difficult housing economics. Slower sales, persistent affordability pressures, and costly incentives continue to strain builder margins, while land acquisition and development require substantial capital commitments long before homes generate revenue.

Hunt’s ownership gives View access to a larger real estate investment organization and a longer-term investment perspective. Its recent partnership with Wafra to establish Strata Land Partners adds another potentially valuable capability.

Strata launched with projects comprising approximately 1,300 single-family lots and a mandate to provide flexible land-financing solutions for public and private homebuilders and developers nationwide. Forsum has described the platform as a capital partner “built by builders, for builders,” emphasizing the need to understand the operational risks and financial requirements of homebuilding businesses.

Gandhi confirmed that View and Strata are already discussing opportunities to work together.

“We are actually already exploring opportunities to where Strata and [View] can partner together,” she said. “There’s definitely opportunity and conversations already in place.”

She did not identify specific transactions or financing structures under review.

Still, the potential relationship illustrates how Hunt’s residential investments could create complementary advantages. View brings homebuilding operations, local market relationships, and demand for future lots. Strata brings a platform designed to finance land acquisition and development while managing builders’ capital exposure.

Whether those capabilities translate into direct financial or operational advantages for View will depend on the transactions and terms the companies ultimately pursue. Strata’s mandate extends well beyond Hunt-owned businesses.

Gandhi said she has assembled the leadership team she believes can execute View’s next phase, including experienced executives recruited during the restructuring process.

“It’s your people that get you the results,” she said. “It’s your people that help you navigate a tough market.”

That leadership investment comes as View prepares to expand into Sterling Ranch, a master-planned community in Douglas County, Colorado, near Denver.

View currently operates in Northern Colorado, Colorado Springs, and Las Cruces, El Paso, and San Antonio. Sterling Ranch gives the company an opportunity to establish a stronger presence in the Denver metropolitan market, where Gandhi sees additional growth opportunities.

She said View is close to completing other land transactions in the Denver area and is pursuing opportunities in additional master-planned communities.

The expansion also offers an early test of the unified brand’s positioning. View intends to compete as a premium regional builder while maintaining a product range that serves buyers across price points.

Gandhi’s transformation is underway as many homebuilders protect cash, reduce land commitments, and prepare for the possibility that difficult conditions could persist through 2027 and 2028. View must balance those immediate pressures with Hunt’s longer-term objective of building a substantially larger homebuilding enterprise.

The company is not simply adding communities to its existing business. Gandhi is working to establish the leadership, systems, product standards, and capital discipline needed to support growth without replicating the fragmented operating structure she inherited.

“My goal, Hunt’s goal, is for View to grow into a premium regional builder,” Gandhi said. “I would like to see View be among the top 50, top 25 home builders in the next five years.”

Achieving that scale will require more than additional land and investment capital. View must demonstrate that its five divisions can operate consistently, protect margins amid changing market conditions, and deliver – or exceed – the customer experience its new brand promises.

#5577. Trump strikes a softer note on immigration; builders need proof

Trump said immigration policy may be too tough and suggested a deal for long-term undocumented workers. Administration signals remain mixed as ICE raids and arrest targets pressure builders ahead of 2027.  AI Summary

On Sunday, President Donald Trump indicated that he is open to negotiating an immigration deal with the incoming Democratic Congress. However, despite softening post-election rhetoric, the Trump administration appears to be sending mixed signals on immigration, clouding the outlook for any potential bipartisan agreement.

The stakes of the nation’s highly contentious immigration debate remain high for homebuilders. After a surge in job site raids by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) this summer and fall, many homebuilders say their workers, including those in the country legally, were swept up in enforcement actions.

Whether a bipartisan immigration deal materializes remains an open and pressing question for the numerous builders facing ongoing job site disruptions.

Speaking to CBS News’ 60 Minutes on Sunday, President Trump suggested his administration’s immigration policies “might be too tough” and may have contributed to last week’s election outcome.

“When you go into a hotel…and you have a woman that’s worked there as a maid, as a cleaner, as a this, as a that, as a waitress – a lot of good things, great jobs – and all of a sudden, they’re being taken out of the country. It’s tough. It’s a tough thing,” Trump said.

Trump added that it may be “doable” to reach an agreement allowing undocumented workers who have lived in the U.S. for many years, construction workers among them, to legally remain in the country.

“Get the killers out. Get the rapists out. Get all the rough ones out. Get the drug dealers out, but let the people that are here, and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them,” Trump suggested.

It’s unclear whether Trump’s softer rhetoric will translate into a bipartisan immigration deal. However, his administration’s decision to promote Stephen Miller, a longtime immigration hardliner, to White House Chief of Staff suggests an agreement may be less likely than Trump implied in his CBS News interview.

And in a post on Sunday, the Official White House Rapid Response account, in a post on X, denied that Trump will push for an amnesty deal with Democrats.

However, Trump has at times shown a willingness to soften his stance on immigration, at least briefly. In June 2025, the Trump administration momentarily directed ICE to pause job site raids in sectors like agriculture, hospitality and restaurants after facing blowback from business leaders worried about staffing shortages.

Within days, however, the administration reversed course. It later set a target of 3,000 ICE arrests per day, leading to a record number of immigration arrests in recent months.

Trump has also helped kill a bipartisan deal before. In early 2024, ahead of the presidential election, he urged Republicans to vote against a Senate border package introduced by Sen. James Lankford (R-OK) that would have tightened asylum requirements, ended releases of migrants into U.S. communities while they await hearings, and let the president close the border when asylum claims surged. The bill ultimately failed.

Some homebuilding organizations, like the National Association of Home Builders, now have their eyes on a different bipartisan measure, the Dignity Act, which would allow certain undocumented workers to remain in the U.S. without citizenship. Trump’s words signaled openness to such a proposal, but the administration’s actions since the election suggest otherwise.

Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, laid out in a post-midterms election post on X that the administration may be open to changing its approach to immigration, with less room for negotiation.

“Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement – by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you,” Vance wrote.

For homebuilders, immigration policy and its impact on the construction labor pool remains among the biggest policy questions heading into 2027. However, history suggests that a bipartisan deal may be a heavy lift, as Washington hasn’t passed comprehensive immigration reform since 1986, under President Reagan.

Whether Washington breaks its four-decade drought on immigration reform, and whether enforcement eases on job sites, remains a key policy wild card to watch in 2027.

#5576. Anthropic launches Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 with science, coding upgrades

Anthropic PBC today pulled back the curtains on Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, its two most capable large language models to date.

The LLMs are identical as far as their core capabilities are concerned. The difference is that Fable 5.2 blocks certain biology and cybersecurity use cases, while Mythos 5.2 includes more relaxed guardrails. The latter model is only available to trusted researchers through a pair of limited-access programs.

Anthropic tested Fable 5.2 against its predecessor across 14 artificial intelligence benchmarks. The model beat Fable 5.1’s score by more than 10% across most of the tests. It’s particularly adept at scientific research: Fable 5.2 scored 74.6% on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, a 22% improvement over Fable 5.1.

Earlier this year, Anthropic used an unreleased LLM to generate a computer-verifiable version of a famous mathematical proof. The project took 11 days. According to Anthropic, Fable 5.2 reduced the workflow to 30 hours by spinning up 1,000 agents to parallelize calculations. In a separate project, it answered two open questions about a theoretical physics concept related to black holes.

The company also tested Mythos 5.2, the invite-only version of Fable 5.2. It asked the model to study the protective shells of harmless viruses called AAVs. AAV shells, or capsids as they’re known in scientific parlance, are used by some therapies to deliver drugs.

Mythos 5.2 accurately modeled the structure of 28 out of the 34 AAV capsids it studied. The result is notable because capsids comprise dozens of different proteins. Other cutting-edge models that are optimized for biology research, notably Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold2, can only model the structure of individual proteins. The creators of the latter model won one half of the 2024 Nobel Prize in chemistry.

Fable 5.2 includes guardrails that block most research biology questions and many cybersecurity-related prompts. If users enter a request that falls into either of those categories, the model sends it to Opus 4.8 or Opus 5. Anthropic says Fable 5.2 is 55% less likely to erroneously block safe prompts than Fable 5.1.

The model outperforms its predecessor by more than 13% across two coding benchmarks called FrontierCode 2.0 FrontierSWE 2.0. According to Anthropic, one of its engineers put the model’s programming capabilities to the test by asking it to build an operating system. Fable 5.2 spun up up 1,000 agents that completed the task in about eight days. The operating system they created can run on a laptop, offers network access and features a Claude sidebar.

Anthropic sees customers using Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 to speed up highly complicated, open-ended technical tasks. The company says more day-to-day workflows can be automated more efficiently using Opus 5.5, an LLM it introduced in July. Users can also combine the models by having Opus 5.5 ask Fable 5.2 or Mythos 5.2 for advise when it encounters a bottleneck.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are priced at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. That makes them 20% more affordable than Anthropic’s previous-generation models. Both LLMs offer a high-performance mode that generates prompt responses 2.5 times faster than the standard tier for double the price.

#5575. Nvidia and Jensen Huang sued by shareholders over alleged Chinese spy affair

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The class-action complaint seeks unspecified damages for investors who bought Nvidia stock between Oct. 9 and Nov. 8

David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Nvidia $NVDA and CEO Jensen Huang face a shareholder lawsuit alleging they misled investors regarding Huang's affair with a woman believed to be an agent of Chinese intelligence, according to The Associated Press.

The complaint, which retail investor Mark Kistenmacher submitted to a California court on Monday, alleges that the company and Jensen Huang never revealed the affair, according to The Associated Press. It also accuses them of making false statements about Nvidia's relationship with the company of Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the reports. The complaint says this posed a "material risk" to Nvidia's reputation and business prospects.

The suit is meant to cover all purchasers of Nvidia stock between Oct. 9, the day news of the affair surfaced, and Nov. 8, the day Nvidia announced it was looking into reports that Jensen Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort," according to The Associated Press. It demands a jury trial and damages in an amount it does not specify.

"As a result of Defendants' wrongful acts and omissions, and the precipitous decline in the market value of the Company's securities, Plaintiff and other Class members have suffered significant losses and damages," the complaint said, according to The Associated Press. It adds that investors would not have bought Nvidia stock at "artificially inflated prices" had they known the truth.

The suit was filed in federal court in San Jose, California, by the Rosen Law Firm, according to CBS News.

Nvidia stock fell $7.97 on Monday, erasing about $190 billion in market value. The stock was down before the opening bell on Tuesday.

Jensen Huang has acknowledged the affair and apologized, according to The Associated Press. He told Nvidia employees in a message released Sunday that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife, according to CBS News.

The New York Times reported that American intelligence agencies had concluded Alice Huang, a onetime executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, was collecting information on behalf of the Chinese government, according to The Associated Press. Megaspeed purchased Nvidia chips valued at over $4.8 billion during the last two years, according to The New York Times. The two Huangs are unrelated.

President Donald Trump said Monday that Jensen Huang told him he did not know the woman was an alleged spy. Trump said he believes Huang and that the FBI is reviewing the issue.

The Justice Department is conducting a criminal probe of Megaspeed, which is suspected of illegally funneling Nvidia AI chips to China. China's Foreign Ministry has called the allegation against Alice Huang unsubstantiated. Nvidia's board is conducting its own scrutiny of the affair.

#5573. Century Communities names Jim Francescon as president

Century Communities Inc. announced that Jim Francescon, currently executive vice president of corporate operations, will be promoted to president effective Jan. 1, 2027. In his new position, Jim will oversee homebuilding operations, land and related corporate functions, building on his work leading recent acquisitions in Texas and Tennessee.   AI Summary

Century Communities Inc. (NYSE: CCS) announced on Monday that Jim Francescon has been promoted to president, effective Jan. 1, 2027, as part of the company’s long-term succession planning process.

The company, ranked 13th by sales volume in the HousingWire Homebuilder Rankings, said Dale Francescon will continue to serve as executive chairman. Rob Francescon, who currently serves as chief executive officer and president, will remain CEO.

As president, Jim Francescon will oversee Century Communities’ homebuilding operations, land and related corporate functions and will help drive the company’s strategy and growth, according to the announcement.

“Today’s announcement reflects the implementation of a succession plan that our Board, Rob, and I have been planning and executing over the past two years,” Dale Francescon, executive chairman of Century Communities, said in a statement. “We have been very thoughtful in how we have approached succession, with the goal of best positioning Century for long-term alignment with shareholders, success and growth.”

“Jim has played an integral role in shaping our strategic direction and our growth into one of the largest homebuilders in the country, including leading our recent acquisitions that have deepened our footprint and strengthened our platform,” Rob Francescon, CEO of Century Communities, said. “I look forward to continuing to work closely with Jim and our entire executive team as we position Century for continued success.”

Jim Francescon said he is “honored to take on this role and grateful to our Board, Dale and Rob for their confidence.”

“We have built a strong operating platform and a talented team, and I am excited about the opportunities ahead as we continue to grow and deliver on our promise of A Home for Every Dream®,” he said.

Francescon joined Century Communities in 2019 and most recently served as executive vice president, corporate operations, overseeing much of the company’s corporate operations, including homebuilding, land, strategy, business development, and mergers and acquisitions.

In that role, he led the company’s acquisition strategy, including recent acquisitions of HistoryMaker Homes, Anglia Homes and Landmark Homes of Tennessee, which expanded Century’s presence in Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston and Nashville, respectively.

Before serving as executive vice president, Francescon was president of Century Living, the company’s multifamily platform, and earlier served as corporate vice president. Prior to joining Century, he worked in private equity at GoldPoint Partners, a subsidiary of New York Life Investments, and in investment banking at J.P. Morgan Securities LLC.

He holds a Bachelor of Science in business administration with a concentration in finance and real estate and a Master of Science in finance from the University of Denver. Francescon also serves as a trustee of the University of Denver, Children’s Hospital Colorado Foundation and ACE Scholarships Colorado.

#5572. Sorted Launches the All-in-One App for TCG Players and Collectors

The next evolution of TCG collection management, from Collectivus Holdings

LISBON, Portugal, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Collectivus Holdings, a leading distribution, consumer goods, and services company supporting retailers and brands across the trading card game and hobby industries, today announced the official launch of Sorted, a trading card game (TCG) collection management app built for players and collectors. Now out of beta, Sorted brings collection tracking, card valuation, deck building, and more into one intuitive app. It solves a problem every serious collector knows well: managing a growing collection across multiple games, platforms, and tools.

Sorted supports all major TCGs including Magic: The Gathering, PokÃ©mon, One Piece, Yu-Gi-Oh!, Lorcana, Flesh & Blood, and its most recent additions of Riftbound and Gundam, with more games and formats on the way. Whether a user collects across one game or several, Sorted consolidates their entire portfolio into a single, searchable collection.

Sorted is powered by proprietary card scanning technology built to be one of the fastest in the industry. Through its recently launched Bulk Scanner feature, players and collectors can now catalog hundreds or thousands of cards in a fraction of the time it takes with manual entry or other scanning tools. Sorted also launched its Wishlist feature which helps collectors track the cards they need to complete their collection and decks.

"Sorted was built by collectors, for collectors. That shared passion with the community drove every decision we made to deliver an experience that makes managing a collection faster, easier, and more rewarding for every type of TCG enthusiast, from those building their first deck to devoted fans managing thousands of cards," said Alice Sanches, Product Owner, Sorted. "We're proud of what we've launched, but we're just getting started, and we can't wait for fans to see what's on the roadmap."

Sorted is available now for download on the App Store and Google Play. To learn more, visit www.tcgsorted.com or follow Sorted on Discord and Instagram.

About SortedSorted is the premier collection management app built for trading card game (TCG) players and collectors. Powered by its proprietary card scanning technology, Sorted elevates the experience with powerful collection organization tools, card valuation features, and a single destination for collection management across all major TCGs. Designed for everyone from casual collectors to competitive players, Sorted is setting a new standard for how the hobby tracks, values, and manages its cards.

Sorted is part of the Collectivus Holdings portfolio of consumer brands serving the global TCG and hobby industry.
